hd9jab.text: Broadcom has released security updates to fix a critical VMware vCenter Server authentication bypass vulnerability that Chinese-linked hackers have exploited in zero-day attacks since September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, affects the VMware Directory Service in vCenter Server, a management platform organizations use to manage VMware virtualized environments. According Broadcom, the flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker with network access to a vulnerable vCenter Server to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access. Successful exploitation can allow attackers to obtain administrative access to vCenter, giving them control over the virtual machines managed by the server. Broadcom patched the vulnerability on November 19 in VMSA-2026-0009, which also fixes four other vulnerabilities affecting VMware SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows. "You are affected if you are running any version of VMware vCenter, SDDC Manager, or VMware Tools for Windows prior to the versions listed as "fixed" in the VMSA," Broadcom's security advisory reads. "This includes vCenter and SDDC Manager deployed standalone and as part of VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure, as well as VMware Tools installed in Windows virtual machines." The company considers the vCenter vulnerability as an emergency update, urging organizations to install the patches as soon as possible. Broadcom says there are no official workarounds for the vulnerabilities, although network restrictions and firewall controls can help reduce exposure. Furthermore, the vulnerability affects vCenter regardless of whether Enhanced Linked Mode is enabled. While Broadcom has not confirmed that the flaw was exploited, researchers at Google's Mandiant have documented attacks exploiting CVE-2026-123890. Chinese hackers exploited VMware zero-day In a report published today, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) revealed that a suspected Chinese state-sponsored hacking group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-123890 in early September 2026. "Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local," explains Mandiant. "Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp." Armory Castle is a cyberespionage group known for exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in enterprise network appliances, including Citrix NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure devices, to breach corporate networks and deploy custom malware. The group was also recently linked to attacks exploiting a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day, tracked as CVE-2026-102764, which has been exploited since late August. Mandiant says the VMware exploitation was part of the same intrusion campaign, with the attackers first compromising BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances before moving laterally into internal Linux systems and targeting VMware infrastructure. After gaining access to an internal Linux appliance, the hackers deployed the "SLIMSAVAGE" web shells to maintain persistent access, escalated privileges to root, and scanned the internal network for VMware systems. SLIMSAVAGE webshell deployed on Linux servers S​​ource: Mandiant The attackers then used a custom Golang exploitation tool named BONESAW to exploit CVE-2026-123890 and compromise a VMware vCenter Server. Mandiant observed the tool successfully creating a vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) administrator account and stealing the server's directory database, which can be used to extract further credentials. BONESAW can also extract SAML signing keys, allowing attackers to forge authentication tokens and gain administrative access to VMware environments. Following the exploitation, the hackers deployed another tool called SAWSNAKE, which enables so-called Golden SAML attacks to forge authentication tokens, bypass multifactor authentication, and impersonate legitimate users. During the attack, the attackers also deployed additional web shells and backdoors, including CAGEMATCH, BEARBONES, and LAZYBONES, to execute commands, transfer files, steal credentials, and maintain access to compromised systems. Armory Castle attack flow Source: Mandiant The attacks ultimately allowed Armory Castle to move deeper into the victims' virtualized environments, access ESXi hosts, and extract sensitive information from virtual machines, including Windows Active Directory database files. Mandiant says the use of two zero-day vulnerabilities in the same campaign, along with multiple malware families tailored to the targeted platforms, demonstrates the threat actor's technical expertise. The researchers urge admins to apply the VMware security updates as soon as possible and configure additional security controls to protect their virtualization infrastructure against future attacks. 1iyz7jc.text: SBC Medical Group has warned in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) that two cybersecurity incidents exposed sensitive customer and employee information, including personal data belonging to 1.6 million people. SBC Medical Group is a clinic management company whose main business is in Japan, but it also has a limited presence in the U.S., is traded on Nasdaq as SBC, and holds a minority stake in the medical spa chain OrangeTwist. Its clinics receive 7 million patient visits annually. The first compromise concerns the SBC databases, while the second involves unauthorized access to clinic administrator accounts on Tribeau, a third-party booking platform. The company discovered the database breach on November 16 and was notified of the Tribeau compromise the same day. Both incidents affected its Japan-based businesses. "On November 16, 2026, unauthorized access occurred to certain databases within a website system managed and operated by SBC Medical Group, Ltd., the Company’s, Japanese subsidiary, in connection with its management services in Japan," reads a FORM 8-K filing with the SEC. "The Company confirmed that an unauthorized third party accessed and extracted customer information. The method of intrusion and full scope remain under investigation." The incident impacting SBC databases exposed basic personal information belonging to 1,624,000 people, including: Full names Contact details Dates of birth Patient card numbers Member IDs Passwords Survey responses Not all of the above data types were exposed for all 1.6 million people. Additionally, the incident exposed 255,416 reservation requests, 217,769 inquiries submitted to SBC websites, and thousands of treatment description records, image filenames, and customer reviews. The company said the attackers also stole approximately 20,000 employee account records, including names, IDs, and passwords. For a small subset of 459 employees, the affected data also included bank account and tax information. The second incident involved administrator accounts on the Tribeau booking platform, a service used by 56 clinics. The operator reported access to reservation information for 12,641 people, as well as access to treatment names, dates, and fees for 6,804 people who received treatment. SBC noted that it has not confirmed unauthorized access to electronic medical records or information from its mySBC reservation site in the database breach. As of November 18, when the Form 8-K was submitted, the company has not seen any evidence of misuse of the exposed data. SBC said the investigation remains ongoing, and at this time, it could not estimate the financial impact of these cybersecurity incidents. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1qvqrec.text: A bipartisan group of than two dozen House lawmakers announced Thursday they are joining a new AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to confront the security risks posed by evolving and increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence models. The July breach of Hugging Face by an OpenAI agent that escaped a sandbox — and the subsequent Anthropic warning that its own AI models also broke out of testing environments to obtain unauthorized access to third-party organizations — have “underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions,” according to a press release from Rep. George Whitesides (D-CA), a caucus co-chair. “As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the potential consequences of catastrophic misuse, loss of control over advanced systems, and threats to national security.” Whitesides and co-chairs Reps. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) and Don Beyer (D-VA) called for bipartisan collaboration to forge basic guardrails in the face of accelerating risks, citing Americans’ well-documented concerns about the technology. Seven of 26 founding members of the caucus are Republicans, a notable number given the White House’s steadfast opposition to regulating AI. The caucus is focused on finding “targeted” solutions that will not imperil innovation, Whitesides said in a statement. The lawmakers will push bipartisan legislation to augment AI safety and quickly respond to AI security incidents by gathering AI developers, independent experts and government officials to brief lawmakers and help develop solutions, the press release said. It will aggressively pursue relationships with outside experts who can help lawmakers navigate complicated AI policy decisions, focus on raising public awareness and give members outside of relevant committees the tools needed to contribute to relevant legislation and debate, according to the press release. Midterm polling showed more than half of American voters considered AI a major issue, and 43% said they trust neither party to properly manage the issue, according to the press release. “By automating vulnerability discovery and exploit development, AI tools have drastically reduced the technical skills required for offensive cyber operations,” a caucus one-pager said. “As threat actors deploy these capabilities at scale, they pose acute risks to critical infrastructure, sensitive personal data, and financial sector stability.” No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

m85ku8.text: ASUS released Control Center Express v1.7.29 to fix three critical vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers gain administrative control of the management console and the devices it manages. Of the three, one is a maximum-severity vulnerability (CVSS score: 10.0) tracked under CVE-2026-114202, arising from a hard-coded cryptographic key used in the product. The flaw lets an unauthenticated remote attacker forge an authentication token and gain administrator privileges, without requiring any privileges or user interaction. The second flaw is CVE-2026-114204, also a hard-coded key problem, which lets a remote attacker with low privileges forge a session token for a recently logged-in account. The third is CVE-2026-114205, an authorization flaw that lets a low-privileged user create an administrator account. ASUS Control Center Express is a central dashboard that IT administrators use to monitor and remotely manage fleets of PCs. ASUS markets it to businesses and IT service providers and lists support for more than 200 of its business, workstation, and Corporate Stable Model motherboards. While all three vulnerabilities are rated critical, CVE-2026-114204 has a recent-session prerequisite, and CVE-2026-114205 requires a low-privileged account, whereas CVE-2026-114202 enables remote administrative access with no prerequisites. ASUS’s security bulletin says versions earlier than v1.7.29 are affected. However, the CVE records only list affected versions through v1.7.27, leaving the status of v1.7.28 unclear. Impacted users are advised to install v1.7.29, then update the agents on managed devices through Select Function → Client Agent Updater, and verify their versions. Also yesterday, ASUS released security updates for Control Center Enterprise, its centralized IT management platform, and Armoury Crate, a hardware configuration utility. Specifically, ASUS patched CVE-2026-126574, a critical authorization flaw that lets a remote user with the low-privileged Viewer role change an administrator’s password and take over the account. The flaw affects Control Center Datacenter 4.0.0.2 and earlier and Control Center Enterprise 3.1.0.8 and earlier. The Armoury Crate update addressed CVE-2026-112115, a high-severity privilege escalation flaw. The flaw affects all versions up to and including 6.7.2 and could allow a low-privileged local user to trick an elevated process into loading a malicious library. eyi2w7.text: The easiest way to fool someone is to give them something they already expect. A job offer. A message about a service outage. A familiar app. Nothing looks strange at first. And that's the problem. This week's stories show how ordinary things are being used to steal data, spread malware, and get people to hand over access.There's another shift worth watching. AI is making some attacks easier to run and harder to spot. Stolen data can now be searched like a shopping catalog. Phishing emails can be tested and rewritten until they get through. At the same time, researchers are finding that even powerful AI systems have safety gaps of their own.And while everyone is watching the new tools, the old problems haven't gone anywhere. Third-party breaches, years of hidden spying, ransomware, and security fixes still need attention. Some stories are clever. Others are painfully simple. Here's what caught our attention this week.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. Faster, more secure AI coding Google has unveiled Gemini 4 Neon, its latest frontier model capable of delivering reasoning faster and more cost-efficiently. According to the company's DeepMind division, it also produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench, achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). "Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost-efficient than large frontier models," Google said. "Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge." Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program. Major leap in AI cyber capabilities OpenAI has introduced GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol with a "significant jump" in cyber capabilities. "They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and produce better patches, with substantial token-efficiency gains on several evaluations," OpenAI said. "Like GPT‑6 Astra⁠, 6.2 Astra and Sol meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework⁠." The company also said it has made defensive capabilities a core focus by allowing the models to write secure code from the start. The development comes amid a disclosure from the U.K. AI Security Institute (AISI) that it developed a universal jailbreak against two pre-release versions of OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra in half the queries required for GPT-6 Astra, adding it identified a "substantial regression in jailbreak robustness relative to GPT-6 Astra." OpenAI has since addressed the regression. Urgent WordPress security update WordPress has released WordPress 7.1.5 with fixes for multiple security issues. "Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately," WordPress said. The patches have also been backported to all branches eligible to receive security fixes (currently through 4.7). Independent AI safety assessments OpenAI will embed independent evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot to help support its safety work. The embedded assessors will focus on model alignment and monitoring, training run monitoring, post-training alignment evaluations, and assessing "whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior." "Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases," the company said. "Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated." OpenAI's safety practices have been under intense scrutiny since July, when two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and hacked a company called Hugging Face. The pilot, however, limits how much researchers can disclose, with OpenAI reserving the right to redact evidence or confidential information to substantiate the outcome of their evaluations. $500 million ransomware extortion case Roman Khlynovskiy, 43, a Kazak national, has been extradited from Italy to the U.S. to face charges for his alleged role in a ransomware and extortion conspiracy that targeted U.S. schools, hospitals, and healthcare entities. "Khlynovskiy and other members of the '8-Digits Team' repeatedly targeted hospitals and schools, extorting victims and threatening to release highly sensitive information," said FBI Director Kash Patel. "This widespread extortion campaign resulted in over $500 million in ransom demands." The 8-Digits Team is said to have been affiliated with the INC and Lynx ransomware, and targeted victims in at least six states, including both schools and hospitals. Khlynovskiy was arrested in Italy in July 2025 while vacationing with his family. He is facing a maximum penalty of 27 years in prison on computer fraud, money laundering, wire fraud, extortion and identity theft charges. AI model extraction tactics exposed An exclusive report from Reuters has revealed that Chinese entities are adopting sophisticated methods to conduct distillation attacks against American AI models and use the outputs to train domestic rivals, according to a review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures, recruitment notices, and government documents. "Chinese researchers [are] using U.S. models to produce answers to questions, build computer code and find solutions to difficult problems, with Chinese companies then developing software to automate the process and specialist workers preparing material for training smaller domestic models," the report said. AI-driven stolen data marketplace A criminal marketplace promoted on underground forums is selling data stolen from computers infected with infostealer malware, along with AI-written profiles of their owners, according to Hudson Rock. The seller has claimed registration for the service is open and free. "The reviewed listings present each computer with a description of its apparent owner, workplace, applications, and potentially valuable data," Hudson Rock said. "Buyers can search those descriptions using natural language and combine the results with filters such as country, operating system, and price. The result is a catalog in which a compromised machine can be presented as a clinic’s reception desk, a defense contractor's household computer, or a government employee's family workstation. The service is marketing the context around the stolen data as part of the product." North Korean ransomware campaign The North Korean hacking group known as Kimsuky group has been observed distributing the Funhouse ransomware via a malicious Hangul document that was disguised as a resume. "The Funhouse ransomware was identified as a variant of previously disclosed endpoint ransomware, and the tools used in this attack — such as Quasar RAT — as well as the overall attack chain shared numerous similarities with Kimsuky’s endpoint ransomware distribution cases observed since the first half of 2026," AhnLab said. Gemini chat retention extended Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change is expected to roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks. It marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period. "Even if Gemini History is turned off, future chats will still be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers," Google said in a revised policy update on November 17, 2026. The change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become increasingly capable. Anthropic and OpenAI, by comparison, have said they may keep temporary or incognito chats in ChatGPT and Claude for 30 days by default or up to 30 days. €11 million data privacy penalty Ireland's data protection regulator said it will fine Match Group €11 million ($10 million) as a result of the dating app Tinder allegedly failing to provide users with their personal data held by the company upon request. The investigation was launched in January 2020. "The Download My Data tool was presented to Tinder users as a way to request a copy of their personal data," the Data Protection Commission (DPC) said. "It failed to provide users with all of their personal data. Certain categories of information were omitted without notice to the user, or provided in summary form only." In addition to the fine, Match Group has been ordered to bring its processing into compliance within three months. Rapid-fire domain impersonation Malicious actors registered one-letter lookalikes of new domains for a number of major brands a day after each real domain was registered. "Every lookalike was registered within the next working day of its authentic counterpart, which suggests the actors monitored new registrations made through brand-protection registrars," Broadcom said. "Most authentic domains appeared to be designed to host campaign sites for well-known brands, including Abbott Laboratories, Bayer, CarMax, McDonald's, Procter & Gamble and Sanofi, such as patient-savings programs, sweepstakes, claims portals and legal settlements." The fake domains have been found to serve parked pages, deceptive search portals, and brand-themed blogs whose ads routed visitors to scam sites. The typosquatting campaign has focused on clients of two brand-protection registrars, Corporation Service Company (CSC) and MarkMonitor. EU targets Russian cyber operations The Council of the European Union has issued sanctions against Social Design Agency (SDA), a Moscow-based company known for running large-scale disinformation campaigns tracked as Doppelgänger. Also sanctioned are 24 individuals working for SDA and a pro-Russian hacktivist group known as NoName057(16). "SDA systematically manipulates the media and social media environment, spreads pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation and foreign information manipulation and interference campaigns," the Council said. "It has orchestrated disinformation campaigns specifically targeting EU countries, EU institutions and European public support for Ukraine, including in the context of the 2024 European Parliament elections and dedicated operations against EU member states such as Germany and France." Android espionage targets defense jobs An active GravityRAT surveillance campaign is using a fake recruitment portal ("recruitersglobal[.]net") to trick job seekers into downloading malicious Android apps. The campaign is targeting job seekers in India looking for work at foreign defense contractors. The activity has been attributed to Pakistani threat actors SpaceCobra and Cosmic Leopard. Once victims are lured into downloading the malicious app, it can steal contacts, call logs, and other sensitive information, and upload the data to the attackers' servers in less than 30 minutes. Over the past 12 months, GravityRAT has been detected across 14 devices from India, per Lookout. Similar variants of the malware have been tracked publicly as HeavyLift. Third-party breach exposes sensitive data DNS threat intelligence company Infoblox has disclosed a third-party breach that allowed criminals to access sensitive customer and staff data. The incident impacted a third-party data migration vendor that had access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, allowing the attackers to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint. This also includes employees' financial information such as direct deposit details, along with contact information, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. The scale of the compromise remains unknown, nor has the company named the third-party migration vendor that was hacked. Microsoft 365 outage fuels phishing Microsoft has identified a "coordinated, high volume" global phishing campaign designed to exploit the recent Microsoft 365 outage, which began on 11:20 a.m. EST on November 12 and lasted for more than 22 hours. The phishing emails were designed to exploit individuals' and employees' urgency to reconnect to Microsoft 365 services, attempting to trick them into clicking a malicious link and potentially capturing their credentials. The campaign targeted organizations across multiple sectors worldwide. "The messages created a false sense of urgency by claiming that emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them," Microsoft said. "The available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext." AI-powered phishing evasion toolkit A new phishing kit called TheMailer is capable of orchestrating most elements of the attack through AI functionality, including designing email lures tailored to bypass content filters. The self-hosted phishing platform runs on AI models like Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, Mistral, and DeepSeek, and personalizes lures for each mail provider and rewrites them until they bypass spam filters. The tool has been advertised on a cybercrime network since March 2026. "The clearest example of how far things have moved is TheMailer’s Inbox Loop," Varonis said. "It sends a test email and checks whether the test was filtered as spam. If so, the tool uses AI to rewrite the message and retry until it reaches the victim's inbox. TheMailer also writes HTML lures from short prompts, turns real brand emails into templates, tailors content to each mailbox provider’s filters, and strips 'AI patterns,' so the text is harder to detect." A lifetime license costs between $3,000 and $6,000 in cryptocurrency. New federal cybercrime disruption unit The U.S. Homeland Security Task Force's (HSTF) National Coordination Center (NCC) has announced the launch of the Threat Disruption Center, a new unit aimed at stopping the flow of victim funds to foreign criminal networks behind scams, cybercrime, and sextortion schemes targeting Americans. "It gives investigators tools to triage victim complaints and map the networks responsible," HSTF said. "It also provides a direct channel to the private-sector organizations best positioned to facilitate outreach to victims and disrupt criminal operations, as well as dedicated technical support." Five-year government cyber espionage Bulgaria has uncovered a five-year-long hacking operation that's estimated to have accessed tens of millions of pages of ​documents on a wide range of government databases. Since 2021 more than 130 GB, ​or 62 million pages, of documents had ​been downloaded. The Ministry for Innovation and Digital Transformation said there is no evidence that Bulgarians' personal data had been compromised. The agency has attributed the activity to "several international hacking groups" ​without naming one. The campaign was first discovered in August 2026 after a new national cybersecurity monitoring system was deployed. $40.5 million ransomware crackdown Ukrainian authorities, in partnership with the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have arrested four suspected members of an unspecified international ransomware organization alleged to be linked to more than $40.5 million in ransom payments from at least 28 companies across the world. The group has targeted organizations in the oil and gas, pharmaceutical, manufacturing, logistics, financial, and critical infrastructure sectors. Some of the victims included Warren Oil Company, Maxxis International-USA, Newpark Resources, and Quantum Health. PNG-based malware delivery technique An evolving malware loader called BubbleLoader has been observed hijacking common benign software by hooking and adding two PNGs to convert it into a distribution mechanism for malicious payloads. Early BubbleLoader artifacts emerged in February 2026 and have been observed as recently as last month. "By patching and adding two PNGs to otherwise legitimate software, BubbleLoader is able to convert any executable to a malicious payload delivery mechanism," ReversingLabs said. "It targets common software as its host, such as WinRAR, x64dbg, Windows Media Player, Firefox Launcher, and virtiofs. The patch is a series of instructions that are applied at the exact address of the host PE’s entry point. The entry point patch allocates memory and copies the PNGs into that location. The second, fake PNG houses both a small area of second-stage shellcode and the XOR-encrypted third stage. Once executed, this shellcode uses the first PNG as a rolling XOR key to decrypt the third stage. The third stage decrypts the final payload PE and then performs a reflective loading process that includes a set of anti-analysis features. The final payload is variable depending on the malware family being distributed." The strange part is how normal much of this has become. A fake email, a trusted tool, a third party nobody thought to question. Small things that can lead to expensive problems. The methods keep changing, but attackers still count on people being busy, systems being trusted, and warning signs being missed.That's it for this week. Keep an eye on the boring stuff. It has a habit of becoming the next big story.

2m7x8b.text: Transport for London (TfL) has announced that around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers may have had their account details exposed in a data breach. TfL is London's public transport authority, operating the Underground, Overground, buses, trams, and the Elizabeth line. It recorded 3.53 billion passenger journeys in 2025/26, including 1.78 billion bus journeys and 1.20 billion Tube journeys. Oyster photocards are travel smartcards with the holder's photo that give eligible passengers free or discounted travel. The organization discovered the security incident on November 16, 2026, after receiving customer reports about emails requesting them to create an account, which came directly from TfL's mail systems as a result of a compromise. The Oyster photocard website has now been taken offline and the organization is sending impacted individuals data breach notifications. Oyster photocards remain valid for travel, and customers who need to renew their cards or check their journey history can still do so by contacting TfL's Customer Services. These notifications, with one shared on Reddit, state that the following customer data may have been exposed: Full names Phone numbers Email addresses Home addresses Dates of birth Security questions and answers TfL's current assessment is that passwords, bank and payment card details, journey information, and the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were not compromised. The transportation organization also said it has found no evidence so far that the affected data has been misused. TfL estimates that around 265,000 photocard customers may have been impacted, up from an estimated 250k previously, but the investigation is not yet complete and the figure may increase further. TfL says it has now contained the incident and contacted affected customers. It has also notified the UK's Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). Those who received the previous email urging them to create an account on the platform should ignore it. The leak of security questions and answers is particularly concerning, as those may be used in account access restoration, so customers should remain vigilant for suspicious activity and report it to the organization as soon as possible. Once the Oyster photocard portal is restored, all photocard customers will be prompted to change their password, security question, and answer. However, if those same security questions are used at other sites, they should be rotated to new questions and answers. It is also recommended to change passwords on other services where the same information was used. In 2024, Scattered Spider members breached TfL's network and stole customer data and disrupted online services, including Oyster refunds. The attack cost the agency £29 million in losses and recovery costs, while two of the hackers pleaded guilty in June 2026 and were sentenced to five years and six months in prison. ak1x25.text: The Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security announced Thursday the creation of a new task force aimed at disrupting the flow of victim funds to foreign criminal networks powering scams, cybercrime and sextortion schemes that target Americans. The departments are partnering on the Threat Disruption Center to better triage victim complaints, map cybercriminal networks and provide a direct channel to private sector organizations that work with victims. Senior FBI official Heith Janke said Threat Disruption Center members have already worked together on efforts to warn thousands of victims before they lose money to scammers, and the center will allow them to better coordinate their efforts. “The Threat Disruption Center builds on those efforts by providing advanced tools and operational capabilities that enable faster action at greater scale, strengthening the work of every agency on the task force,” Janke said. TRM Labs, which is providing technology support for the effort, said that the center has already moved to take down more than 1,600 scam websites, added more than 6,600 scam-linked cryptocurrency wallet addresses to a screening network and identified 101 new fraud networks for investigation. The center is part of the federal government’s efforts to implement an executive order issued in March centered around stopping cyber scams, which continue to siphon billions of dollars each year from unwitting Americans. Cyber scam losses reported to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) grew to $20.9 billion in 2025 — a number that does not account for the thousands of people who never file victim reports. The staggering losses have prompted multiple concurrent efforts by the federal government and Congress to disrupt the scams and provide better avenues for victims to report crimes. Much of the center's work will focus on collaborating with tech companies that get a firsthand view on criminal network activity because of how many gangs use social media platforms, web hosting, domain infrastructure, cryptocurrency services and banking systems. “The Center establishes a standing mechanism for law enforcement and participating companies to appropriately share intelligence in near real-time, and convert that intelligence into action, for example, by pausing victim payments; taking down malicious web domains; or banning social media accounts used by scammers,” federal officials said in a statement. “Participating private-sector companies can take these actions independently under their terms of service, while law enforcement agencies proceed with investigations, prosecutions, and court-authorized seizures.” The center is being housed within the Homeland Security Task Force — a permanent interagency law enforcement network of more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners that focus on transnational criminal organizations, cartels and foreign terrorist organizations. Prince Group sanctions The initiative is just one part of a multi-prong effort the U.S. is undertaking to address cyber scams. On Thursday, for example, the Treasury Department issued more sanctions on scam operators in Myanmar and affiliates of the Prince Group, a Cambodian company accused of managing an empire of scam centers across Southeast Asia. The sanctions include Zhao Hui, a Cambodian national who leased a scam center from Prince Group and paid the company fees to run the compound. U.S. officials accused Zhao of being directly involved in the scam center’s operations — which targeted Americans and Europeans with cryptocurrency investment scams. Two of Hui’s companies, Bei Fang Bo Lin Construction Decoration and ZHZ Investment, are included in the sanctions. The Treasury Department also sanctioned two leaders running the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), an armed group backing scam centers located along the Thailand-Myanmar border. General Saw Shwe Wah is the commander-in-chief of the DKBA and Colonel Saw A One is a commander who runs the Three Pagodas Pass in Karen State near the Thai border. Both own land along the border and provide security to scam compound operators. "These scammers rarely stop after one payment — they drain a victim's savings, or their retirement, over months and years," Esteban Castaño, CEO of TRM Labs, said of the DOJ and DHS joint venture. "Stepping in sooner changes everything: a warning before the next payment, a scam website removed before it victimizes another family, or stolen funds frozen while they can still be recovered. That's the difference between a recoverable setback and a loss from which an entire family may never recover.” No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

1n1mny7.text: President Donald Trump’s pick to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on Thursday vowed to uncover any “gaps” within the organization that have been created by massive personnel and funding cuts. “I'm going to get involved and understand where the gaps are and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis,” Mike LoSapio, Palantir’s chief information security officer, told the Senate Homeland Security Committee. LoSapio was nominated earlier this month to helm the nation’s cyber defense agency, which has been without a Senate-confirmed chief for almost two years. A previous nominee, Sean Plankey, withdrew from consideration earlier this year after spending months in limbo on Capitol Hill. Nick Andersen has led CISA in an acting capacity since February. The agency has been a target of Trump’s ire over the role it played in debunking the conspiracy theories he spread that the 2020 presidential election was rigged. Since he returned to the Oval Office, CISA has lost one-third of its staff and had its budget slashed by millions. In a brief nomination hearing, LoSapio described CISA as “effectively the cybersecurity version of the 911 system. You pick up the phone, you say you have an emergency, you need help.” “If confirmed, I intend to bring together the community and the national labs to help collaborate and coordinate and to give defenders the tools they need to defend their networks,” including AI tools, he told the panel. In his written statement to the committee, LoSapio also pledged to “recruit and keep talented people, give them clear priorities, and make sure every dollar Congress provides is spent with discipline and tied to measurable results.” However, he demurred when asked to weigh in on the recent technical outages that have upended key sectors of the U.S. as he’s “not inside” the agency today. And he stopped short of saying CISA’s budget needed to be increased to meet digital threats. “I don't necessarily believe more money means more security. I believe spending money on the right solutions in the right ways actually decreases risk,” LoSapio told Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.). He later testified that if analysis showed the need for more funding he would “come back to this committee and request for more resources.” When asked by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) who won the 2020 presidential election, LoSapio repeatedly declined to directly answer. “I'm not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” he said. “My only involvement in the 2020 election was voting for the president of the United States.” LoSapio also disagreed with Blumenthal when the policymaker asked if the Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021. “No, I don't believe there was an attack. No,” he said under persistent questioning. In response, Blumenthal told LoSapio he was “disqualified from the position that you've been nominated to fill.” The committee likely won’t vote on LoSapio’s nomination until after next week’s Thanksgiving recess. If advanced, he could face a full floor vote during the final weeks of the lame-duck session of Congress. No previous articleNo new articlesMartin Matishakis the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.

1nkc3gn.text: PHP's default file-based session storage can be made to return objects an attacker chose, by cutting off a session write at the right moment. When combined with a second weakness, such as a suitable gadget chain in the app, those objects can allow the attacker to run code on the server. Today's PHP releases fix the flaw, called phpAfterShell. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-126714 and rated 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 scale by PHP's maintainers. Depthfirst, a security company, says it found the flaw and reported it to the maintainers. The October 21 PHP releases, which fixed two critical flaws known as PHP2Shell, do not contain this fix. Servers updated then remain affected until they install today's releases. Neither the maintainers nor the company reports any attacks using phpAfterShell. Who Is Affected and What to Do These releases are affected, according to the maintainers' security advisory: Branch Affected releases Fixed release PHP 8.2 Before 8.2.36 8.2.36 PHP 8.3 Before 8.3.37 8.3.37 PHP 8.4 Before 8.4.28 8.4.28 PHP 8.5 Before 8.5.13 8.5.13 PHP 8.6.0, also released today, includes the fix. The flaw is in the files session handler, which PHP uses by default. Sessions kept in Redis, a database, or another store are outside this defect, though each store's handling of a cut-off update needs its own check. Whether an attacker needs to log in depends on how the app exposes its session handling. On the path the company tested, the attacker uses upload progress, a PHP feature that records the progress of a file upload in the user's session. Where the feature is on, a multipart form upload that carries its field makes PHP write to the session before the app's own code runs. The app does not need an upload page, only any page that opens the session later. PHP 8.1 and older are end-of-life. The official end-of-life mitigation branches for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are not affected, but older unpatched builds of those versions are, according to the company. The company's remediation guidance sets out these steps: Install the fixed release for your branch, as listed above. If you run PHP 8.1 or older, move to a supported branch. Rebuild any container images and redeploy. Check that the PHP version serving web requests is the new one. If you cannot update yet and your app does not use upload progress, set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini or the server's PHP settings, then restart the PHP workers. Also limit the untrusted data your app stores in sessions. Switching the feature off is not a full fix. It closes the upload path, but apps that put attacker-controlled data into sessions in other ways remain affected, the maintainers say. The maintainers listed the same setting on October 21 as a temporary measure for one of the PHP2Shell flaws. Servers that have kept it off since then still need the update. Moving sessions to a store that replaces records in one step also avoids this defect. The update is still the recommended fix for sites that keep the files handler. Linux distribution packages may include the fix without changing the PHP version number, according to the company, so the version number alone may not indicate whether a server is fixed. Once installed, the fixed releases empty the session file before each write and stop the write if that step fails. A cut-off write can still lose session data, but it can no longer leave old data behind for an attacker to use. The updates also switch upload progress off by default. The Hacker News compared PHP's source code for the October 21 releases and today's. The built-in setting is on in 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, and off in 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6.0. The release notes do not mention or explain the change. The sample php.ini files still show the old setting in a commented-out line. A php.ini file, distribution package, or hosting panel that switches the setting on will keep it on. Where nothing else sets it, apps that rely on upload progress will need it switched back on after the update. The same releases also fix other PHP security flaws. How the Attack Works The attack starts with the session write that upload progress makes before the app's code runs, Depthfirst's researchers say in their technical analysis. A PHP session file stores each value as a name followed by serialized data. Length fields in that data tell PHP where each string ends, and nothing in the file marks a write as finished. PHP locks the file while it writes, but the lock cannot undo a write that stops halfway. If the worker process dies partway through, the file can retain the start of the new data and the end of the old data. By setting the lengths in the new data, an attacker can make text that sat harmlessly inside the old data read as a separate record, including a serialized object. The next request that calls session_start() loads that record and creates the object. The researchers' public proof uses a harmless built-in object, stdClass, which appears in the session once the file is mixed. The emergency PHP2Shell fixes on October 21 addressed an earlier attack via the same step. "The original exploit stopped working, but the underlying problem was still there," the researchers say of the PHP2Shell patch. That exploit needed objects to become active while PHP recorded upload progress, so the maintainers limited which classes can load at that moment. The change did not touch the file write. The object data still reaches the disk and becomes active later, when an ordinary request calls session_start(). The attack depends on stopping the write at the right moment. The maintainers say one way is a hard memory-limit failure in another thread of a threaded PHP build, which can kill the process mid-write. Code execution then still needs a suitable gadget chain in the app, and the flaw can also corrupt session state. In the researchers' own Linux tests, PHP's execution timeout fired only after the write had finished, so they used an out-of-memory kill to stop the worker mid-write instead. The planted object appeared on the 11th attempt in a fresh run. That count measures getting the file into the right state on their servers, not how often code execution succeeds. Their own chain needed no gadget from the app, the researchers say. It used a second bug instead, memory corruption in one of PHP's built-in classes. They are holding back its details for coordinated disclosure and have not said whether that bug is fixed in today's releases. The same trick can also replace ordinary session values, such as who is logged in, their permissions, or a CSRF token, before the app checks them, the researchers say.

xjzxup.text: The PHP dev team released security updates for 18 vulnerabilities, including critical flaws that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. The updates were released Thursday, November 19, for all supported PHP branches, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 now available. Security firm Aikido reports that the updates address 18 CVEs affecting PHP's core engine, session handling, PHP-FPM, CGI, and other components. One of the most serious flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-129289, is a critical PHP-FPM request smuggling vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.2. According to Aikido, the flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to execute PHP code remotely on vulnerable servers that reuse connections to PHP-FPM under certain conditions. The vulnerability affects certain nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM. Standard nginx and Apache configurations that do not reuse backend connections are not affected by the attack. Other important vulnerabilities fixed in the updates include: CVE-2026-129474: A use-after-free vulnerability involving magic method backtraces that could lead to remote code execution. CVE-2026-129496: A timezone cache use-after-free vulnerability that could lead to remote code execution. CVE-2026-126714: A vulnerability involving partially overwritten session files that could lead to remote code execution. CVE-2026-115560: A session serializer mismatch vulnerability that could lead to remote code execution. CVE-2026-129291: A PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free vulnerability that could lead to local privilege escalation. CVE-2026-128090: A PHAR OpenSSL signature bypass vulnerability involving an algorithm downgrade. Additional fixes address memory corruption, information disclosure, cross-site scripting, denial-of-service issues, and potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs. The releases follow a warning issued Wednesday by the PHP security team that the upcoming updates would address vulnerabilities affecting all supported PHP versions, with the highest severity rated critical. "The issues rated CRITICAL require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups," the PHP security team warned. One of the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-115560, was already disclosed in an October 23 informational advisory and relates to how PHP handles session data under certain configurations, potentially leading to remote code execution. As a temporary mitigation, PHP recommended disabling session upload progress by setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restarting PHP workers. This setting was also recommended to mitigate the recent PHP2Shell flaws. For CVE-2026-129289, administrators who cannot immediately install the security updates can mitigate the vulnerability by disabling persistent backend connections between their web servers and PHP-FPM, ensuring connections are closed after each request. Aikido warns that these mitigations do not address all vulnerabilities fixed in the November updates and recommends ensuring PHP-FPM and LSAPI listeners are not directly exposed to untrusted networks. Although the official security updates are limited to supported PHP branches, third-party maintainer Ondrej Surý has also released patched packages for unsupported PHP versions dating back to PHP 5.6. Aikido has similarly released hardened PHP container images containing backported security fixes for unsupported versions, including PHP 5.6, 7.0, 7.1, 7.2, 7.4, and 8.1. PHP administrators are urged to upgrade to PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, or 8.2.36, depending on their supported branch, to address the newly disclosed vulnerabilities. 1vmghxv.text: The British government served Apple with a secret legal notice targeting the company’s cryptographic protections for iCloud accounts, a tribunal has confirmed, ending almost two years of official refusal to acknowledge what had been widely reported. In a judgment handed down Thursday, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal — the only court in the country that can hear certain national security cases — rejected the government’s “neither confirm nor deny” policy based on the argument that even confirming the existence of the notice would damage national security. The court’s three judges stated explicitly that the government “has given Apple a technical capability notice,” referencing the legal power which the government used to demand that Apple retain the ability to access the content of iCloud accounts. At the core of the dispute is Apple’s Advanced Data Protection (ADP) feature which generates and stores encryption keys on users’ own devices instead of Apple’s servers. Because Apple never holds the keys, it is technically unable to access the content of iCloud accounts even when served with a lawful request. Last February, Apple withdrew ADP for British users entirely after receiving the technical capability notice, as was first reported by The Washington Post. Although the details of the notice are not public, it appears that Apple effectively complied by withdrawing ADP for British users. Since the initial report about the notice, Westminster officials have continued to repeatedly state they do “not comment on operational matters, including for example confirming or denying the existence of any such notices.” Addressing Parliament earlier this year, Security Minister Dan Jarvis again declined to respond after the issue was raised by a lawmaker, and said that not doing so was “a long-standing position held by successive Governments for obvious reasons of national security.” Those “obvious reasons” were challenged by the tribunal, as well as in comments from both within the U.K. intelligence community and from academic experts. In a preliminary judgment last April, the tribunal cited numerous public comments by senior U.S. politicians, including President Donald Trump, that appeared to confirm the existence of the notice, with Trump comparing the British government’s move to “something that you hear about with China.” The then-U.S. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard ordered a legal review of the secret directive in February 2025, and said she had a “grave concern” about its implications. In its judgment, the tribunal also referenced numerous British media reports about the notice, citing government officials as sources, as additional justification for finding against the “neither confirm nor deny” policy. Experts, including from Britain’s own intelligence community, have argued the government’s attempts to access encrypted messaging platforms should be more transparent. Academics described the Home Office's ongoing refusal to either confirm or deny the legal demand as unsustainable and unjustifiable. Tim Stevens, the head of the King's Cyber Security Research Group at King's College London, previously told Recorded Future News that a default of no comment left the government unable to control the story when details came out. Sir Jeremy Fleming, the former director of GCHQ, told the Munich Cyber Security Conference in 2025 that greater transparency was needed to protect the agencies’ “license to operate.” In 2018, GCHQ technical officials argued in an essay for Lawfare that the details of any exceptional access scheme would probably become public anyway, and that criminals would not simply switch services once it was known to exist. The tribunal found that confirmation of a notice’s existence would not tell adversaries anything that they could not already find elsewhere. Andrew Dwyer, a lecturer in information security at Royal Holloway, University of London, argued that a notice capable of removing an encryption service from millions of users is not like a live operation and should not be shielded in the same way. The ruling does not make a finding about whether the notice issued to Apple is lawful. A substantive hearing has been scheduled for the first half of 2027. The tribunal's April 2025 judgment, quoted again in this ruling, noted that the government can choose to withdraw or settle proceedings rather than depart from its “neither confirm nor deny” approach. A government spokesperson said: “Terrorists, child abusers and organised crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public. “A judge can authorise access to a criminal’s home, a parcel they’ve sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company’s communications systems or data. “Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so. “Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies.” Editor's note: Story updated at 19:35 GMT with a government spokesperson's statement.
