4xlpc9.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security The PHP Foundation has released security updates to address multiple critical security flaws that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution on affected deployments, including CVE-2026-115560. The release of the patch follows an advance notice in which the project maintainers alerted users to multiple critical vulnerabilities affecting all supported PHP versions under specific conditions, including non-default configuration or uncommon setups. At a high level, successful exploitation of the defects could pave the way for remote code execution, session corruption, denial-of-service, memory corruption, or local privilege escalation. The list of vulnerabilities is as follows - CVE-2026-115560 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could result in remote code execution, file modification, session corruption, or denial-of-service. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in memory corruption and possible full remote code execution, as in the case of CVE-2026-109619. (Fixed in PHP 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-126714 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerability that could result in the execution of arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker. Successful exploitation requires an attacker's influence over the session data, an interruption at a useful point in the write, and an application with a suitable deserialization gadget chain. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An inconsistent interpretation of HTTP requests vulnerability that could result in execution of attacker-controlled PHP code as the worker without another user's interaction or a non-default PHP configuration. Successful exploitation requires a front end that enables persistent backend connections and an application path that opens "php://input" without reading it fully, such as nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, HAProxy FastCGI applications that retain backend connections, and LSAPI. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in remote code execution on PHP 8.5 and later. Successful exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point. (Fixed in PHP 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129481 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could cause an application's session cleanup to fail and potentially corrupt memory, crash a reused PHP worker, or potentially allow remote code execution. (Fixed in PHP 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code with their privileges on an affected deployment. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) CVE-2026-129291 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in local privilege escalation. Successful exploitation requires local code execution in an FPM worker, an affected pool with catch_workers_output enabled, the epoll event backend, and the ability to manipulate worker lifetimes and retain inherited pipe descriptors. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0) Depthfirst, which has codenamed CVE-2026-126714 "phpAfterShell," has described it as a critical flaw that can enable a remote attacker to run arbitrary code on affected servers. "If a pwrite()/ftruncate() update is interrupted, PHP may leave behind a malformed session file that is later loaded by session_start(), yielding an arbitrary deserialization primitive," Depthfirst said. "Chained with another of our PHP-native deserialization-to-RCE findings, this leads directly to remote code execution." Put differently, the vulnerability turns an interrupted file write into a potential remote code execution primitive by manipulating how PHP writes session data to disk, causing it to interpret previously harmless data as executable object data. It then exploits the unexpected session state where the PHP worker either dies while the write process is underway, leaving a partially updated file, or dies after the write is complete, but before content from the previous session is removed. Both scenarios lead to a mixture of two different session states. "Depending on where the interruption happens, part of the new Session may already have been written while bytes from the previous Session remain on disk," security researcher Yuhang Wu said. "The result can be a Session file containing the prefix of the new serialized data and the tail of the old one." "By carefully choosing the length fields in the new prefix, an attacker can make PHP's Session decoder interpret leftover bytes that were previously just part of an ordinary string as separate Session entries and serialized objects. Nothing needs to be deserialized during the upload-progress callback itself. The attacker only needs to leave the right bytes on disk and wait for the application to call session_start(), at which point PHP reads the modified Session and deserializes those objects." Once the prefix of one valid session is spliced with the tail of a replacement session, a subsequent session treats the corrupted data as a legitimate server-side state. This, in turn, causes PHP to interpret it as a "different, valid Session" and ultimately enable remote code execution by chaining it with a memory-corruption in a PHP-native class. It affects any application that runs an affected PHP version with file-based sessions. If immediate patching is not possible, it's advised to turn off session upload progress. Patches for the flaws are available in the following versions - PHP 8.2.36 PHP 8.3.37 PHP 8.4.28 PHP 8.5.13 PHP 8.6.0 Users who are using existing 8.2.x, 8.3.x, 8.4.x, and 8.5.x versions of PHP are advised to update to the latest version for optimal protection.

1tc6fbg.text: The European Commission confirmed Thursday that it had been hit by a cyberattack last month involving a publicly available artificial intelligence tool, following media reports of the incident. Speaking to journalists, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the first signs of the attack were detected October 22. He described the incident as an “AI-generated cyber campaign” but did not identify the tool used or the attackers’ apparent motivation. POLITICO first reported that the Commission had been impacted by the cyberattack. It said CERT-EU had identified the attackers’ use of ARTEX, an open-source AI hacking platform that the FBI last week warned was being used both by criminals and state-sponsored groups. The attack reportedly disrupted the European Commission’s personnel systems for more than 10 days, including payroll, leave requests, medical reimbursements and translation services. A commission spokesperson confirmed to Recorded Future News they had “taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign,” including taking several services offline as “a protective measure.” They said they had notified affected individuals and were “preventively checking other systems” while keeping in touch with CERT-EU and the European Data Protection Supervisor. Regnier said investigators had found no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff broadly and were unaware of any ransom demand. He said the investigation remains open. Asked why the incident was not disclosed earlier, Regnier said publicizing defensive measures could undermine their effectiveness. “There was no hiding whatsoever,” he told journalists. The incident follows an alert issued in June by the Five Eyes intelligence alliance, which said AI would fundamentally transform both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities. “The timeline is not years, it is months,” it said at the time. The FBI warned last week that ARTEX was being used prolifically by cybercriminals and nation-states to breach government agencies and dozens of critical sectors worldwide, “with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.” The open-source framework, which was released in July, uses commercial AI models to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation. “The key takeaway here is not that threat actors are using Artex,” said Shaun Williams, a senior director at SentinelOne, “but that the widespread availability of AI-powered tools like Artex have allowed threat actors to find and exploit vulnerabilities in internet facing devices faster, more effectively, cheaper, and with less skill than ever before.” The attack is the Commission's third disclosed cyber incident this year, following breaches involving Ivanti software in January and its cloud infrastructure in March. Officials have not linked the incidents. No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

1hndris.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security A critical flaw in VMware vCenter lets an attacker with network access bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system, Broadcom, which owns VMware, said in an advisory published today. Fixed versions are out for all supported branches, and the company lists no workaround. vCenter is the central console for managing an organization's ESX hosts and virtual machines. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-123890 and is rated 9.8 on the CVSS scoring system. "VMware vCenter contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service," the advisory says. In an FAQ published with the advisory, the company says the issue "qualifies under ITIL methodologies as an emergency change," and urges organizations to consult their security staff immediately on timing. The company has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, or any public exploit code. It also does not say what level of access an attacker gains after the bypass. Credit for reporting the bug goes to Google-owned Mandiant. The bug is present in vCenter 8.0, 9.0, and 9.1, and in the vCenter builds that ship inside VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, and the Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure products. That includes the older Cloud Foundation 5.x line. It is there whether or not Enhanced Linked Mode is in use. Older versions are not cleared. The company no longer evaluates versions past end of support, and says vSphere 6.5 and 6.7 should be presumed affected. The same goes for vSphere 7.0, which left general support in October 2025, and whose customers can request a patch under an extended support contract. None of the five flaws in the advisory lets code run on an ESX host from inside a virtual machine, and ESX itself is not affected, the advisory FAQ says. There is no fallback for systems that cannot be updated yet: asked whether a workaround exists, the FAQ answers "Not as listed by Broadcom," while noting that mitigations may still exist in an organization's own defenses. The updates are cumulative and cannot be installed through vCenter Quick Patch. Virtual machines continue running while vCenter installs the update, though management access drops briefly, and some encryption operations against a Standard Key Provider become unavailable until vCenter is back online. One warning applies to upgrades already in progress: installing vCenter 8.0 U3m or 9.0.2.0200 blocks a later upgrade to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1, a conflict the FAQ calls a "Back-in-Time" issue. The options are to upgrade vCenter to 9.1.1 first and apply the security update there, or to wait briefly for VCF 9.1.2. The bypass is the second critical authentication flaw in the VMware Directory Service this year. The earlier vCenter flaws, patched on July 29, included CVE-2026-59309, another 9.8-rated bypass in the same component per the July advisory, alongside a directory-traversal bug, CVE-2026-59310. Attacks on that traversal flaw began five days after its disclosure, German incident response firm QUIRSO assessed in August, linking them with moderate confidence to a suspected China-nexus actor. The August attacks compromised an estimated 361 IP addresses in 47 countries and deployed Babuk-derived ransomware on ESXi hosts. Broadcom has reported no attacks on the new bypass. The advisory also fixes four lower-severity flaws, rated 6.7 to 8.1: a SQL injection (CVE-2026-123891) and a command injection (CVE-2026-123892) in SDDC Manager, a privilege escalation to root on the SDDC Manager appliance (CVE-2026-123893), and a SAML token signature bypass in VMware Tools for Windows (CVE-2026-123894), exploitable only where Guest Alias mapping is configured. Each needs an authenticated or already privileged actor, and the last one stays inside the guest virtual machine.

1yavs9.text: Ask many IT teams how they would recognize ransomware, and the answer is still “when files start changing extensions.” By then, the intrusion may already include credential theft, privilege escalation, defense evasion, recovery sabotage, lateral movement and data exfiltration. Encryption is often a late-stage action, not the beginning of the attack. In data-extortion attacks it never happens at all: the operators steal data and threaten to leak it without encrypting anything. Recent attacks against on-premises SharePoint servers illustrate that sequence. After exploiting internet-facing systems, operators used stolen credentials and legitimate administration tools to move through victim environments before deploying ransomware. The practical lesson is simple: defenders need to detect the behaviors that precede encryption, not only the encryptor itself. Acronis Cyber Platform (formerly Acronis Cyber Protect Cloud) natively integrates cybersecurity, data protection and endpoint management through a single agent, console and policy framework. When the relevant capabilities are licensed and enabled, Acronis Active Protection, EDR, MDR and XDR can help detect, contain and recover from ransomware-related activity before widespread encryption occurs. Five high-value signals deserve immediate attention: Defense tampering: Attempts to stop security services, modify protection agents, load vulnerable drivers or clear event logs. Privilege escalation and lateral movement: Unexpected privileged accounts, remote-execution tools spreading across hosts or unusual server-to-server remote access. Data exfiltration: Unusual outbound transfers from systems that do not normally upload large volumes of data. Recovery sabotage: Deletion of shadow copies, backup catalogs or recovery options with tools such as vssadmin.exe, wbadmin.exe or bcdedit.exe. Pre-encryption file behavior: Rapid file enumeration, repeated read-write-rename activity and encryption-like changes across local or network locations. How do ransomware gangs typically gain initial access to corporate networks? Ransomware attacks rarely begin with the ransomware payload itself. Operators first need an initial foothold, and common entry paths include exploitation of vulnerable internet-facing systems, abuse of stolen credentials, and social engineering. An unpatched externally accessible service can provide a route into the environment, while compromised credentials can allow an attacker to enter through legitimate remote-access or cloud services. Social engineering adds another path by targeting users and the processes around identity and access. Once attackers establish access, the initial compromise can become the starting point for credential theft, privilege escalation, defense evasion and lateral movement. Organizations should reduce unnecessary internet exposure, prioritize patching of high-risk systems, strengthen identity and access controls, and protect email and collaboration channels. Monitoring endpoints for suspicious post-compromise behavior provides another layer when preventive controls do not stop the initial intrusion. The article already establishes these pre-encryption stages as important signals defenders should detect. Acronis Cyber Platform supports this layered approach from one platform. On the detection and response side, endpoint protection, built on Acronis Active Protection and EDR, identifies and contains malicious activity once an attacker gains a foothold, while email security and XDR extend that detection to the attack surface beyond the endpoint. On the prevention side, vulnerability assessment and patch management reduce exploitable exposure, security posture management and security policy management close configuration gaps, and data loss prevention limits what an intruder can take. Together these create a progression from reducing opportunities for initial compromise to detecting and responding to activity after one occurs. How does ransomware protection prevent an attack instead of only detecting it? Stopping ransomware is rarely about a single control. Organizations need to reduce the opportunities attackers have to get in, detect and contain malicious activity when they do, and have a reliable way to recover if systems or data are affected. That makes prevention, detection and response, and recovery different parts of the same ransomware defense strategy. Acronis brings those layers together in one platform. On the prevention side, patch management reduces exploitable exposure, security posture management and unified endpoint and security policy management close configuration gaps before an attacker can use them, data loss prevention limits what can leave the environment, and data protection with immutable backups removes the leverage that recovery sabotage depends on. On the detection and response side, Active Protection, EDR, XDR and email security identify and contain malicious activity across endpoints, email and the wider environment. Integrated backup and recovery then provide the path to restoring affected systems and data. That last layer is critical for getting operations back online, but it does not undo data theft, an important distinction in double-extortion attacks. How do detection tools stop ransomware before it encrypts files? Ransomware rarely goes straight to encryption. Endpoint detection tools can spot the suspicious activity that comes first, from attempts to disable defenses to lateral movement and unusual file activity. The table below breaks down five signals worth watching, the controls that can address them and how Acronis supports each response. Signal Recommended control Acronis implementation Recovery sabotage Alert on recovery-tool abuse; stop the malicious process; maintain off-host, immutable recovery points. Active Protection blocks ransomware behavior and restores affected files. Self-protection helps defend Acronis components and backups. Immutable Acronis Cloud Storage protects eligible recovery points. Defense tampering Use agent self-protection, exploit prevention, vulnerable-driver controls and off-host logging. Self-protection helps prevent unauthorized changes to the Acronis agent. EDR/XDR and SIEM integrations add incident visibility, subject to configuration. Privilege and lateral movement Monitor privileged-account changes and remote-execution activity; isolate affected endpoints. EDR/XDR correlates activity across workloads, presents the attack chain and supports endpoint isolation and response actions. Data exfiltration Monitor unusual data flows and apply controls appropriate to systems and users, based on least-privilege principle. XDR correlates endpoint activity with supported telemetry sources. Acronis DLP controls sensitive-data transfers on supported endpoints. Pre-encryption file behavior Use behavioral detection and automated rollback; protect local data, network folders and servers. Active Protection uses behavioral and AI/ML-based detection to stop ransomware and restore affected files. Network folder and server-side protection extend coverage where supported. What should an organization do immediately after detecting ransomware? The first actions should limit spread, preserve evidence and create a safe path to recovery. Organizations should pre-authorize automated actions for clearly defined, high-severity conditions and test them before an incident. Isolate the affected workload while preserving the management channel needed for investigation. Stop malicious processes and quarantine confirmed malicious files. Protect evidence, including process trees, command lines, network connections and relevant logs. Identify and disable the compromised account, token or remote-access path. Patch the exploited vulnerability or close the exposed service after containment. Restore affected files or workloads from a known-good recovery point, then validate the recovered environment before reconnecting it. Escalate to incident-response, legal, privacy, insurance and communications stakeholders according to the organization’s response plan. Acronis EDR and XDR support investigation, isolation and response actions from the incident view. Recovery actions depend on the applicable backup and recovery licenses, available recovery points and configuration. Acronis MDR by Acronis TRU adds 24/7 expert monitoring, investigation and response; managed remediation and recovery are included in the Advanced service tier within the agreed scope and permissions. Turn pre-encryption signals into tested controls The value of an early ransomware warning depends on what happens next. The five signals above can give defenders an opportunity to contain an attack before encryption spreads, but only if the response is already defined and tested. Whether it is an attempt to delete shadow copies, data exfiltration, unexpected remote execution or a sudden burst of encryption-like file activity, suspicious behavior should trigger a clear containment and recovery plan. Acronis Cyber Platform can connect prevention, detection, response and recovery through one integrated platform. Capabilities vary by edition, deployment model, configuration and licensing. He works at the intersection of cybersecurity, product strategy, and go-to-market, translating complex security challenges and technology trends into practical insights for businesses and service providers. 8qupty.text: Two critical NGINX vulnerabilities dubbed "nginx2root" allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable web servers, with researchers demonstrating how the flaws can be chained with a Linux kernel bug to gain root access. The two HTTP/2 vulnerabilities were discovered independently by researchers at Xint, Wiz, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, and Rapid7, while Xint also discovered three additional NGINX RCE flaws. Censys later reproduced the underlying memory corruption conditions in four of the five flaws through lab testing, but did not achieve remote code execution. The first of the two "nginx2root" flaws is CVE-2026-123007, a flow-control bug that can corrupt memory in an NGINX worker. It impacts all versions from 1.31.8 down to 1.9.5, released in 2015. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution on a server hosting ordinary static files over HTTP/2 with TLS, while Xint demoed root access by chaining it with a separate Linux kernel flaw. Xint says the separate vulnerability affects the Linux kernel's SCTP subsystem and can be used to escape an NGINX Docker container and gain root privileges on the underlying host. The second flaw is CVE-2026-123633, a use-after-free problem that affects NGINX when it accepts HTTP/2 connections and proxies requests to a backend. It impacts all versions from 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. When the worker runs low on connection slots, it can close an active connection and free memory that a request still uses. Wiz also demonstrated remote code execution via CVE-2026-123633, but the firm is not publicly releasing its proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits at this time. The other three flaws the researchers discovered and F5 fixed are CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-123634, and CVE-2026-113425, all use-after-free vulnerabilities affecting HTTP/3 reverse proxying, DNS resolution with subrequests, and mail proxy authentication, respectively. The flaws were fixed in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 stable and 1.31.9 mainline. NGINX Plus users should update to versions 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1. F5’s latest security update also addresses five more vulnerabilities not highlighted in the Wiz or Xint reports. The most notable is CVE-2026-118899, a high-severity issue that allows an unauthenticated attacker to cause a worker to enter an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3, resulting in denial of service. For system administrators, it is recommended to upgrade immediately to the latest NGINX release, or temporarily disable HTTP/2 until an upgrade is possible. However, this mitigation only covers the two "nginx2root" flaws. Evaluating the risk Regarding the real exploitability risk of "nginx2root," security researcher Florian Roth says it's worse than Node2Shell and Java2Shell, but doesn’t appear to be an imminent threat for most NGINX deployments. Commenting on X, Roth said the flaws are exploitable in non-default configurations, warning that claims of widespread exposure based solely on NGINX version numbers are misleading. Xint previously reported that 98.9% of NGINX hosts disclosing recognizable versions were running software within the affected range, but this does not account for whether HTTP/2 is enabled or security fixes have been backported. The two HTTP/2 flaws require an unpatched server with HTTP/2 enabled on a listener an attacker can reach, while CVE-2026-123633 also requires NGINX to proxy requests to a backend. Roth scanned a sample of a few hundred NGINX HTTPS endpoints from Shodan and found that roughly 66% of them support HTTP/2, but confirming actual exposure requires checking the server’s configuration and whether a fix has been backported. According to Censys' live exposure tracker, approximately 8.8 million NGINX services were potentially exposed to CVE-2026-123007 as of November 19, based on affected version numbers and HTTP/2 support. The company reports that more than 511,000 previously exposed services have already been patched or mitigated, while another 104 million NGINX services do not disclose their versions, making it difficult to determine whether they are affected. 9pdlfw.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Under specific conditions, a critical vulnerability in Drupal core can allow an attacker without login credentials to use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site. That can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, and the project rates the vulnerable configurations as uncommon. Fixed releases for all supported branches shipped yesterday. The Drupal Security Team disclosed the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, yesterday and rated it critical, 18 out of 25 on the project's risk scale. The installer ships in every copy of Drupal core as the file /core/install.php and stays on the site after installation. Core's default .htaccess rules do not block requests to it, so blocking it is left to each site. No attacks are reported in the security advisory, which rates exploitation as complex and records an existing proof-of-concept exploit. Some exploit paths are blocked where the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php. The team had told site owners in an advance notice earlier this week to set aside time for the update, warning that exploits may be developed within hours or days. Every release below 10.6.22 is affected, along with Drupal 11 releases from 11.0.0 before 11.3.22 and from 11.4.0 before 11.4.13. What to Do Now The fixed versions, detailed in the project's release notes, are: Drupal 11.4.x: update to 11.4.13 Drupal 11.3.x: update to 11.3.22 Drupal 10.6.x: update to 10.6.22 The team recommends blocking the installer even after updating. Sites that cannot update yet should follow the project's installer guidance, updated yesterday, which describes three options: a deny rule in the web server configuration, an .htaccess rule, or removing the file and keeping it removed with Composer scripts. Sites that use the Drupal Steward protection service are already protected from known attack vectors, according to the team, and should still update in case new vectors emerge. Drupal 11.2.x and earlier, 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 8 and 9 are end-of-life and get no fix. The 11.3.x branch and Drupal 10 lose security coverage altogether in December under the project's support schedule. In the week of November 8, 154,485 of the 528,430 sites reporting usage data to drupal.org, about 29 percent, were running end-of-life branches. The flaw was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, an automated service the AI company launched on October 8 to look for vulnerabilities in open-source projects that opt in. Findings go to maintainers without human review, each with a reproducer and, where available, a candidate patch, according to its launch announcement. Drupal's security team said on November 2 that a surge of security reports, which it attributes to AI tools, is more than it can sustain at its current funding, and that it is cutting security coverage for core minor versions from 12 months to 8 starting in 2027. This is the second critical remote code execution flaw fixed in Drupal core in two months, after the Field UI flaw patched on October 14, which also had at least one exploit path that needed no login.

d5zf6n.text: The Drupal Security Team has patched a critical remote code execution vulnerability that can let attackers take over vulnerable sites. This content management system (CMS) is commonly used by large organizations that manage multi-site installations and massive data structures, including government entities, educational organizations, major research universities, and high-profile enterprise and media organizations. The security flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-132165) was discovered by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, and anonymous users can exploit it to reinstall the Drupal CMS. "Drupal core ships with an install.php file for installing Drupal core. Under specific conditions, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal. This can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution," the Drupal Security Team warned in a Wednesday advisory. "Some exploit paths are mitigated if the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php." Admins whose websites use the paid Drupal Steward Web Application Firewall (WAF) service are already protected from known attack vectors, but should still upgrade to Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, or 11.4.13 in case other attack vectors are discovered. Those who can't immediately upgrade should secure the Drupal installer by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root. On Wednesday, Drupal also addressed a moderately critical gadget chain vulnerability (CVE-2026-132166) that attackers with admin privileges can exploit to gain remote code execution on a targeted site if the application deserializes untrusted data due to another security flaw. "The Drupal Security Team urges you to reserve time for core updates at that time because exploits might be developed within hours or days," the security team said in a Monday advance warning. "The vulnerabilities are currently rated as critical and at least one can be exploited by anonymous users." In May, Drupal also confirmed that attackers were actively exploiting an SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-9082) in the database abstraction API that could let them escalate privileges, access sensitive information, or achieve remote code execution on unpatched servers. More recently, Drupal warned that a critical access bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-118539) in the Commerce Core module is being abused in attacks. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged 5 Drupal vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild since November 2021, two of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks. 1ab09ah.text: One of the early targets of PHP2Shell exploitation was the firewall. On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. Both flaws let anyone execute code on the web server without authentication. The disclosure itself went a little wrong. Details leaked on October 20, ahead of the coordinated release, and the PHP project shipped an emergency patch the next day. The vulnerabilities require no authentication, but they are not easy to exploit reliably. It takes skill and additional knowledge about the target system. Where it matters a lot is appliances, which run identical, often outdated software that an attacker can study in advance. That is the bigger picture. An awful lot of web applications control critical devices in your network. Almost anything is a web application to some extent. That often goes unrecognized, and as a result those applications aren't adequately protected. Everything is a web application. That is the motto of the SANS course I teach, SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices. Web application security has traditionally been treated as a developer issue, yet anyone protecting a network must understand how web applications work to properly defend them. Why Appliances Are the Softer Target On ordinary web servers, address space layout randomization (ASLR) is one of the features that makes exploitation harder. It shuffles where code and data sit in memory, so an exploit can't rely on fixed addresses. VulnCheck's early analysis found the bugs exploitable on ARM64 systems and on x86 systems without ASLR. Few public exploits bypassed ASLR on x86-64, and the one VulnCheck confirmed worked only against a single PHP build. VulnCheck's own exploit chained a memory leak to get code execution with ASLR enabled. Appliances change that math, not because the protections are missing, but because every device on a given software version runs the same binaries, so an attacker can work out memory offsets in advance. The PAN-OS exploit still had to defeat ASLR, leaking the libphp.so base address through the Set-Cookie header, and SELinux confined the resulting shell. PAN-OS also ships end-of-life PHP versions (8.0.30 and 7.4.33). Israeli security firm Dream, working with Palo Alto Networks on the investigation, found the attacker had obtained PAN-OS firmware, decrypted it, extracted the PHP libraries, and built precise memory profiles for nine software versions. The actor then chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw (Fragnesia, CVE-2026-46300) to gain root on 25 systems (24 firewalls and one management server) in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Web application security tends to focus on large, cloud-based applications. It's often the little things, the mosquitoes on the internet, that do you in. Appliances run predictable, often outdated software, and they are everywhere. HTTP Is More Complex Than Your Defenses Assume HTTP is a very complex protocol with lots of options. To upload a file, a client doesn't have to send it in one piece. It can send the body in chunks without declaring its total length, and, if the server decompresses request bodies, compress it, which makes it difficult for a web server to calculate how much memory it needs to store it. Memory-safety bugs remain common as a result, in web applications and in the web servers running them. In PHP2Shell, a crafted multipart upload pushes PHP past its memory limit while it is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. The bugs are in what PHP leaves behind when it aborts the request: uninitialized request memory (CVE-2026-109618) and a pointer to freed memory (CVE-2026-109619). The request doesn't need to be large, either. Deeply nested, empty file fields make PHP allocate far more memory than the body contains, so a request well under the default 8 MB post_max_size can still exhaust the default 128 MB memory limit. Defenders must understand the protocol to know what these vulnerabilities look like, for example to write signatures that detect the exploits. The same complexity limits the middle boxes we rely on. They can even interfere in ways nobody planned. Intruder found that nginx in front of PAN-OS buffered chunked request bodies, which broke public exploit chains. Web application firewalls are often not adequate, and file uploads are key functionality for a lot of web applications, so blocking them outright isn't an option. That takes out many of the traditional defenses. What remains is knowing where your critical web applications are. Identify them, starting with the admin interfaces on your firewalls and other network equipment, and restrict access to them. Palo Alto's own guidance for PHP2Shell was to remove internet access to management interfaces and limit them to trusted internal IP addresses. If you rely on a web application firewall, configure it properly and understand how much protection it does and doesn't provide. Risk Was the Hardest Call The clearest lesson from PHP2Shell is how difficult it can be to accurately determine the risk from a vulnerability like this. Prioritization is always a big issue for defenders, particularly with today's flood of vulnerabilities, and this one was hard to read from every angle. The scores told different stories. The PHP project rated both flaws 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and Fortinet's PSIRT listed 9.8 under CVSS v3. Palo Alto initially scored the issue 8.7 for its own products and listed it at moderate urgency, raised it to 9.2 Critical with the highest urgency on October 27, and confirmed exploitation a week after its advisory went out. Many public proofs of concept didn't work, so a flood of attempts in your logs said little about whether a given server was at risk. And PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard warned that one early workaround, turning off session upload progress, was not enough on its own. We are adding these lessons to SEC522: how to assess risk, how protections like ASLR reduce it, and why appliances remain softer targets. Defending What Runs on HTTP I will be teaching SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026, December 14-18 in Washington, D.C., and Live Online. The course starts with how HTTP works, including HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and covers file upload handling, API security, and AI endpoints across 17 hands-on labs and a Defend the Flag capstone. It is built for the people who defend web applications, whether or not they wrote them. Register for SEC522 at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026. Note: This article has been written and contributed by Dr. Johannes Ullrich, Dean of Research at SANS Technology Institute.

11ho73c.text: ​Microsoft is developing a new Edge security feature to reduce the attack surface by disabling the WebGL, WebGL2, and WebGPU APIs. Inspired by Apple's Lockdown Mode, the new feature shares the same name and builds on Edge Enhanced Security Mode (also known internally as Super Duper Secure Mode), which disables Just-In-Time Compilation (JIT) from the V8 processing pipeline. The new Edge Lockdown Mode offers optional, extreme protections for users facing highly targeted attacks who are willing to sacrifice website compatibility for stronger defenses. "Lockdown Mode is designed for users who are at particular risk of being targeted in cybersecurity campaigns. This may include journalists, executives, security researchers, and administrators," said Partner Security Group Manager Gareth Evans. "Individuals whose threat model justifies accepting reduced compatibility in exchange for stronger protection. It may also apply to devices operating within highly restricted environments." Evans also warned that websites that use the disabled APIs (especially those with interactive graphics like games or maps) may not work as expected when this security feature is toggled on. Edge users can test Lockdown Mode by switching to the Canary release channel, enabling the #edge-sdsm-plus flag, restarting the browser, then toggling on Strict mode for "Enhance your security on the web" and blocking WebGL graphics and WebGPU graphics. After enabling it, users will see a new "Lockdown Enabled" indicator in the address bar when WebGL or WebGPU is blocked on a web page. Lockdown Mode indicator (Microsoft) ​While the current Edge Canary Lockdown Mode blocks websites from using WebGL, WebGL2, and WebGPU APIs to stop attacks that try to escalate privileges and escape the sandbox, Microsoft plans to extend the feature in upcoming releases. "The initial set of Lockdown Mode mitigations focus is the GPU process, a more privileged component that handles complex graphics workloads across browser code, third-party libraries, and device drivers," Evans added. "Results from this experiment will inform the finished Lockdown Mode experience, including clearer descriptions of restricted capabilities and site-level exceptions that restore trusted sites without weakening protection everywhere else." According to the company's estimates, this new security feature would have blocked around 60% of privilege escalation attacks targeting Edge users in the wild. Last year, Microsoft also introduced a new Edge scareware sensor to ensure Defender SmartScreen blocks scam pages faster, and restricted access to Edge's Internet Explorer mode after learning that hackers were leveraging zero-day exploits in the Chakra JavaScript engine to access target devices. 10dta0t.text: Microsoft has shared a workaround for installation and launch issues affecting Office and third-party applications after installing this month's Windows 11 hotpatch. In a service alert seen by BleepingComputer, Microsoft told IT administrators that these problems may appear during installation, launch, or even during normal app use on systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later. "Devices which installed the November 2026 hotpatch update (the Originating KBs listed above), might experience an error when installing, launching, or running some applications. Resulting from this issue, errors similar to "ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099)" are displayed," Microsoft said. "Current investigation suggests this issue occurs for applications which load the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL, found as msi.dll. This can happen more frequently with 32-bit applications, but can also occur for 64-bit applications under certain conditions." Microsoft added that this known issue should not impact systems that have installed the standard November 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates, but only those that have installed the hotpatch updates pushed through the Windows Autopatch, the company's cloud-based enterprise service that automates Windows and Microsoft 365 software and security updates. Until a fix is available, Microsoft has shared a workaround to help IT admins temporarily mitigate the bug on affected systems. To do that, they have to edit the Windows Registry to increase the HotPatchTableSize using the following procedure: Open the Windows Registry by opening the Start menu, typing "regedit", and selecting Registry Editor from the results. Using the folders and address path, navigate to the HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management folder. In the right-hand panel, locate the "HotPatchTableSize" registry key, open it, and set the Value to "2000". Click OK. Close the registry editor and restart the device. "Before you modify the registry, back it up and make sure that you know how to restore it if a problem occurs. For more information, see How to back up and restore the registry in Windows," Microsoft said. Microsoft said in March that it would turn on hotpatch security updates by default for all eligible Windows devices managed through the Microsoft Graph API and Microsoft Intune, after the May 2026 Windows security updates are installed. One month later, it fixed a Windows Autopatch bug that caused driver updates restricted by administrative policies to deploy on some Autopatch-managed Windows devices belonging to customers in the European Union. Microsoft first announced Windows Autopatch in April 2002, saying it would be available for free to customers with a Windows 10/11 Enterprise E3 license or greater starting in July 2022. The feature reached public preview in early June and has been generally available since July 2022. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 48lpmk.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 19, 2026Cloud Security / Email Security N-able on Wednesday disclosed that unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to one of the servers in the Mail Assure and Spam Experts Hosted Cloud, causing it to disable management interfaces and APIs. "We have taken steps to mitigate the threat and are continuing to harden our services to reduce the risk of recurrence," N-able said. "The investigation is ongoing, but at this time we do not have evidence that customer data was compromised, including access to tenants' mailboxes." The following services remain impacted - Mail Assure (Americas) Mail Assure (APAC) Mail Assure (Europe) SpamExperts (Americas) SpamExperts (APAC) SpamExperts (Europe) The discovery comes after N-able began an investigation into a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026. While it was initially traced to a combination of platform configuration and service dependencies within the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud environment, it has since been determined that the disruption was actually caused by a security incident. N-able said it's continuing to work on restoring Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud across all regions, while core mail flow and inbound and outbound mail filtering remain available. "The management portal (UI), APIs, quarantine, and logging remain offline while our teams work to restore them securely. Access will be restored once validation is complete," it said. The company also noted that it has directly reached out to Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud partners with "information relevant to their environment and whether action is required or not." As of November 19, 2026, at 8 a.m. UTC, N-able said the restoration process is still underway, and that it's making steady progress on validating and hardening the management portal and its supporting services. It's worth noting that the incident is unrelated to the discovery of multiple vulnerabilities impacting N-central referred to as Able2Shell, 4EverAble2Shell, and Agent2Shell. (This is a developing story. Please check back for more details.)

1rfy8lm.text: NVIDIA is investigating claims of a security breach after the Gentlemen ransomware group has added the company to its dark web data leak site. Although the ransomware operation now lists the American multinational tech giant, it has not yet shared any proof of the breach. On their leak site, the cybercrime gang threatens to release data and has added a countdown that ends in nine days, on November 28. While the company told BleepingComputer it hasn't found evidence that its systems were compromised, it said it's now looking into a separate incident that may have affected one of its service providers. "NVIDIA is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner," an NVIDIA spokesperson told BleepingComputer when asked to confirm the cybercrime gang's claims. "We have found no indication that NVIDIA systems or networks were affected. We continue to monitor the situation." NVIDIA entry on data leak site (BleepingComputer) ​NVIDIA confirmed a data breach earlier this year, in May, when it told BleepingComputer that some Armenian users' information (including their names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and usernames) had been exposed after a regional GeForce NOW Alliance partner was hacked. However, the company added that the May breach did not affect its network or NVIDIA-operated services. The tech giant also disclosed another data breach in March 2022 (claimed by the Lapsus$ extortion gang) that affected more than 71,000 employees after attackers accessed its network a month earlier. The Gentlemen surfaced last year as a closed ransomware group and then switched to a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) model, offering affiliates up to a 90% cut of ransom proceeds (compared to the typical 70%–80% other ransomware groups offer). It operates as a double-extortion group, exfiltrating sensitive data from victims' networks before encrypting their systems and pressuring them with the threat of leaking the stolen information online. Since it emerged, The Gentlemen has claimed more than 1,100 victims from various sectors, spanning manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, energy, education, financial services, and more. 1e55q2c.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Software Security Ruby contains seven memory-safety flaws in its regular expression engine and its string case-conversion code. For five of them, its maintainers say, proof-of-concept exploits, or PoCs, have shown that crafted input can run code on the machine. "We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution," the maintainers said. The project released fixed versions yesterday: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14. Whether an application is at risk depends on whether an attacker can get crafted patterns or strings into the affected code, and the advisories report no attacks so far. The other two flaws are weaker. The maintainers say one has proof-of-concept code that corrupts memory under an attacker's control but has not been shown to run code, and the other can only read memory it should not or crash the program. The project set the seven out in a security announcement and a separate advisory for each. The advisories rate three flaws critical, three high, and one moderate, and say which carry the remote-code-execution PoCs. In order of severity: Critical. GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5, a one-byte heap overflow when Ruby changes the case of a string in certain single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252. It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory) Critical. GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x, a double free when Ruby compiles a crafted regular expression that uses a character-class intersection (&&). It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory) Critical. GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w, a heap overflow when the size of a compiled regular expression overflows during compilation. It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory) High. GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a heap overflow when a case change produces a result larger than 4 GiB. It has a remote-code-execution PoC, though the size needed puts it out of reach for most requests. (GitHub advisory) High. GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4, a heap overflow when Ruby turns a crafted compiled regular expression back into text with Regexp#to_s. It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory) High. GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r, an out-of-bounds read during case-insensitive matching. Its PoC shows attacker-controlled memory corruption, and the maintainers say remote code execution is possible but not shown. (GitHub advisory) Moderate. GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h, an out-of-bounds read when Ruby matches a case-insensitive backreference against a crafted subject string. The advisory says it "may disclose memory contents or crash the process." (GitHub advisory) The project credits Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics and Anthropic with four of the findings, and baba__yaga, aphantom, Hiroya Fujinami and Hiroshi SHIBATA with the other three. Which Applications Are Exposed The flaws are in Ruby's own code, so every application on an affected version carries them. Whether an attacker can reach one depends on how the application handles external input. The regex flaws need an application that builds a regular expression from input an attacker controls and then compiles or runs it. Matching untrusted text against a pattern the developers wrote themselves does not pose the same risk, except in one case below. The two case-conversion flaws do not involve regular expressions at all. They fire when the application changes the case of a crafted string, so code that runs case conversion over imported or outside text is worth checking. The one case is the moderate read flaw, which fires when the application matches a crafted subject string against a fixed pattern that uses a case-insensitive backreference. The announcement and advisories do not include the proof-of-concept code. The fixes are in Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14. The affected ranges are: Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9, fixed in 4.0.10. Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, fixed in 3.4.13. Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, fixed in 3.3.14. Ruby 3.2 and earlier, end of life and not fixed. Those older versions will not get a fix, and the project recommends moving to a supported line. With 3.3.14, the maintainers renamed the Ruby 3.3 phase from security maintenance to legacy maintenance, and support still ends at the end of March 2027. Because the fixes ship inside Ruby, updating an application's gems or framework does not replace a vulnerable interpreter. The version that matters is the Ruby running on application servers, background workers, and container images, which must be updated and then restarted or rebuilt. The seven do not have CVE numbers yet. The project says it has requested them, and until they are assigned, the GitHub advisory IDs are the only way to track flaws in scanners and software inventories. It is the second time in a month that the project has patched its regular expression engine. In the October fixes, released on October 23, it shipped Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13 to patch compilation bugs GitLab found, which sat behind four critical GitLab flaws. One of those GitLab flaws drew an attempted attack on Alpine Linux's own GitLab server. CISA later added it to the KEV catalog, its list of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, as actively exploited. Those are different bugs from this week's seven, and the new advisories do not say that GitLab or any other named product can be attacked through them. What the October case showed is that a regular expression built from user input can become a real way onto a server, not just a theoretical one.

1jsjljs.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Database Security Low-privilege database accounts that cannot read a single application table can still be used to run code on the database server itself, a researcher has shown, by reaching memory-corruption bugs in the engine code behind ordinary SQL. The exploits, published yesterday, are the researcher's proofs of concept against PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, plus a separate Oracle chain that needs no login. None has been seen in a real attack. The work is by Zheng Yu, a researcher at Depthfirst. A database account's SQL permissions control which tables and schemas it can access, the researcher argues, not the memory-unsafe C and C++ code the engine runs to read, plan, and execute a query. Common grants give an account enough room to reach that code. PostgreSQL's default TEMPORARY privilege, or the right to create temporary tables in MySQL and ClickHouse, allows an account to create objects or send input that triggers a memory bug. Four of the flaws now have vendor CVEs and fixes, but the full attack chains were not reproduced independently, and the research reports no sign that any of them has been used in an attack. In PostgreSQL, the flaw CVE-2026-116331 allows an account that can create database objects to run code as the operating system user that runs the database. It was fixed last week in a security advisory, and the CVE record credits the researcher for the report. The researcher's technical analysis shows a plain login role building the objects it needs in its own temporary schema, without touching application data, then turning a type-confusion bug into control of the server. MySQL has a similar flaw in its query optimizer, CVE-2026-101786, in Server and Cluster versions 26.7.0 to 26.7.1. Oracle's MySQL October advisory rates it as needing high privileges. The researcher reached code execution on the 26.7.0 image with an account that could only create temporary tables and could not read existing ones, a narrower kind of access than that rating suggests. Oracle Database is the one case where an attacker needs no account at all, the researcher says. A bug in Oracle Text and a flaw in the GraphQL interface of Oracle REST Data Services, chained against an exposed web endpoint, reach the engine code and run commands before any login. Oracle patched the Oracle Text bug, CVE-2026-114819, rated 9.9, earlier this week in its November update, and the GraphQL flaw, CVE-2026-91609, in the October update. On their own, the company rates neither as exploitable without a login. ClickHouse is the fourth target. The researcher reports an integer-overflow write in how it reads a binary row format, reached by a user who sets a single option, format_binary_max_string_size, to zero, and reproduced a shell on version 26.7.5.10. This one has no CVE and no confirmed fixed version, so operators should check with the vendor for the fix. Software Identifier Affected versions Fix PostgreSQL CVE-2026-116331 Versions before 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, 14.25 Fixed November 12 MySQL Server and Cluster CVE-2026-101786 26.7.0 to 26.7.1 Fixed October 20 Oracle Database (Oracle Text) CVE-2026-114819 19.3-19.32, 21.3-21.24, 23.4.0-23.26.3 Fixed November 17 Oracle REST Data Services CVE-2026-91609 24.2.0 to 26.2.1 Fixed October 20 ClickHouse No CVE assigned 26.7.5.10 tested No confirmed fixed version Beyond installing the updates, the other move is to review what accounts can do, not only what they can read, and to take away the TEMPORARY privilege and broad temporary-table rights from accounts that do not need them. That step does not close the Oracle path, which starts without any account.

1l0aqfd.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added four vulnerabilities impacting Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An unsafe reflection vulnerability in Apache Axis that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. CVE-2026-90817 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A code injection vulnerability in REDCap that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. CVE-2026-40217 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An unprotected alternate channel vulnerability in LiteLLM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via bytecode rewriting at the /guardrails/test_custom_code URI. CVE-2024-10441 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper encoding or escaping of output vulnerability in Synology DSM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via unspecified vectors. "An attacker could exploit this via crafted HTTP requests that access an unintended controller route from a public survey context and supply a crafted file-path or stream parameter during data import processing," CISA said about CVE-2026-90817. "Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash." The addition of CVE-2026-90436 to the KEV catalog follows reports that the flaw is exploited in conjunction with the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities affecting N-able N-central to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. Rapid7, in its own analysis of the flaw, said it detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment by taking advantage of the fact that the corporate workspace platform uses the Axis library as part of its XML-RPC and SOAP APIs. "To be vulnerable, the Confluence instance must have the 'Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)' enabled," Atlassian said. "Please note that this setting was turned off by default for new installations starting in Confluence 3.0. This feature was fully removed in Confluence 10.0." In the activity documented by Rapid7, threat actors are said to have weaponized the flaw to run shell commands and scripts fetched from temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains, followed by enumerating the compromised environment. The incident was flagged on November 13, 2026. "Just over three minutes after the first observed execution, the attackers were authenticating to MySQL with Confluence's own database credentials, querying page bodies, application links, and attachments with names associated with credentials, tokens, VPN configurations, and private keys," Rapid7 said. "The attacker's scripts, likely AI-generated, then targeted files in Confluence's default location for uploaded page attachments (/var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/attachments/v4/), parsed Office documents, searched for credentials, and hunted for payment card numbers, using Luhn checks to filter out false positives." In addition, the attackers have been found to map various internal services, use a Confluence application credential to query the internal Atlassian Crowd API for users and group memberships, and attempt to carry out a Kerberos-based credential harvesting technique called AS-REP Roasting. Although these efforts were unsuccessful, the threat actor managed to acquire a service account credential and queried a production cloud data warehouse. About 12 hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from "192.238.253[.]176." CVE-2026-90436, which affects Axis 1.x versions, remains unpatched as Axis 1 has reached end-of-life (EoL) status. It's recommended to migrate to a different SOAP engine, such as Apache Axis 2/Java. Alternatively, users can use a build of Axis with the patch from a July 12, 2026, commit applied. As for CVE-2026-90817, Safe Security said in a report published late last month that it observed an unknown threat abusing the flaw to "stage a transient web shell, followed by an in-memory loader that retrieved XMRig disguised as image files, masqueraded the miner as syslog-ng, and established persistence through cron and an added SSH key." The exploitation of CVE-2026-40217 stems from a Google Threat Intelligence Group report this week in which threat actors have leveraged the vulnerability to elevate limited-access inference keys into full administrative credentials and establish persistence as part of LLMjacking attacks aimed at financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region. Rounding off the list is CVE-2024-10441, which Synology disclosed earlier this month as being exploited in ransomware attacks targeting Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices. The attacks have been found to result in the deployment of C3RB3R ransomware. In light of active exploitation, federal agencies have been recommended to apply fixes or necessary mitigations for DSM, REDCap, and Axis flaws by November 21, 2026, and for the LiteLLM flaw by December 2, 2026.

13fgm1a.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security The maintainers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday issued an advisory announcing an upcoming security release that addresses critical flaws. The release is scheduled for November 19, 2026, between 2 and 2:30 p.m. UTC. "These releases are part of PHP's regular four-week release cycle and will address security vulnerabilities affecting all supported PHP versions," the maintainers said. "The highest severity is CRITICAL." However, the project also noted that issues rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups. It did not disclose any additional specifics. The update is expected to include CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution flaw that succeeds only if the following conditions are met - An application sets session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration, and its code switches the handler to php with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress is enabled, which is PHP's default. As mitigations, users were urged to set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release and restart the PHP worker for the setting to be applied. The development comes nearly a month after PHP released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively tracked as PHP2Shell that enable unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) via specially crafted HTTP requests. The shortcomings have since come under limited active exploitation, targeting publicly-accessible Palo Alto Networks management interfaces and Check Point Security Gateways to launch attacks against Active Directory and deliver backdoors. In a report published on October 30, 2026, Hunt.io said it identified 616 PHP2Shell-related files, spanning shared exploit kits, cloned proof-of-concepts (PoCs), custom heap exploits, scanners, and post-exploitation tooling, across multiple hosts, even as participants in underground forums have sought exploits, discussed prerequisites, and whether circulating PoCs worked. "Exploit developers are unlikely to create a single universal exploit that works reliably across all affected PHP deployments," CrowdStrike said. Last month, PHP also released patches to address a critical flaw in Brotli (CVE-2026-111497 aka Node2Shell or Broccoli2Shell), an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the decoder library that could result in arbitrary code execution. Users are advised to apply the updates as soon as they become available.

tx5qp0.text: Ukrainian authorities, working with the FBI, have arrested four suspected members of an international ransomware organization linked to more than $40.5 million in ransom payments from at least 28 companies worldwide. The arrests come after a two-year investigation into a cybercrime organization comprising at least 27 individuals from Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Russia, and other countries. Investigators say the organization was connected to a larger cybercrime network of more than 60 members operating across eight jurisdictions, including former members of the notorious Conti ransomware gang. According to Ukraine's National Police, the group targeted organizations in the oil and gas, pharmaceutical, manufacturing, logistics, and financial sectors, as well as critical infrastructure. The attackers researched their victims' financial standing, assets, employees, and IT vulnerabilities before launching attacks designed to steal corporate data, encrypt systems, and extort cryptocurrency payments. Speaking in an exclusive interview with Ukrainian news outlet Censor.NET, acting National Police chief Maksym Tsutskiridze said investigators had identified at least 28 companies that paid more than $40.5 million in ransoms. "We have identified at least 28 companies that transferred more than $40.5 million in ransom payments to the hackers, equivalent to approximately UAH 1.8 billion. This is money that has already been paid. We are still establishing the full extent of the damage," Tsutskiridze said. In one attack, the hackers stole 1.4 terabytes of data from a U.S. company and expanded their attack to other companies within the same corporate group. The attackers initially demanded $10 million but ultimately received $5 million after negotiations. As first reported by French cybersecurity news outlet LeMagIT, Ukrainian court records identify several victims of the criminal organization, including Warren Oil Company, Maxxis International-USA, Newpark Resources, and Quantum Health. The court documents identify Warren Oil Company as the victim of an August 2024 attack in which hackers copied 1.4 TB of data before receiving an 84.5 BTC ransom payment, equivalent to approximately $5 million at the time. The records also allege that Newpark Resources paid $1.5 million in December 2024, while Quantum Health paid $5 million in June 2026 following an initial $15 million ransom demand. LeMagIT also noted that the BlackSuit ransomware gang claimed Maxxis International as a victim in November 2024, while Ukrainian court records identify Chaos as the ransomware used by the criminal organization. The Conti ransomware operation shut down in May 2022, with its members dispersing into smaller ransomware gangs and other cybercrime operations. One of the groups linked to former Conti members was BlackSuit, which initially operated as Quantum ransomware in January 2022 before becoming Royal. In June 2023, Royal began operating under the BlackSuit name after testing a new encryptor and carrying out high-profile attacks, including one against the City of Dallas, Texas. However, Ukrainian authorities have not identified the four arrested suspects as former Conti members or confirmed their individual affiliations with BlackSuit or Chaos. AI-powered IT support impersonation To breach corporate networks, the cybercriminals impersonated IT support personnel and used a custom-developed platform with AI-generated voice messages to automate fraudulent phone calls. During these calls, they tricked employees into disclosing login credentials or installing remote-access software, allowing the attackers to access internal corporate systems. In one documented incident, an attacker kept an employee on the phone while another attacker accessed the company's systems, with the call ending only after the attackers confirmed the intrusion was successful. "They created their own platform featuring voice messages generated by artificial intelligence. They called company employees, posing as IT support specialists. Under the pretext of providing technical assistance, they persuaded employees to disclose their login credentials or install remote access software. This allowed them to gain access to corporate networks," Tsutskiridze explained. The Ukrainian court records provide additional insight into these attacks, describing how the hackers used phishing pages impersonating corporate VPN services, spoofed phone numbers, and remote-access tools such as TeamViewer and AnyDesk. During the Warren Oil Company attack, the records allege that the attackers tricked an employee into entering credentials on a phishing page, then obtained a two-factor authentication code that granted them remote access to the corporate network. Once inside the network, the attackers stole sensitive information and encrypted files using ransomware, disrupting the victim's operations. The gang then demanded cryptocurrency payments in exchange for restoring access to encrypted systems while threatening to publicly release stolen corporate data. "They would deprive a company of access to its own data and then demand millions of dollars in exchange for decrypting it. At the same time, they threatened to publish the stolen information. Victims were put under pressure from both sides, forcing them to pay the ransom in cryptocurrency," Tsutskiridze said. Ukrainian authorities conducted 66 simultaneous searches across Kyiv and 11 regions of Ukraine as part of the joint operation with U.S. law enforcement. Four suspected key members of the organization were detained, although authorities did not disclose their exact arrest locations. During these searches, investigators seized computers, mobile phones, bank cards, nearly $370,000 in cash, and €20,000. Four alleged key members of the organization were formally notified of suspicion and are currently in custody. The suspects face charges related to participating in a criminal organization and unauthorized interference with information systems under Ukrainian law. If convicted, they face up to 15 years in prison. Ukrainian authorities say the investigation is ongoing as law enforcement works to identify additional members of the international network and determine their involvement in other cyberattacks. The National Police also released a video showing footage from the investigation, including law enforcement raids, seized cash, interviews with investigators, and a suspect being questioned. The video also contains audio from an alleged ransomware extortion call demanding $15 million after claiming to have stolen more than 1.5 TB of corporate data. ro82fm.text: Coinbase says it blocked $4.7 million in cryptocurrency transfers to scammers promoting a fake giveaway using an AI-generated deepfake of Elon Musk during a Tesla livestream that attracted more than 500,000 viewers. The deepfake took place during Tesla's "flying car" demonstration, when scammers created a fake YouTube livestream that appeared to broadcast the event. The fraudulent stream featured an AI-generated video of Musk, cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and a QR code, promising viewers that any cryptocurrency they sent would be doubled. According to Coinbase, hundreds of its customers attempted to send millions of dollars to the scammers over about two hours, including many longtime users of the exchange. However, the company says its AI-powered fraud-prevention systems detected the scam and blocked about 91% of the attempted transfers, totaling $4.7 million. Unlike traditional cryptocurrency theft involving compromised accounts or stolen credentials, victims in this campaign voluntarily made the crypto transfer after believing the livestream was real. Coinbase explained that this makes scams like these difficult to detect because the transactions are created and approved by legitimate account holders. "Most fraud defenses are built to spot activity the customer didn't authorize," Coinbase explained. "That's not what happened here. The customer was logged in, the customer pressed confirm, and the customer believed it was the opportunity of a lifetime." AI agents intervene to stop transfers Coinbase says its scam prevention system uses machine learning models to analyze outgoing cryptocurrency transfers in real time, identifying suspicious activity associated with giveaway scams, brand impersonation, and newly created wallet addresses. When a suspicious transfer is detected, an AI agent engages the customer in a short conversation, explaining the characteristics of the suspected scam and asking questions intended to help them recognize the fraud. The system also assigns confidence scores to the agent's responses before presenting them to customers, allowing it to determine when additional safeguards may be necessary. Coinbase says its AI agent had never encountered this particular campaign before but recognized the underlying scam techniques, including promises to multiply cryptocurrency, time pressure tied to a live event, and irreversible transfers. The company claims the entire detection and intervention process operated automatically, without human involvement. "What's notable is that the agent had never seen this scam. Deepfake giveaways tied to a live product launch weren't in its training," Coinbase said. BleepingComputer contacted Coinbase to ask how many transfers reached the scammers and how much cryptocurrency was stolen, but has not yet received a response. Elon Musk and his companies have long been popular lures for cryptocurrency scams, with fraudsters hijacking verified Twitter accounts, sending fake giveaway invitations via email, and flooding TikTok with fraudulent promotions. Scammers have also used deepfake videos of Musk to promote fraudulent cryptocurrency investment platforms, while a separate campaign involving compromised verified Twitter accounts stole more than $580,000 in cryptocurrency in just one week. To avoid falling victim to these types of scam campaigns, users should independently verify cryptocurrency promotions through official websites and social media accounts rather than trusting livestreams or QR codes displayed in videos. 1flzb7u.text: A reported cyberattack on Wellington IT has exposed sensitive information belonging to members of 50 credit unions, the majority of which are located in Ireland. Wellington IT is a Belfast-based supplier whose services are used by about 50 credit unions, including 43 in Ireland. While the company has not publicly disclosed a security incident, Minister of State Robert Troy confirmed to RTÉ that Wellington IT is the third-party service provider linked to the cybersecurity incident involving credit unions, resulting in the exposure of data from about 40 credit unions in Ireland. The company reportedly notified affected organizations of a data breach that posed a risk of financial fraud, impersonation, and targeted phishing to their members. According to the Irish Examiner, which saw the notices, Wellington IT informed customers that an automated script made five million requests to exploit an authorization flaw in the company's infrastructure. The attack unfolded between October 2 and 4, 2026, and the attacker accessed private records using valid credentials. However, the firm said it lacked activity logs that would specify which member data was compromised and therefore cannot verify the impact on individual payees. Minister R. Troy characterized the massive delay in Wellington IT notifying the credit unions as "not acceptable." At this time, the total number of impacted individuals is unknown. Sensitive information exposed At least six credit unions have independently disclosed impact linked to the incident, including Capital Credit Union, Phoenix Credit Union, St. Canice's Credit Union, First South Credit Union, Malahide Credit Union, and Limerick & District Credit Union. The announcements confirmed unauthorized access to payee information, with some noting that members' login credentials and funds haven't been affected, while others are working to determine exactly what was exposed. The notices list the following payee records saved in online banking platforms as potentially exposed: Payee name or name associated with the payee's bank account Nickname the member used to save the payee, if provided International Bank Account Number (IBAN) Bank Identifier Code (BIC) Bank account number Bank sort code Payee address information Payment reference information entered for the saved payee The records could also reveal which credit union member saved a particular payee. Account passwords, PINs, payment card details, and online banking credentials were unaffected, but union members are advised to remain vigilant for phishing and impersonation attempts. BleepingComputer has contacted Wellington IT to learn more about the incident, and we will update this post with their response once we receive it. 1v7l5x8.text: A flaw in NGINX's HTTP/2 support can allow an attacker to run code on servers with HTTP/2 enabled, without needing to log in. The decade-old flaw, CVE-2026-123007, dubbed "nginx2root," has been present in NGINX's open-source code since version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015.
