Fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 came out today. F5, the company behind NGINX, says attackers can run code where ASLR is turned off or can be bypassed. Security researchers at Wiz said they bypassed ASLR and ran code through the flaw in tests. Xint's researchers said they ran code through it with nothing more than a reachable HTTP/2 port. Code run this way gets the permissions of an NGINX worker process. Getting root on the host takes a second way to raise privileges, according to CIRCL, the Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg. In Xint's tests, code running as a worker could get root on the host through a separate bug in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, even when NGINX ran inside a Docker container. Neither the vendor nor the Wiz and Rapid7 researchers have reported any attacks exploiting the flaw so far. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog did not list it as of today. Proof-of-concept code for the flaw is publicly available on GitHub, but its notes state it is suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started Docker container on the same machine. Every open-source release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is vulnerable, according to NGINX's security advisories. That includes 1.31.8 from October 21, as well as the October 14 security releases 1.31.7 and 1.30.6. Wiz PoC NGINX Plus is affected too, in 37.x releases before the fixed builds and in R34 to R36, according to the vendor advisory. Today's releases also fix four more flaws that the vendor says can lead to code execution under the same ASLR condition. It scores all five 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0. Each flaw can be reached only in a particular setup: Flaw What it needs CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 turned on CVE-2026-123633 HTTP/2, with requests passed to a backend server while the worker is running low on worker_connections CVE-2026-123634 A proxied server name built from variables, plus a server-side include (SSI) or mirror subrequest to a location that looks up the same name CVE-2026-121810 HTTP/3 turned on CVE-2026-113425 NGINX used as a mail proxy HTTP/2 is on where a listen directive includes http2, or where http2 on is set. Running openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against a server shows whether it accepts HTTP/2: the output reads ALPN protocol: h2 if it does. Behind a CDN, test the NGINX origin itself, because an origin that accepts only HTTP/1.1 cannot be attacked through HTTP/2. Fixes, Workarounds and Signs of Attack These releases fix CVE-2026-123007, according to F5: NGINX Open Source 1.31.0 to 1.31.8 (mainline): fixed in 1.31.9 NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 to 1.30.6, including older branches such as 1.28: fixed in 1.30.7 NGINX Plus 37.1.0 to 37.2.0.1: fixed in 37.3.0.1 NGINX Plus 37.0.0 to 37.0.7.1: fixed in 37.0.8.1 NGINX Plus R34 to R36: no fix listed Versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix all five flaws, according to NGINX's release notes. On NGINX Plus, 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 fix four of the flaws, and the CVE-2026-123633 fix was introduced in the earlier builds 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1. After upgrading, restart NGINX fully or use its live binary upgrade. A reload alone leaves the old executable running, and existing connections can stay on old worker processes. The official Docker images for NGINX had 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 tags as of today, including Alpine variants. Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages as of today. Ubuntu's CVE status page listed nginx as vulnerable on its releases from 16.04 to 26.10, and Debian's security tracker listed it as vulnerable in bookworm, trixie, forky and sid. A distribution package can carry a fix without changing the version number that nginx -v reports, so compare the full package version with the distribution's own advisory. Xint PoC The vendor lists workarounds for only two of the five flaws. For the resolver flaw, CVE-2026-123634, avoid SSI and mirror directives, and do not build a proxied server name from variables. For the mail proxy flaw, CVE-2026-113425, limit listeners to trusted networks. CIRCL's response guidance lists turning off HTTP/2 as a temporary mitigation until you can upgrade. That blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, but not the other three flaws. Turning off HTTP/3 where it is used removes the setup that CVE-2026-121810 needs. On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in each affected server block and remove http2 from its listen directives. On 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove http2 from the listen directive, so listen 443 ssl http2; becomes listen 443 ssl;. Then restart NGINX where needed and rerun the openssl check to confirm the server no longer accepts HTTP/2. Until the Linux kernel's SCTP bug is fixed, the same guidance advises that hosts not using SCTP, a network transport protocol like TCP, block its kernel module from loading. One way is to add the line install sctp /bin/false to a .conf file in /etc/modprobe.d/. That does not unload a module already loaded or turn off SCTP built into the kernel. For signs of an attack, CIRCL suggests looking for NGINX workers that start unexpected programs, workers that exit abnormally or leave core dumps, long-lived HTTP/2 connections with heavy incoming traffic but few logged requests, and unusual outbound connections or DNS lookups. A clean access log does not rule out an attack, because HTTP/2 control frames do not normally show up there as requests. None of these signs is proof on its own. Rapid7's version of the attack needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, according to its technical analysis. The attack took two and a half minutes in its demonstration. On links slower than about 300 Mbit/s, the transfer would run past NGINX's default one-hour connection limit, and the attack would fail. The method also depends on a glibc memory-copy routine that is chosen on x86-64 CPUs with the avx512f and avx512vl features. Wiz ran its tests on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds, using HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems, according to its disclosure post. Xint's attack worked against its test servers on AWS, GCP and Azure, including over a public IP address, according to its research report.

1ta6vep.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 18, 2026Network Security / Vulnerability Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts. Each flaw needs a specific setup on a virtual server: an iRule that uses a particular command, or an APM policy that includes two particular kinds of agent. F5, which makes BIG-IP, disclosed the flaws today and says they may also allow remote code execution. The company has released engineering hotfixes and lists no workaround. The company rates all six 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.3 under CVSS v4.0. They are stack-based buffer overflows in BIG-IP's data plane, the part that processes almost all of its network traffic. The management side is not exposed, according to the company. None of the company's advisories says the flaws have been exploited. WatchTowr researcher Sina Kheirkhah reported four, and the company found the other two itself. Five of the flaws are in iRules, a BIG-IP feature that administrators use to manage traffic, and one is in BIG-IP's APM module. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and BIG-IP CNF, part of the company's BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition. Each flaw needs the setup listed below on a virtual server: CVE-2026-123637: an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents. Affects BIG-IP APM only. CVE-2026-121805: an iRule that uses PEM::subscriber on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP PEM, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF. CVE-2026-120292: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses MR::message route. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. CVE-2026-120285: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses PSC::ip_address. Affects BIG-IP (all modules), BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF. CVE-2026-116953: an iRule that uses GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. CVE-2026-120722: an iRule that uses DNS::scrape on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP DNS and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. The company's advisory lists BIG-IP CNF as not vulnerable, but its CVE record, updated today, lists CNF as affected. F5's security notification lists the 22 advisories it published today, including 10 for NGINX. For the six critical flaws, the only fixes are engineering hotfixes, builds that the company issues between its normal software releases. No scheduled release is listed as a fix, and the advisories provide no workaround until a hotfix is installed. The company warns that "engineering hotfixes do not undergo the extensive QA assessment of scheduled software releases." Its hotfix policy adds that they come with no warranty or promise that they will work. A system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from the company's support team. BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes is fixed in BNK-2.4.2-EHF1, BNK-2.3.4-EHF1 and BNK-2.2.5-EHF1, for versions 2.4.0 to 2.4.2, 2.3.0 to 2.3.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.5. BIG-IP CNF, on the same version ranges, is fixed in CNF-2.4.2-EHF1, CNF-2.3.4-EHF1 and CNF-2.2.5-EHF1 for CVE-2026-121805 and CVE-2026-120285. The company checks only versions that are still within technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe. Today's flaws differ from CVE-2026-94127, an APM flaw that F5 disclosed on September 22 and that was later exploited. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day. That flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow in APM setups that serve as OAuth authorization servers, allowing attackers to run code without logging in. Today's six are stack-based overflows that need different settings. Six Other BIG-IP and BIG-IQ Flaws Today's advisories also cover six lower-rated flaws in BIG-IP and BIG-IQ, each with its own fix. The scores below are CVSS v3.1: CVE-2026-125274 (iControl SOAP, 8.8): A user with network access and at least the Guest role can send an unauthorized management request. The company says this may allow them to run system commands, create or delete files, or disable services. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10 and 17.1.3.6, and in BIG-IQ 8.4.2.3. Until then, the SOAP advisory explains how to limit iControl SOAP access to trusted networks and warns that blocking it on self-IP addresses may break high-availability setups. CVE-2026-120718 (iControl REST, 8.1): iControl REST tokens may not expire as expected. An attacker who already holds a token may be able to extend how long it stays valid unless its owner deletes it. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.2, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6. As a workaround, scripts that create tokens can be changed to delete them when they are no longer needed. CVE-2026-125272 (APM, 7.5): When an APM access profile on a virtual server has a per-request policy with a form-based Logon Page, an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes as the six critical flaws. CVE-2026-126822 (APM SAML, 7.5): When an access profile is set up as a SAML Service Provider (SP), an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes. Until then, the company suggests removing the SAML Auth agent if SAML SP is not needed, and limiting access to that virtual server to trusted client networks. CVE-2026-126336 (APM SAML, 7.5): A SAML SP agent with encrypted assertions turned on lets an attacker crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6, and the company recommends a high-availability setup to reduce the impact. CVE-2026-121812 (APM and SSL Orchestrator, 7.5): A per-request policy with the tmm.access.policytrace database key turned on lets an attacker crash TMM. The key is off by default. APM is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes, and for SSL Orchestrator the advisory lists fixes on the 21.1 and 17.1 branches only.

rhcn9h.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 18, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack A critical security flaw in Apache Roller, an open-source, Java-based blogging platform, has come under active exploitation in the wild, according to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of unauthenticated deserialization in the XML-RPC endpoint that could lead to remote code execution. "Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code," project maintainers said. "The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester." ASF also noted that the vulnerability is the same as CVE-2026-82384 (CVSS score: 9.8), which was patched in September 2026 and listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. "This issue is being actively exploited," it added. ASF did not share any details on how the vulnerability is being exploited, or who is being targeted as part of these efforts. A security researcher named n0mi1k has been credited with finding the flaw, and Matt Raible has been acknowledged for reporting it. Users are advised to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled. If immediate patching is not an option, it's recommended to set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and then restart Roller. "Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting," ASF noted.

fqqind.text: The suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group behind the sophisticated EggStreme malware has rebuilt its toolkit as it continues to target government organizations in the Philippines. "When attackers are exposed, the cheap response is to rotate," Bitdefender said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "A file hash changes with every recompile, a domain costs a few dollars, and a new IP address costs less." "The EggStreme operators did more than rotate – the agent we now see uses a different network protocol, has an enhanced command set, and comes in a passive variant that never beacons out. The infrastructure appears to be moving away from the one certificate authority that tied its older servers together." The end result is that the changes allow it to bypass static signatures and heuristic detections built around the EggStreme malware framework when it was first exposed in September 2025. Delivered via an as-yet-unknown initial access vector, EggStreme's defining characteristic is the use of DLL sideloading to execute payloads. It features multiple components as follows - EggStremeFuel (aka RawCookie), which conducts system profiling and deploys EggStremeLoader EggStremeLoader, which sets up persistence and decrypts and executes EggStremeReflectiveLoader EggStremeReflectiveLoader, which executes EggStremeAgent EggStremeAgent (aka Gorem RAT), the core component and a full-featured backdoor that enables system reconnaissance, lateral movement, data theft via an injected keylogger called EggStremeKeylogger, and reverse shell and file upload/download capabilities via a secondary backdoor called EggStremeWizard It's worth noting that some components of the framework, such as EggStremeFuel and EggStremeLoader, have been put to use by another cluster tracked by Palo Alto Networks as CL-STA-1048 between March and September 2025. The latest findings from Bitdefender show a significant retooling of EggStreme's capabilities, including removing the keylogger from every agent build observed since then. Within two weeks after public disclosure, the threat actors are also said to have made other changes - The method EggStremeFuel uses to protect its configuration EggStremeLoader's cryptography and payload format, moving from RC4 to RC5 and to a custom cipher by the end of October 2025 Added commands in EggStremeAgent that facilitate Active Directory reconnaissance, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) querying, TCP traffic forwarding, and execution of PowerShell, Portable Executable (PE), .NET assembly payloads Moving from a single certificate authority to campaign-specific certificate authorities In addition, where lateral movement previously relied on Impacket-like tooling and on EggStremeAgent itself, newer incidents make use of an unmanaged system that sits outside of the organization's endpoint management but is still reachable by other workstations to stage the payloads and launch them via DLL sideloading using a Visual Basic Script (VBScript) file remotely run over Server Message Block (SMB). Some of the newer builds have been found to run in passive mode by opening a listening port and waiting for the operator to connect in as opposed to contacting an external command-and-control (C2) server. There is also some evidence that the attackers have also targeted Taiwan, but it has been treated with low to medium confidence. "The speed of the loader changes says as much about the operators' maturity as about the cost of exposure," Bitdefender concluded. "The build-time design appears to be what makes rebuilds this fast. What they did not change is how they operate: sideloaded DLLs under system library names, staging through file shares, running from memory, and requiring mutual TLS." Mustang Panda Targets Philippine Government Using ASEAN Summit Lures As of late October 2026, Philippine government officials have also been targeted by Mustang Panda, a prolific China-aligned cyber espionage group, using ASEAN Summit lures to deliver PlugX using established tactics like DLL sideloading. Mustang Panda attack chain "The package impersonated a Laos–Philippines bilateral meeting agenda from the Lao Ministry of Foreign Affairs," Dream Research Labs said in a report published last week. "It named five officials and referenced plausible diplomatic priorities, requesting that the reader provide confirmation before the summit. Behind it was a delivery chain that installed PlugX remote-access malware while displaying the decoy agenda." Earth Alux Uses Stealthy Tradecraft to Strike Southeast Asia The disclosure comes as a China-nexus threat actor tracked as Earth Alux (aka Ink Dragon, Jewelbug, REF7707, and UAT-11587) has been attributed to a fresh set of attacks targeting Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has assigned the activity the designation TGR-STA-0049 (formerly CL-STA-0049). "The defining signature of the threat actor behind the activity is the targeting of government entities, combined with the use of advanced custom payloads that are designed for high-stealth intelligence collection operations, with an emphasis on evading security detection tools," Unit 42 researcher Tom Fakterman said. Attacks mounted by the group have historically deployed an advanced backdoor known as FINALDRAFT (aka Squidoor) since 2023. However, it has since expanded its malware arsenal to include two previously undocumented remote access trojans (RATs) called PerfectPioneer RAT (in July 2025) and KUKURAT (in March 2026). Initial access to target networks is achieved via exploitation of vulnerable, unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers to deploy web shells like ASPXSpy and Godzilla, which are then used to deploy the RAT payloads. Alternatively, Earth Alux has leveraged phishing emails using decoy PDFs and lookalike domains to compromise victim hosts. PerfectPioneer RAT is a Go-based malware that's launched via three different methods - DLL sideloading to launch a malicious DLL that reads, decrypts and executes XOR-encrypted shellcode containing the RAT Decoy installers for Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect that installs the legitimate program but also writes the malware to disk and executes it in the background Disguising executable files as PDF documents in phishing emails that, once launched, opens a decoy PDF document while the malware is launched in the background The malware supports a number of features that enable the operator to gain remote control of the infected host. It facilitates file operations, shell execution, process management, keylogging, SOCKS5 proxy, screenshot capture, Window enumeration and manipulation, and CPU and memory utilization monitoring. PerfectPioneer RAT execution chain It also ensures a connection to the C2 server remains active at all times and systematically cleans up temporary files and runs garbage collection if memory usage exceeds 100 MB to minimize forensic traces. Furthermore, select variants of the malware come with an "isDangerousCommand" feature to avoid running administrative commands that would be highly destructive or noisy, thereby allowing it to be detected by security programs installed on the host. These include rm, curl | bash, wget | bash, and powershell -e, among others. KUKURAT, in contrast, functions as a modular implant that's executed in networks already compromised by PerfectPioneer RAT. Written in C++, the backdoor implements its functionality as a separate DLL module that's loaded dynamically at runtime directly from the C2 server. This allows the malware to be highly evasive and adapt its capabilities on the fly in response to shifting operational objectives. It supports the following features - Send system information and receive a configuration from the C2 server Take screenshots Log keystrokes Enumerate and terminate processes Perform file operations Execute shell commands via cmd.exe and PowerShell Conduct lateral movement via PsExec Carry out SMB credential brute-forcing Run Beacon Object Files (BOF) Facilitate local privilege elevation Ensure the malware remains active by means of a standalone watchdog executable What's more, KUKURAT initiates bogus, legitimate-looking activity on the endpoint to camouflage and cover up its tracks based on a command issued by the threat actor. This includes - Generate 10 decoy HTTP requests per operational cycle to randomly selected domains that are extracted from a hard-coded list of 15 popular websites using randomly generated URL paths with an aim to blend C2 communications Mimic legitimate Google Chrome browser behavior by writing random data to the registry path HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\BrowserCrashRecovery, reading the data back, and deleting the key Create temporary files with random names and randomized content inside the system %temp% directory, and delete them "Both PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT use HTTP/3 as the primary method for communicating with C2 infrastructure," Unit 42 said. "While the adoption of HTTP/3 is rare across the broader malware landscape, its deployment in this campaign reflects an emerging trend among advanced threat actors." The attacks have also been found to leverage established tools like PsExec, WMI, and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) to move laterally across compromised enterprise networks; collect credentials using Mimikatz, ProcDump, and SharpDPAPI; compromise Domain Controllers to deploy KUKURAT on local endpoints; and exfiltrate sensitive data such as files and emails. "Through the deployment of KUKURAT and the PerfectPioneer RAT, the attackers behind this activity are actively evolving to stay ahead of traditional network defenses by implementing protocol-level evasion via HTTP/3 and QUIC over UDP," Unit 42 concluded. "What makes this group particularly evasive is the extensive effort invested in maintaining operational security and remaining hidden on compromised endpoints. The group demonstrates a mature understanding of modern defensive ecosystems. They have even gone so far as to embed hard-coded administrative safety switches within their binaries to prevent their own operators from running loud or destructive commands that might trigger security alerts."

1dk4xjg.text: On AMD-based PCs and some Intel PCs, the TPM lockout for Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs can be reset by someone who opens the PC's case, researchers at Technische Universität Berlin say. That leaves short PINs open to guessing. In lab tests, the researchers found a four-digit Hello PIN on an AMD laptop and a 6-digit BitLocker PIN on an Intel laptop this way. Both PINs were set by the researchers and found within 236 tries. From the speeds they measured, they calculate a worst-case of 40 hours for a four-digit Hello PIN, compared to 69 days with the lockout working as documented. For a default six-digit BitLocker PIN, the worst-case time drops from 19 years to 20 days. AMD confirmed yesterday that its processor firmware has a flaw that allows the attack on some PCs with its chips. It plans fixes for most of those chips between November and February 2027. For now, the researchers advise adding at least two digits to Hello and BitLocker PINs. The TPM in these PCs is a firmware TPM, built into the processor. Unlike a separate TPM chip, it has no secure storage of its own, according to the research paper the researchers posted late last week. So it keeps its saved state, including the count of wrong guesses, encrypted on the mainboard's flash chip. If someone copies that saved state and later writes the old copy back, the count goes back too, unless the PC detects it. Newer PCs try to catch this with counters inside the flash chip, called RPMC, that can only go up. On AMD PCs that use these counters, the processor's firmware never verifies that a counter actually increased. A small board placed between the processor and the flash chip can block the update and report success, causing the PC to accept the old state. RPMC chips from flash maker Winbond have a different weakness, the researchers found. A brief drop in the chip's power supply, called a voltage glitch, can cause the chip to reveal the secret key that signs its counter values. With that key, which took about a second to extract with their best settings, the board can forge any counter value. On the Intel laptop they tested, one glitch was enough: the laptop's firmware feeds the chip the same value at every boot, so the leaked key kept working after each restart. For the Hello test, the researchers attacked a locked HP OmniBook 3 with an AMD Ryzen AI 5 330 processor and a BitLocker-encrypted drive. Their setup typed PINs from 1000 upward and reached the correct one, 1235, after 236 tries in 57 minutes. Windows still forced a restart after every 5 incorrect PIN attempts on that laptop, but no lockout delay was applied. Microsoft's lockout defaults lock the TPM after 32 wrong tries and forget one failure every 10 minutes. The BitLocker test ran on a Framework Laptop 13 with an Intel Core Ultra 5 125H processor and Winbond flash. BitLocker's startup prompt adds no limit of its own, so each reset gave a fresh 32 tries. The setup found the PIN, 123457, after 236 tries in 6 minutes and 55 seconds. In both tests, the researchers took the flash chip off the mainboard and wired in their own board. A script read the screen, typed PINs, and restarted the laptop through a KVM switch. They also changed firmware settings to slow each laptop's link to the flash chip, because their board could not keep up at full speed. The researchers make two further claims that their tests did not cover. Either method could be used against either PIN. A recovered Hello PIN can also unlock keys tied to the device and enable Hello-based single sign-on at work, and, in some configurations, pass a multi-factor check. The researchers have published their attack firmware, board designs, and scripts. They say reproducing the RPMC attacks is not plug-and-play and needs one of their boards. Neither the paper nor the vendor notices published so far describe attacks outside the lab. Which PCs the Attack Works On and What Vendors Say Whether the attack works depends on the processor and the flash chip: AMD-based PCs with RPMC flash: open to the board that blocks counter updates. The chipmaker has confirmed the firmware flaw behind this and plans to fix it. AMD-based PCs without RPMC flash: on two AMD desktops in the researchers' tests, writing an old copy back with an ordinary flash programmer reset the count, requiring no board. They conclude that AMD processors likely have no other protection against this, though two desktops may not be representative of all AMD systems. PCs that rely on Winbond RPMC flash: the researchers say these are open to the leaked-key method whatever the processor, and that only a new chip design can fix it. Intel PCs without RPMC-like flash: three Intel systems detected the same write-back in those tests. The researchers expect the AMD firmware flaw to affect AMD PCs that use the Microsoft Pluton security core as their TPM, but did not show this. On an AMD PC, the owner can boot Linux, for example from a live USB stick, and run the command grep . /sys/bus/pci/drivers/ccp/*/rpmc_* from the researchers' exposure check. The output indicates whether RPMC flash is present and enabled, which tells the owner which of the two methods applies. Missing files do not mean the PC lacks RPMC. For Intel PCs, the researchers know of no such check. Owners would have to open the PC and look for a Winbond chip marked 25R or 74M. AMD tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-43613 and assigns it a CVSS score of 5.1 in a security bulletin published yesterday. The chipmaker says attacks requiring physical access fall outside its product security threat model, but that "RPMC is intended to stop this type of interposer attack." The researchers first told it about the flaw in February. The chipmaker's fix targets run from November to February 2027 across Ryzen, Ryzen AI, Ryzen Threadripper, Athlon and EPYC chips, and one unnamed product has no date yet. These are planned dates for its own firmware, not updates already out for PCs. The bulletin does not cover AMD PCs without RPMC flash. It also does not say whether the update will prevent an attacker from installing older, unfixed firmware on the PC, which the researchers say a fix must prevent. Intel, whose processor was in the BitLocker test laptop, said in a security announcement earlier this week that the research "did not demonstrate a vulnerability in an Intel component". That matches the tests, in which the attack on the Intel laptop needed the Winbond chip's flaw. According to the researchers, Intel's security team called the reused value a weakness rather than a vulnerability. The researchers told Microsoft in April. According to them, the company rated the Windows Hello report as "moderate severity" and below its bar for an immediate fix, issued no CVE or bounty, and committed to raising its recommended minimum Hello PIN length to six digits. At the company's request, the researchers filed the BitLocker finding as a separate report for a different team. The company declined to give them any further written statement for the paper. Separately, a Windows 11 test build released late last week makes six digits the minimum for personal-account Hello PINs, with an option to use four. The release notes give no reason, and features in that test channel may never reach regular releases. According to the researchers, Winbond was first told about its chips' weakness to voltage glitches in January 2025 and received a second report in April showing that a glitch also leaks the key. The flash maker is studying the issue, possibly including a new chip design, but has not committed to a fix or a date. What Owners and Admins Can Do Two extra digits make a large difference in the researchers' figures: Worst-case time to find a numeric PIN PIN length With the documented lockout Hello attack (AMD laptop) BitLocker attack (Intel laptop) 4 digits 69 days 40 hours 5 hours* 6 digits 19 years 168 days 20 days 8 digits 1,903 years 46 years 6 years * BitLocker accepts a four-digit PIN only if an admin lowers the six-digit minimum. The times are worst cases calculated from speeds measured on one laptop each. In May, Microsoft advised moving BitLocker from TPM-only to TPM+PIN to block the YellowKey bypass, as part of its YellowKey mitigation. The same TPM lockout guards that PIN. Steps for each setup: Windows Hello for Business: raise the Minimum PIN length policy, under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > PIN Complexity. If it is not set, Windows requires six digits, a worst case of 168 days in the table above, and admins can set it as low as four. The PIN policy settings page lists it on the PIN settings tab. BitLocker: raise the Configure minimum PIN length for startup policy, which allows 4 to 20 digits and requires six by default. Turning on "Allow enhanced PINs for startup" lets letters and symbols, which the BitLocker PIN guidance recommends for older hardware. AMD-based PCs: install the firmware update with the chipmaker's fix when one is available for your PC. Until then, the chipmaker advises keeping PCs under physical control and watching for signs of tampering. PCs that rely on Winbond RPMC flash: the flash maker has not committed to a fix, according to the researchers. Intel advises its customers to ask their PC maker about updates.

1d9ubp3.text: The Hacker NewsNov 18, 2026Penetration Testing / Artificial Intelligence TL;DR Attackers move first. On average, exploitation now starts before a patch exists (Mandiant M-Trends 2026). In 1H 2026, 23% of vulnerabilities VulnCheck added to its exploited list were hit on or before disclosure day. AI pentesting vendors aren't interchangeable. Most look convincing in a demo. The gaps show up in your logged-in flows, your coverage, and your production safety. Make them prove it on your own web apps. Score each vendor on context, reach, validated findings, guardrails, and retests. Choosing an AI pentesting vendor? Get 15 questions, red flags, and a scorecard to test what vendors deliver, not just what they demo. Download the free checklist → AI is speeding attackers up For the first time, Google's Threat Intelligence Group identified a threat actor using a zero-day exploit it believes was developed with AI: a 2FA bypass rooted in a logic flaw that conventional fuzzing and static analysis can easily miss (GTIG). Agentic pentesting can close that gap, and 87% of US security leaders surveyed are planning, piloting, or using it. Choosing the agent is the hard part. Every Demo Looks Good. Your App Is the Real Test. Picture three agents that all demo well. The first finds real flaws but stops at your login page. The second navigates your app but can't answer a basic question: coverage of what? The third exploits real issues but has no hard limits for production. Each looks impressive on the vendor's target. The difference shows up on yours. A structured bake-off surfaces it before you sign. Ask What the Agent Knows Before It Attacks Every tester has to learn your site before the first payload. That recon is real attack work. The cost is redoing it from scratch on every engagement, when most of the map hasn't changed. In CyCognito's model, recon and analysis take 20 to 30 of a manual pentest's 63 to 95 hours. Agents differ here. Some start from a blank URL and rebuild the map on every run. Others start from an existing model of your site and keep it current between runs. Ask which one you're buying, what carries over between runs, and whether the agent keeps discovering beyond its starting map. A starting map should be a head start, not a boundary. Without context, an AI agent behaves like a smart scanner. With context, it can reason about your application. That changes what it finds, not just how fast. When a security researcher hunted for flaws in Apache Airflow, their AI assistant called the search a dead end. Testing how the deployment’s parts trust each other, instead of reading the code, turned up an unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2026-68982). Ask for Proof, Not Suspicion A suspicious pattern is not an exploitable vulnerability. Ask whether the agent exploits what it suspects, reproduces its findings, and hands over evidence your team can verify. A list of suspected issues is not a validated pentest. Here is what proof looks like. During an authorized assessment of a major insurer's production website, an AI pentesting agent found that the one-time passcode request could send login codes to any email address. It proved the flaw by logging in with a code sent to its own inbox, and guardrails then stopped the test. The insurer said it had pentested the site about six months earlier (Reflectiz case study on The Hacker News). Three Questions That Expose a Weak AI Pentesting Vendor A demo can look convincing without proving that the agent reaches your logged-in workflows, validates what it finds, or confirms your fixes. Here are three of the 15 checks to run before you choose. The other 12, covering starting context, coverage proof, attack chaining, access across roles, data handling, and guardrails, are in the full checklist. Run a Bake-Off, Not a Demo Demos run on the vendor's target. Bake-offs run on yours. Same target, same week. Same app, test accounts, and scope for every vendor. Log three timestamps. Access granted, discovery complete, first test. Score every check. The checklist's scoring sheet weights what matters and gates on safety. What's Inside the Checklist 15 checks, each with the question to ask and the red flag Checks for attack chaining, roles, guardrails, and retesting A 36-point scorecard and a per-check scoring sheet The best AI pentesting agent isn't the one with the best demo. It's the one that can show what it tested, prove what it found, and run safely on your application. Use these 15 questions to find it. Download the free AI Pentesting Checklist and vendor scorecard →

derguv.text: A Java flaw called Java4Shell can let attackers without an account run their own code on Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak, and three other widely used applications, says Calif, the security research firm that disclosed it this week. The flaw is present in Java 17.0.6 and later, and the vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 Intel and AMD chips that support the AVX-512 VBMI feature. Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, the fix was released today by Oracle and the OpenJDK project, whose open-source code underpins Java builds from many vendors. Amazon has fixed its Corretto Java builds, but Red Hat is still preparing fixes for its own. The researchers are holding back their attack code for the six applications, and other labs have so far reproduced crashes and a memory leak but not the code execution. Canada's Cyber Center said this week that it was not aware of any attacks exploiting the flaw. Servers often decode Base64-encoded data, such as HTTP Basic login headers, SAML artifacts, and CSRF tokens, before checking whether a user is logged in. That is how an attacker without an account can exploit the flaw. The flaw is in a faster version of Java's Base64 decoder that runs on chips with AVX-512 VBMI. Java switches to it after compiling the decoder for speed, which it does for code that runs often. A malformed string that ends with an extra = makes this decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past the end of its output. Java rejects the string, but only after the write. The bytes written past the end are fixed, so an attacker controls only where they land. For that reason, early readings of the source code had pointed to a crash rather than code execution, as The Hacker News noted in an earlier report yesterday. The attacks worked without a login under the default settings of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, Calif says in its technical write-up. The researchers' lists are incomplete, and they rate the flaw as 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. They get past the fixed bytes by arranging the server's memory so that the overflow expands a neighboring array. They then use that array to write bytes of their choosing and a second array to read back from memory, a step they call JavaBleed. From there, the researchers say, the attack reaches the parts of Java that run code. There is no single exploit that works everywhere. Each target requires its own memory layout and timing, and some attacks are sensitive to network delays. A proxy that waits for complete requests, as nginx does by default, blocks some attacks but not all. A failed attempt can crash Java, and an attacker can often try again. Security company Upwind reproduced the memory corruption on an AWS server with an Intel Ice Lake chip, where it damaged the next object in memory and eventually crashed Java, according to its lab results. Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group crashed a test Spring Boot application by sending about 28,300 malformed login requests over roughly 20 seconds, without ever logging in. The group also used the JavaBleed step in a local test to read a secret stored next to the overflow, which worked in all 30 runs. It did not reproduce remote code execution, its test results show. Oracle scores the flaw 8.1 out of 10 under CVSS 3.1, rating it hard to exploit but requiring no login. The description in its CVE record says, "Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE." Red Hat also rates it as requiring no login, with a preliminary score of 9.8 out of 10. Amazon scores it 8.8 out of 10 and describes the risk in its Amazon Linux entry as "a JVM crash for unauthenticated users or, in certain application environments, code execution by an authenticated low-privileged user." Canada's Cyber Centre also describes the flaw as exploitable remotely without authentication in its government alert. The flaw was not in the KEV catalog of exploited vulnerabilities, kept by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), when The Hacker News checked it today. Who Is Exposed The vulnerable code is in Java 17.0.6 and later on the Java 17 line, and in Java 21, 25, and 27. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 do not contain it, but the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf is affected. GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21.0.3, GraalVM for JDK 21.0.13.0.3, and GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.0.3 are also affected. It runs only on x86-64 chips that support AVX-512 VBMI. These include Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, and Granite Rapids chips, as well as AMD Zen 4 or newer chips. ARM64 chips do not run it. Because the vulnerable code runs only on these chips, the same container image can run it on one server and not on another. On Linux, this command shows whether a server's chip has the four features the vulnerable code needs, and all four must appear in its output: grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$' The attacker also needs malformed Base64 to reach Java's standard decoder, through paths such as the login headers and tokens described earlier. Calif also says a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if the program runs no service of its own. The exploit for this came from another researcher, samczsun, and the researchers have not published how it reaches the decoder. Fixes and Workarounds The OpenJDK project's vulnerability advisory lists the flaw as fixed in this week's releases, and Oracle's security advisory lists the affected versions of its builds. For Oracle Java, the fixed builds are the new .1 releases in the table, all released this week. The release notes for 17.0.21.1 say it includes the update's security fixes, and the notes for 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1 say the same. For the Java 8 Performance Pack, the latest build is 8u513, available in both standard and Performance Pack versions. For GraalVM, the November security releases are GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21.1, GraalVM for JDK 21.0.13.1, and GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.1. Java build Affected versions Fixed release Oracle Java SE 17 17.0.6 to 17.0.21.0.3 17.0.21.1 Oracle Java SE 21 21.0.13.0.3 and earlier 21.0.13.1 Oracle Java SE 25 25.0.5.0.3 and earlier 25.0.5.1 Oracle Java SE 27 27.0.1.0.3 and earlier 27.0.1.1 Amazon Corretto 17, 21, 25 and 27 Earlier builds, from 17.0.6 on for Corretto 17 17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2 and 27.0.1.1.4 Azul Zulu 17, 21, 25 and 27 Earlier builds, from 17.0.6 on for Zulu 17 17.70.201, 21.54.201, 25.38.201 and 27.30.201 (free builds) Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10, and Red Hat build of OpenJDK 17, 21 and 25 17.0.6 and later, including 21 and 25 None yet The Corretto changelog for 17.0.21.1.2 lists the flaw as fixed, as do the changelogs for the new 21, 25, and 27 builds. Amazon Linux also marks its Corretto 17, 21, 25 and 27 packages as fixed. Azul's November update fixes the flaw in Zulu 17, 21, 25 and 27, according to its Zulu release notes. Red Hat has not yet released fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10, or for its OpenJDK 17, 21 and 25 builds, according to its security bulletin. Containers based on its images need to be rebuilt once updated images are out. SAP released SapMachine 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1 this week, but their release pages do not specify what they fix. Eclipse Temurin, the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, and BellSoft Liberica had not listed fixed builds when The Hacker News checked today. Products that bundle their own Java runtime need an update from the product's maker. After updating, restart Java services, and rebuild and redeploy container images so the running process uses the new build. If you cannot update yet, start the JVM with one of these flags, and remove it once the fixed build is installed: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics turns off only the faster Base64 code, which removes the vulnerable path and leaves other AVX-512 speedups in place. -XX:UseAVX=2 turns off AVX-512 entirely. Use it only on x86-64 servers, because Java on ARM64 does not recognize it and will fail to start. In Upwind's lab, both flags stopped the overflow on every affected version it tested. The company warns that another flag, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, stops Java from starting when it is used on its own. To spot attempts, it suggests checking for the signs below, while warning that none of them proves a compromise and that their absence does not prove a server is safe: Base64 tokens of 32 characters or more that end in = and whose length is not a multiple of 4, especially in Authorization headers Bursts of IllegalArgumentException errors from java.util.Base64$Decoder Unexplained hs_err_pid crash logs or bursts of restarts A malformed input that triggers the overflow was posted publicly on September 9, in a proposed fix submitted to OpenJDK's code repository as a pull request. The proposal described an overflow in the same AVX-512 Base64 decoder code. Its author closed it without merging it in early November, after an automated notice that it had been inactive for more than eight weeks.

xv9x96.text: AI is speeding up how software is built, which means more code, more changes, and more chances for vulnerabilities to reach production. It's speeding up how attackers find and exploit them too, with time-to-exploit now down to a single day. Security testing has to keep up with both. AI pentesting has emerged as a way to run in-depth tests whenever teams need them, instead of waiting for the next scheduled pentest. To see how far adoption has come and what security teams need from it, Intruder surveyed 500 security and engineering leaders across the US and UK. Read on for the top findings. Only 4% of security leaders believe their current testing frequency gives them sufficient coverage 68% of organizations deploy code to production at least daily, and 37% deploy multiple times a day. Understandably, pentesting runs on a much slower cycle. Nearly half (47%) go more than a month between full pentests on their web applications and APIs. Those figures are for each organization's most frequently tested application, so the rest of their estate is tested less often still. Running a human-led pentest as often as code ships has never been realistic, largely because of the cost. But it means a vulnerability introduced in one release can go weeks or months without a pentest, and only 4% of security leaders believe their current testing frequency gives them sufficient coverage. 42% say they accept the risk and ship code without additional security checks between pentests Most teams cover the gap between pentests with a mix of approaches, but 42% accept the risk and ship code without additional security checks in between. Automated scanning in the build pipeline, more frequent manual pentests, internal AppSec teams, and AI-driven pentesting are each used by around half. Concern about the gap is widespread. 88% of leaders running scheduled pentests are worried about unmapped risk introduced between tests, and they split almost evenly on how serious it is. Half call it one of their largest unmanaged cyber risks, while the other half describe it as a known gap they're covering with basic perimeter controls. Fewer than 1% have no plans to try AI pentesting 55% of organizations already use AI pentesting across their environment, a further 36% have tried it but not yet adopted it at scale, and fewer than 1% have no plans to try it. For a category that has only emerged in the past two years, that's fast uptake. The largest organizations surveyed (5,000 to 10,000 employees) are furthest along, with 71% using AI pentesting across their environment. Midmarket organizations have tried it at a similar rate but scaled it less so far, at 54%. Only a quarter see AI testing quality as a top concern Security leaders need confidence that AI pentesting is safe to run on sensitive systems, and a way to check its work. The quality of AI pentesting isn't the main concern, with only a quarter naming it as one of their biggest barriers to adoption. The top barriers relate to how AI tools operate inside sensitive environments: data privacy (40%), safety on production systems (36%), and whether auditors and regulators will accept AI pentest reports (28%). Asked what would most damage their trust in AI pentesting, nearly half (46%) point to a lack of visibility into what was tested (25%) or a lack of reproducible proof of exploitability (21%). DevSecOps leads, who work most directly with the findings security tools produce, are the most skeptical — only 5% say nothing would damage their trust, compared with 19% of CTOs. 56% of teams spend six or more hours a week triaging false positives More than half of teams (56%) spend six hours or more a week validating findings from their security tooling. Working out whether a finding is real is the biggest remediation bottleneck, named by 44% of leaders, and one in five teams spend 11 hours or more a week on it, more than a full working day. Confirming fixes takes time too. Fewer than two in five organizations independently retest a fix in production as soon as it ships, and nearly half take up to two weeks. Until then, there's no way to know the vulnerability has actually been closed. This is the work AI-enabled validation is designed to cut, by confirming findings are exploitable before they reach the team and retesting a fix as soon as it ships. 90% agree the traditional annual pentest is dead Nine in ten security and engineering leaders agree that the traditional annual pentest is dead and that continuous AI pentesting is now required to keep pace. For most, it already is. Only 6% still rely on a single annual pentest. Looking three to five years ahead, most (54%) expect AI to handle the bulk of testing, and only one in six expect manual pentests to remain a primary method of security validation. 28% expect to keep manual pentests mainly to satisfy auditors, regardless of their technical value. What this means for security teams Until now, teams have relied on two kinds of testing, each with a trade-off. Scanning and DAST run often but are generic by design, so they miss flaws specific to how an application works. A pentest goes deep, but it's a snapshot of how the application looked weeks or months ago. AI pentesting brings the depth of a pentest, on demand. That changes what's possible across the testing cycle. Releases can be tested as they ship, instead of waiting for the next scheduled pentest. With findings validated before they're reported, teams spend their time on issues that are real, and fixes can be retested straight away. For teams looking to adopt it with confidence, a few steps help. Start in a staging environment that mirrors production. Run an AI pentest alongside your next manual pentest and compare the results. Look for findings that come with proof-of-concept code and a record of what was tested. And check how your code and data will be handled before you give it access. With AI speeding up how software is built and how it's attacked, AI pentesting makes it possible to keep pace with both. Get the full report or learn more about Intruder’s AI pentesting.

2w5an4.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 18, 2026Enterprise Security / Vulnerability The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical security flaw impacting Perforce Puppet, an enterprise infrastructure-as-code (IaC) and configuration management platform, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing reports of active exploitation. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS score: 9.4), is a case of deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution. "Perforce Puppet Enterprise contains a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Puppet's report-processing code that allows a client with any CA-signed agent certificate to execute arbitrary code on the Puppet Server as the service user by submitting a report containing a crafted rich-data type through a PUT request," CISA said. "If the certificate authority automatically signs requests without strong verification, an unauthenticated network attacker can obtain a valid certificate and exploit the vulnerability." The shortcoming impacts the following versions - Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.0 before 2026.0.1 Puppet Enterprise 2025.0.0 before 2025.12.1 Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.0 before 2023.8.13 Puppet Core 9.0.0 before 9.1.3 Puppet Core 8.x before 8.22.2 It was addressed by Perforce Software on November 3, 2026, in the following versions - Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1 (Puppet Core 9.1.3) Puppet Enterprise 2025.12.1 (Puppet Core 8.22.2) Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.13 (Puppet Core 8.22.2) Puppet Core 9.1.3 Puppet Core 8.22.2 It's worth noting that the issue also affects OpenVox, an open-source implementation of Puppet, and has been resolved in the following versions - OpenVox Agent 9.3.0 and 8.32.0 OpenVox Server 9.2.0 and 8.18.0 Alain Rödel, a security researcher at Neodyme AG, has been credited with discovering and reporting CVE-2026-115731 along with CVE-2026-115732 (CVSS score: 9.0), a critical certificate-name authorization bypass affecting both Puppet and OpenVox. The issues were discovered with artificial intelligence (AI) assistance and precise steering, the German cybersecurity company added. "The impact highly depends on the Puppet server configuration and the orchestration protocols used, if any are enabled at all," Neodyme said in a report published this month. "Independent of the configuration, an attacker with RCE on a Puppet server can grab the CA signing keys and impersonate other hosts." "Puppet is a powerful software, often with full access to a fleet of systems in a corporate network. Remote Code Execution on such a central and important system can lead to worst-case scenarios: Deployment of ransomware, mass data exfiltration, and potentially lateral movement to other parts of the network." As of writing, there are no details on how the vulnerability is being weaponized in the wild. However, a Reddit user named transdimensia noted in a November 4 post that it was being exploited shortly after public disclosure. "After finding a severely misconfigured CA in my fleet, I traced the actions backwards on a [CVE-2026-]115731 intrusion," the user said. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are advised to apply the fixes by December 1, 2026, to secure their networks under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

zz2b0x.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 18, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged organizations to immediately patch a newly disclosed critical security flaw impacting Oracle Java. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (CVSS score: 8.1), refers to a case of out-of-bounds write that can lead to denial-of-service (DoS) or remote code execution under certain conditions. "This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as 'Java4Shell,' affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK)," CISA said. "Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution." Patches for the flaw have been released by Oracle and OpenJDK. As of writing, there is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild. As reported previously by The Hacker News, Java4Shell can enable attackers without an account to execute arbitrary code on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, under default settings. Advisories for the flaw have been released by numerous security and software vendors, including Aikido, Amazon Linux, Blackpoint Cyber, Chainguard, Cisco Talos, Cycode, Datadog, Dynatrace, Endor Labs, Field Effect, Hadrian, Horizon3.ai, Miggo, Orca Security, Qualys, Rapid7, Red Hat, SentinelOne, Sophos, Tanium, Tenable, Upwind, VulnCheck, watchTowr, and Wiz. In an update shared on November 18, 2026, the Keycloak team said an instance can be considered at risk if the following conditions apply - It runs an unpatched OpenJDK build from 17.0.6 onward, including unpatched OpenJDK 21 and 25 builds Its x86-64 host or virtual machine exposes the avx512vbmi CPU feature to Java The running JVM has Base64 intrinsics enabled and has not been limited to AVX2 with -XX:UseAVX=2 "The x86-64 Keycloak container images tagged 26.8.2-1 and 26.8.2-2 bundle an affected OpenJDK 21.0.13 build," the team said. "These image tags alone do not establish whether your deployment is exploitable: check the CPU feature and effective JVM flags." "A Keycloak ZIP or TAR.GZ distribution started directly on a host can also be affected; the conditions depend on its Java runtime and CPU, not on whether it runs in a container." Keycloak is also recommending that users run the below command to check the CPU feature on a host or virtual machine - grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | grep -qw avx512vbmi && echo 'AVX-512 VBMI available' If the output of the command returns nothing, it indicates that the CPU does not expose AVX-512 VBMI and is not known to be affected by the flaw. Keycloak has released temporary mitigations that users can apply until it releases updated Keycloak and Keycloak Operator container images once patched OpenJDK builds are available for them. "The vulnerability could be reached through a local Spring Boot application using Spring Security," Blackpoint Cyber researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal said. "In this environment, approximately 28,000 unauthenticated HTTP requests carrying a malformed Base64 authentication value caused the JVM to terminate after roughly 20 seconds of sustained requests. Additional testing confirmed corruption of nearby Java objects and changes to live application data without necessarily causing an immediate crash." CISA is recommending that organizations take the following steps - Identify affected Java installations. Review software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available. "If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access," CISA said.

tza9no.text: Threat actors have compromised Microsoft's agent-framework package to push a credential stealer, according to reports from Aikido, Chainguard, Endor Labs, OX Security, SafeDep, Socket, StepSecurity, and Google-owned Wiz. The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published 33 minutes apart on November 17, 2026, and are designed to run a credential stealer on every Python start. As of writing, both the release versions have been quarantined on the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. It's unclear how the attacker managed to obtain publishing access. Agent-framework is the meta-package for Microsoft Agent Framework, an open-source framework for building and orchestrating artificial intelligence (AI) agents using Python. "Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint," Socket said in a report. Once either of the versions is installed, the package drops a .pth file in the site-packages root directory, which then gets executed automatically on every interpreter start, causing the credential stealer to run whenever Python is started in an environment, even if the package is not explicitly imported. "Each wheel adds a .pth file to site-packages," Endor Labs said. "Python executes import lines in .pth files on every interpreter start, so the stealer runs on any Python launch in an affected environment, including pip itself, whether or not anything imports Agent Framework." The names of the .pth files are below - agent_framework_meta.pth in version 1.26.1 af_runtime_diag.pth in version 1.26.2 The "agent_framework_meta.pth" file contains a single import statement referencing "agent_framework_meta," which then launches the stealer payload. It's capable of capturing the following data - Environment variables based on substring-based matching Credential files associated with Azure CLI (~/.azure/*.json), .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json, Hugging Face, Microsoft Azure DevOps agents, and .env and JSON files Azure DevOps OIDC tokens Azure managed-identity tokens Azure instance metadata and retains up to 8,000 characters of the response "Besides reading credentials already on disk, the code asks the platform to issue new ones," SafeDep said. "Rotating stored secrets does not cover those." "In an Azure DevOps pipeline, SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are enough to request a federated token for api://AzureADTokenExchange. On Azure compute, it asks the managed identity endpoint for an access token to each of these resources. It uses IDENTITY_ENDPOINT or MSI_ENDPOINT on App Service and Functions, and 169.254.169[.]254 elsewhere. It also pulls instance metadata." It's worth noting that the Azure instance metadata service (IMDS) is a RESTful web service that runs on a local IP address ("169.254.169[.]254"), and provides information about the virtual machine, its region, tags, and the identity token. All the collected information is saved into a JSON document, zlib-compressed, Base64-encoded, and sent via an HTTPS POST request to a hard-coded URL ("webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb"). Version 1.26.2, on the other hand, imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py, collects GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, and expands the search patterns used for harvesting credential-related environment variables. Given that the package attracts about 190,000 downloads a month, users are advised to perform the following steps - Isolate affected hosts and runners Pin the package to the most recent safe version (1.26.0) and restore from a clean environment Check for exposure to the malicious versions between 8:35 and roughly 9:20 p.m. UTC on November 17, 2026 Search proxy and DNS logs for requests to webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb Rotate exposed credentials from a clean system Audit Azure identities and review sign-in and activity logs Audit GitHub Actions workflows that deploy to Azure "The malicious agent-framework shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it," OX Security said. "While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside." Agent-framework is the second Microsoft-related PyPI package to be compromised this year. In May 2026, the threat actors behind TeamPCP pushed three malicious versions of durabletask, Microsoft's Python client for the Durable Task workflow execution framework, to distribute the Mini Shai-Hulud worm.

1ackw67.text: The Russia-linked cyber espionage group known as Cold Relic (formerly COLDRIVER and UNC4057) has been observed weaponizing a single cloud compromise into a launchpad for a series of linked intrusions resulting in third-party compromise. Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it investigated a 2026 compromise at a U.S.-based organization in which the adversary leveraged data, the corporate staff directory, and identities harvested from an earlier attack on another U.S.-based entity in late 2025. Cold Relic, also tracked as Callisto, Gossamer Bear, and Star Blizzard, has a track record of orchestrating sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns to gain access information that may be of strategic importance to the Russian government. The access is abused to register rogue multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices, passkeys, and MFA backup codes to establish long-term persistence and then conduct aggressive data collection and exfiltration operations targeting email, chat, and cloud storage repositories. In addition, the compromised access is used to target the victim's social and professional networks. Attacks mounted by the threat actor have successfully compromised high-value targets, including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across Europe and North America. "Once Cold Relic compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets," Google said. According to the tech giant's cybersecurity and incident response teams, Cold Relic compromised the cloud productivity environment of an unspecified U.S.-based organization in late 2025. Initial access to the network was achieved by means of a residential proxy network located in close geographical proximity to the victim. Using the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account and combining it with an MFA push notification fatigue attack, the threat actor is said to have gained access to the account after the victim accepted an MFA request. This was followed by the attacker registering their own device within the tenant to retain access. The threat actor was also observed using passkeys and MFA backup codes as alternate access mechanisms. "Cold Relic used the privileges of the compromised Super Admin account to download the contents of the entire organization's cloud storage drive by both mass sharing files to a Cold Relic-operated email account and downloading files directly," Google explained. "While operating inside the tenant of the victim organization, Cold Relic accessed the Admin Console, queried Admin security investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, and viewed, modified, and deleted Alert Center notifications to remove forensic evidence of the initial intrusion." These actions ultimately enabled the threat actor to export full employee lists and domain-wide data via the Google Takeout service using the Super Admin privileges. Following mass data theft, the attackers continued to maintain access over several months and perform additional activities - Sync email inbox via OAuth to external email clients. Re-authenticate using unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys that persisted across password and session resets and bypassed device registration controls. Target cloud drive document access related to credentials, email archives, personnel information, and other documents of interest. Even after the attackers were ousted from the victim organization, Google said it observed Cold Relic using email accounts impersonating employees of the victim organization to target both internal employees and associates within the same professional circles as part of a renewed social engineering campaign. The attack then moved to the next phase when the threat actor compromised a Microsoft Entra ID user account of a second U.S.-based organization that used Entra ID as its federated single sign-on (SSO) identity provider for Google Workspace. By impersonating an employee at the first organization, the threat actor established communications with the target over a secure messaging app and then shared phishing links designed to harvest credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID under the pretext of sharing a document containing details about a technical issue. "Upon successful authentication using the stolen credentials, Cold Relic registered and used a new MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion," Google said. "By impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the new target, Cold Relic increased their chance of phishing success. Ultimately, in this case, Cold Relic was able to obtain credentials to the organization and perform bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user's cloud drive." Upon successfully compromising the second organization, the messaging app account used to initiate the conversation had its profile name changed to a different persona. It's suspected that the new persona was likely used to target other organizations in the same professional network. "Cold Relic's campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."

aui57k.text: A malicious widget can bypass the security filter that Telegram added to its Android app last week and run code outside it, according to NebuSec, a security company. Widgets are small interactive blocks that bots send inside chat messages, and their JavaScript runs on the user's phone. The researchers ran their demonstration on a Telegram test server, because only approved bots can send widgets on the live service now. Bots could start sending widgets last week. Two days later, an account called V12 posted a video on X claiming that any Telegram message could now be used to execute remote code. Telegram then put QuickJS, the small engine that runs widget JavaScript, into its own process on Android. It also added a seccomp filter, which can block or record the system calls that the process makes. Both changes appear in the source code it published for Telegram for Android 13.2.2 (7303). NebuSec said in a technical analysis published earlier this week that its researchers got code running outside that filter in two separate ways. One uses a widget bug the filter does not cover, and the other chains a widget bug the filter does cover with a kernel bug. In their video, a bot's Telegram widget on Android 13.2.2 (7303) bypasses the filter and opens the phone's calculator app, the researchers say. Their write-up and their demonstration post on X do not say what the code could reach beyond that, such as the app's messages or the rest of the phone. They also do not say whether the user had to start the bot or tap the widget first. The researchers are holding back the details for now. Their write-up names no CVE identifier and does not say whether the bugs were reported to the app's developers. The widget documentation says widgets run in a sandbox, with rules such as no network access. Those rules live in the engine's own code, the researchers say. A single use-after-free or out-of-bounds write bug in QuickJS lets a script read and write the process's memory, and then the rules no longer protect anything. The new filter names a few dozen system calls, such as ptrace, bpf, and mount, and lets every other call through. The filter's source code leaves ioctl unfiltered. The filter sits on top of Android's own limits on the engine process. One process also runs every widget, so a hijacked widget from one bot shares memory with the widgets of every other bot, the researchers say. In the published source code for Telegram for Android 13.2.2 (7303), that filter is set to an audit mode, The Hacker News found. In audit mode, it still blocks attempts to start new programs or processes, but it only records the other listed calls and lets them run. A comment above the setting says how long that will last: "Audit until the logs from the devices say the engine never makes them." The published code does not show whether the version people install uses the same setting. "Yes, currently, general bots aren't allowed to use widgets even in private chats," a contributor to the telegram-bot-api project wrote late last week in a bug report thread on GitHub. As of this week, no later message in the thread says which bots are still allowed or that the limit has been lifted. The researchers' write-up lists no fixed version, and the published Android source code is no newer than 13.2.2 (7303) as of this week. "No one could be hacked just by receiving a message," Pavel Durov, Telegram's chief executive, wrote late last week in a channel post. His post addressed reports of code execution through widgets in the Android and Windows apps, and came before the researchers' demonstration. He added that a user first had to start a third-party service, and that even that was fully patched on the server side. The company had earlier said that the problem in V12's first demonstration was fixed and that the fix had reached all users. Separately, the security vendor Kaspersky said late last week that it had detected suspected exploitation of a flaw in Telegram widgets when people visited some Telegram channels. In that activity, a PowerShell script ran without the user noticing and downloaded and launched WebRAT, also known as Salat Stealer. The malware allows attackers to control the infected system and steal data from crypto wallets and Telegram accounts. The vendor's malware warning does not identify the flaw or the Telegram version, does not report the number of victims, and does not link the activity to either demonstration. It advises not running widgets until a fix is released.

ukjh1b.text: Oracle is preparing to release security patches for 11 vulnerabilities in Java SE on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, all of which may be exploited remotely without authentication, as separate reports warn of a potentially critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw affecting OpenJDK. The 11 vulnerabilities carry a maximum CVSS 3.1 severity score of 8.1, according to Oracle's advance security notice. The company has not disclosed their CVE identifiers, affected components, or the individual consequences of exploitation. The separate OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, has reportedly been assigned a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 and affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later. However, those details remain unconfirmed, and there is no evidence yet that the reported flaw is among the 11 vulnerabilities Oracle plans to patch. Security firm Calif said in a post on X that it discovered and reported the flaw, which it calls Java4Shell, and that the vulnerability had leaked. Calif said it would publish technical details by 1 p.m. Pacific time on November 17, after Oracle releases a patch. Security company watchTowr acknowledged the reports in a post on X, but cautioned that the technical details were still unconfirmed. Separate analyses of the OpenJDK source code by security companies Upwind and Equixly point to a flaw in Java's Base64 decoder whose likely result is a crash of the Java virtual machine (JVM) rather than code execution. The vulnerability's CVE record remains reserved without a public description. No official advisory has specified the vulnerable component, precise exploitation requirements, affected version range, or the availability of a fix. Oracle's ops.java site now lists the replacement builds below as its current releases. Oracle's advance notice, release notes and download page still showed the earlier builds as of 16:59 UTC. Oracle Prepares Java Security Updates Oracle advises customers to stop using its current builds of Java 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, and 27 after the November 17 security update and move to the corresponding replacement releases. The company's Java release notes contain the update guidance, while ops.java lists the following planned builds: Java line Current build Planned build Java 8 8u511 b33 8u513 Java 11 11.0.33.0.3 11.0.33.1 Java 17 17.0.21.0.3 17.0.21.1 Java 21 21.0.13.0.3 21.0.13.1 Java 25 25.0.5.0.3 25.0.5.1 Java 27 27.0.1.0.3 27.0.1.1 The November security notice identifies the following affected Oracle products and versions: Oracle Java SE: 8u511, 8u511-perf, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1. Oracle GraalVM for JDK: 17.0.21 and 21.0.13. Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. Oracle JavaFX: 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1. Oracle says all 11 Java SE vulnerabilities may be exploited over a network without requiring credentials. That does not necessarily mean they all allow remote code execution or that every application running an affected Java version can be attacked directly. The advance notice does not identify the vulnerable Java components or specify what an attacker could accomplish by exploiting each flaw. Oracle also warns that the information may change before the complete security advisory is published. Critical OpenJDK RCE Report Remains Unverified The reported CVE-2026-114938 vulnerability introduces a separate concern for organizations operating Java applications, particularly those exposed to the internet. However, the public information does not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed. However, Oracle's notice and the OpenJDK advisories do not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed. Upwind said in a technical analysis that its reading of the OpenJDK source points to a flaw in Java's AVX-512 Base64 decoder, and Equixly reached the same finding in a separate analysis. The flawed code runs only on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support, when untrusted data reaches the basic or URL decoder of java.util.Base64. ARM servers do not run it. The code is in Java 17.0.6 and later and in Java 21, 25 and 27, but not in standard Java 8 or 11. A crash is the likely result because the bytes written past the buffer are fixed and not chosen by the attacker. Neither firm reported reproducing the overflow on AVX-512 hardware.
