Oracle's 8u371-perf release notes show that its Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack added a "Base64 Decoding optimization for x86 using AVX-512". Neither firm said whether the Performance Pack is affected. Both firms named two JVM options as stopgaps to keep the flawed code from running: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which turns off the Base64 intrinsics, and -XX:UseAVX=2, which turns off all AVX-512 code paths and can slow other work. Neither option has been confirmed by a vendor for this flaw, the firms said. Oracle's November notice covers Oracle products and does not establish the patch status of third-party OpenJDK distributions. The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group, which coordinates security disclosures affecting OpenJDK source code, had not published an advisory newer than October 24 at the time of the earlier review. Until official details are available, organizations cannot determine from the reported CVE alone whether their Java deployments are vulnerable or which specific update addresses the issue. Oracle began a monthly security patch cycle on May 28, introducing targeted security releases between its quarterly Critical Patch Updates. Its Java security update plan, last updated September 10, identified November 17 as the next scheduled monthly release. Organizations should inventory deployed Java runtimes, identify internet-facing applications, and prepare to test and install the relevant vendor updates once they become available. This is a developing story. We will update this article as Oracle publishes its full vulnerability advisory and additional verified details about CVE-2026-114938, affected versions, and available patches emerge.

1bvv2h5.text: Artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, and logistics sectors across Europe and the U.S. have emerged as the target of a large-scale, industrialized campaign dubbed Trigram. "Trigram is a large-scale campaign that impersonates about 50 brands in the blockchain and AI sectors, to trick developers into executing an infostealer themselves," Stormshield said in a deep-dive technical report published Monday. "Three social engineering scenarios (recruitment, conference, and package tracking), a software supply-chain compromise, and trojanized code repositories all converge on the same infrastructure and the same payload." The activity is assessed to share similarities with intrusion sets linked to North Korea, particularly Kimsuky and UNK_DeadDrop. Some aspects of this campaign have been previously documented by Proofpoint, SafeDep, Jamf, and Genians Security Center. It's worth noting that the cluster tracked as UNK_DeadDrop exhibits similarities with a long-running North Korea-aligned campaign referred to as Contagious Interview. It employs phishing emails using developer role recruitment or code review themes to target developers across finance, cryptocurrency, education, and technology sectors to deploy an information stealer. On Linux and macOS systems, the attack chains lead to the deployment of Overlord, an open-source remote access trojan (RAT) framework to facilitate data theft. Then, in August 2026, Jamf Threat Labs disclosed details of a macOS campaign using a fake Zoom installer to deploy Overlord RAT, although the Apple device management company said at the time that it found no "direct overlap" between the activity and UNK_DeadDrop. "The Overlord variant observed here shares a LaunchAgent label (com.zoom) and plist name (com.zoom.plist) with FlexibleFerret, a DPRK-attributed macOS malware family associated with the Contagious Interview campaign," it added. Overlord has also been distributed as recently as late October 2026 via another channel: a forged commit in the antd-img-crop GitHub repository that installs the malware by means of a prebuild hook ("prebuild.js") as soon as a developer runs the "npm run build" command. The npm package in itself was not impacted. The JavaScript payload is designed to download and run a fake installer that sets up Node.js and fetches an encrypted JavaScript next-stage that runs entirely in memory and locates its command-and-control (C2) server via a GitLab dead drop. The third-stage malware is responsible for harvesting credentials and installing the OverLord framework. "The malware steals browser passwords, cookies, keychains, cryptocurrency wallets, SSH keys and .env files on macOS, Linux and Windows, then installs a remote-access agent disguised as Google software," SafeDep said in an analysis of the malware. The forged commit pushed to "antd-img-crop⁠" on October 31, 2026 On macOS and Linux systems, it also displays a fake dialog asking users to enter their system password so as to "apply system updates and verify drivers and security settings." Interestingly, the same payload is delivered via two other initial access vectors - A fake careers portal impersonating Amber Group, a legitimate cryptocurrency firm A sideloaded Microsoft Visual Studio Code (VS Code) or Cursor extension named "google-dev-tools.google-update-support" that's likely launched via a coding assessment and deleted after it's run "The fake recruiter, the paste-a-command 'verification' step and the focus on developers and cryptocurrency holders match the publicly documented Contagious Interview campaign," SafeDep said. "The match rests on technique and does not prove who the operators are." The third branch of the campaign revolves around another cluster tracked by Genians as Operation GitPower. Attributed to the Kimsuky group, the activity involves operating local large language model (LLM) environments using Ollama and GPT4All to generate decoy documents and use them to target professionals and organizations in the fields of policy, academia, international cooperation, diplomacy, and security research. Present within the phishing email is a Windows Shortcut (LNK) that, once launched, runs PowerShell code designed to retrieve the lure document via GitHub's raw content service and open it, while stealthily downloading additional payloads like AsyncRAT in the background. Kimsuky's use of GitHub for C2 The campaign has since evolved to target Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security, and international policy, utilizing international conference invitations and requests for analytical collaboration to elicit responses from targets and eventually distribute malware in the form of ZIP archives containing malicious LNK files. In at least one case, the phishing emails have been found to trick recipients into clicking on bogus links to harvest their Google account credentials under the pretext of joining a Zoom meeting via Gmail. Another method involves distributing a counterfeit version of a Zoom installer that, in addition to installing the legitimate app, runs malware designed to run arbitrary PowerShell scripts and send the results back. "This attack is particularly noteworthy as it indicates that Kimsuky has expanded its targeting scope beyond its traditional focus on South Korea to include key individuals in Ukraine," Genians noted last month, adding these efforts were mostly unsuccessful. "Kimsuky's attacks against Ukraine may be cyber espionage operations aimed at collecting information on the war, the extent of North Korean troop losses, developments in the questioning and handling of prisoners of war, and the details of consultations between South Korea and Ukraine." The latest findings from Stormshield merge together all of these separate findings into a single, cohesive picture - a toolset comprising a management platform, victim-tracking consoles, and email-delivery infrastructure. The attack chain is a single infection chain that's adapted for three environments - Send the target an email advertising a job opportunity, entice them into clicking a link, and initiate the "recruitment" process. The website masquerades as a recruitment platform where visitors can view job listings and submit job applications. In the background, the web page fingerprints the visitor and uses an IP address-based geofencing mechanism to lock out users from specific regions (possibly China). If access is restricted, users are served a stripped-down version of the home page without any ability to interact with it. If the "applicant" satisfies the filtering criteria, they are served an application form to enter their personal details. The user is then prompted to enter a referral (or invitation) code, indicating that the campaign is aimed at pre-identified targets rather than a broad audience. If the code is rejected, the site displays one of three messages: "Already used," "Locked to another IP," and "Invalid code." If the code is accepted, the candidate is served a confirmation message and is instructed to copy and run a command on the Linux terminal as part of a technical check. Once the command is run, it sends the "nonce" information displayed on the web page to a remote server via an HTTP POST request. No file or script is downloaded or executed on the victim machine at this stage. The web page, which is waiting for confirmation from the server, responds with an error message, stating: "Operation timeout. Please try again. Nonce Refreshed." The attack moves to the second stage when the web page displays the same verification screen but with a modified "Copy" button behavior that injects the malicious command directly into the victim's clipboard. The same pattern is observed even when the target uses the "Ctrl+C" keyboard shortcut to copy the command from the web page. The actual command that gets executed depends on the operating system - On Windows, it launches PowerShell to download and run a file named "v.cmd" On Linux, it launches bash shell to download and run a file named "u" On macOS, it launches bash shell to download and run a file named "verify_m” "These scripts act as loaders: they prepare the execution environment, retrieve the necessary components, and launch a JavaScript payload, install_guard.js, fetched from a remote server," the French cybersecurity company explained. Trigram dropper execution phase This preparatory stage also involves extracting a Base64-encoded script that configures the working directory, establishes a locking mechanism to prevent concurrent installations, and checks for an existing Node.js installation. If a compatible version (minimum version 18) is not found, it proceeds to download and install Node.js version 20.18.1 based on the infected host's operating system and its architecture. It then downloads "install_guard.js," which deploys an infostealer tasked with collecting system metadata, browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and sensitive files present on the machine. The entire operation is powered by a multi-layered architecture comprising fake recruitment (like Amber Group), conference invitation, and package delivery sites; C2 servers that host the JavaScript and are fetched by means of a GitLab dead-drop; and the back office hosted on "170.205.30[.]27:8000" that enables campaign management and victim tracking via a platform called "rms-platform." The tracking console records every action undertaken by the user, while simultaneously keeping tabs on bot visitors and lookalike domains that have been taken down. Each "real visitor" is then rated "important," "moderate," or "useless," suggesting some sort of shortlisting based on their value. Further analysis of the API routes associated with "rms-platform" show that it's capable of identifying potential targets by scraping GitHub profiles, sending phishing emails, managing decoys, issuing access codes, viewing and exporting collected data, and cryptocurrency wallet monitoring. Trigram infrastructure architecture "These three levels rely on abused legitimate services: GitHub and GitLab for code and configuration hosting; Brevo, Resend, Mailgun, and Smartlead for email delivery; and FullStory for visitor session recording," Stormshield explained. "The tracking consoles are not standalone applications: they are delivered within the same JavaScript code as the decoys. The same bundle is served to all visitors, and a check on the hostname or URL path determines which interface is displayed." The technical indicators that point in the direction of UNK_DeadDrop and Kimsuky are listed below - eros1030109@gmail[.]com, a super-administrator account for the consoles that matches with an email address used in Operation GitPower. 0xapp123, a Medium account that discusses Web3 trends and lists "eros1030109@gmail.com" as the contact email address as far back as June 2022. silviattech1129_db_user, an identifier that appears as a username for a MongoDB database associated with "rms-platform" and in the history of the GitLab dead-drop file used in the "antd-img-crop" repository hijack as "silviattech1129." alexlopez-g/rms-platform, a backup GitHub repository hosting "rms-platform," with the user having contributed to a separate project named "Foxtopia-NFT/foxtopia-frontend" that includes a ".vscode/tasks.json" file mirroring tactics outlined in UNK_DeadDrop. The commit is signed with an email address "harper.danie95@gmail[.]com," which has been used to target designers on Contra with fake job offers. asteara[.]org, a domain flagged as "related infrastructure" for UNK_DeadDrop that has been used to host or serve the Trigram back office. pichi_finance_hr, a Telegram account that impersonates the human resources department of Pichi Finance, a decentralized finance (DeFi) platform that went offline in January 2025, and is likely used as a way to approach targets by posing as recruiters. "Based on these infrastructure and tooling overlaps, we assess with high confidence that Trigram represents a continuation of the UNK_DeadDrop cluster, while illustrating an evolution in its delivery tactics," Stormshield concluded. "Trigram stands out through the diversification of its initial access vectors and the remote retrieval of its final payload, rather than embedding it directly within the trojanized repository." "This system automates the targeting of users on GitHub, orchestrates massive phishing campaigns through four email providers, monitors the compromise of each victim in real time, and launders the stolen funds through cryptocurrency wallets."

1wvbpq4.text: The Hacker NewsNov 17, 2026Supply Chain Security / DevSecOps Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it. In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check. The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it. The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it. That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't. Immutability Is Not Provenance Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected. GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it. But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered: Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned. Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project. Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen. With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely. GitHub's Lockfiles Help. They Don't Finish the Job. GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later. That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server. Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you. What You'll Learn Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers: What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions Who Should Attend Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you. Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either. Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning, pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

11we243.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 17, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security A now-patched flaw in Apple's audio service let apps on iPhones and iPads record audio even after the user tapped "Don't Allow" on the microphone prompt. The first security updates with the fix came out on August 17. Neither Apple nor the two researchers who found the flaw report that it was used in attacks. Nik Tsytsarkin of Meta Red Team X published the technical details last week. Mustafa Calap, a security engineer who reported the same flaw separately, published his own analysis the same day. On iPhones, an orange indicator shows when an app is using the microphone. On one of the researchers' earlier test builds, that indicator stayed off while the app recorded. In Tsytsarkin's tests, the prompt appeared the first time the app opened. Declining it did not stop the recording, and the prompt did not reappear on subsequent launches. In the earlier build of his technical analysis, the system logs showed no record of the app using the microphone. They named the audio service itself as the recorder. His demo video shows the indicator while the test app records with no microphone permission. He wrote that the video "was filmed on a later build that appears to have restored the orange microphone indicator." Calap's test app recorded while its permission still read denied, according to his detailed write-up. No orange indicator appeared in the Dynamic Island or in Control Center. He does not say which of his two test builds that was. Neither researcher describes a way for users to check whether an app recorded them before the fix. Calap reproduced the bypass on iOS 26.6, released July 27, and on an iPadOS 27 beta. The bypass needed an app already installed on the device. His two test apps were sandboxed apps with no added entitlements. Their only privacy key was NSMicrophoneUsageDescription, which makes the microphone prompt appear. In his tests, recording had to start while the app was in the foreground. Once started, it continued after the app went to the background and after the device was locked. The background version also set UIBackgroundModes = audio. Both apps were installed from Xcode and never went through App Review. So the tests do not show whether App Review would have stopped such an app. The Meta analysis compared two iOS 27 test builds. Neither researcher reports testing macOS, tvOS, watchOS, or visionOS, though fixes are listed for those systems too. The bypass covered microphone capture through the audio service only. It did not give the app other privacy permissions. These releases fix the flaw, which is tracked as CVE-2026-65339: iOS 26.6.1 and iPadOS 26.6.1 (August 17), for iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 3rd generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 1st generation and later, iPad Air 3rd generation and later, iPad 8th generation and later, and iPad mini 5th generation and later iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 (October 26), for iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and iPad 7th generation macOS Tahoe 26.6.2 (August 17) macOS Sequoia 15.8 (September 14) tvOS 27 (September 14), for Apple TV 4K 2nd generation and later watchOS 27 (September 14), for Apple Watch Series 9 and later visionOS 27 (September 14), for Apple Vision Pro (all models) The researchers describe no setting that blocks the bypass, so installing these updates is the fix. The iOS 27 notes do not list the flaw, nor do those for later iOS 27 updates as of today. Meta's timeline says the fix shipped in iOS 27.0 beta 5 on August 10. CISA gives the flaw a CVSS score of 5.0 out of 10. The agency's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities does not list it, as of the catalog's update late last week. Apple's notes for the August 17 updates describe the flaw only as one that may let an app leak sensitive user information. Tsytsarkin wrote: "That description leaves out the most striking part: the app could record after permission was denied, without the orange indicator appearing." In his own tests, the indicator was missing only on the earlier build. An app does not decide for itself whether it may record. That decision goes through the Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC) system, which checks which process is asking. The audio service, called audiomxd, accepted the app's own word about which process was asking. An audit token identifies a process. An app could send the service a token that named audiomxd itself. The service then treated the app as itself. It took a shortcut meant for its own internal audio and allowed recording without asking TCC. The kernel itself provided the app with the details it needed to impersonate the service. The fix makes the service check the real caller's identity, which the kernel supplies. Outside callers now need the private entitlement com.apple.private.audio.client-audit-token-override to replace the client identity the service relies on. An app cannot grant itself that entitlement.

4vhjcc.text: Government sectors in Asia and Africa have been targeted by an active cyber intrusion campaign that delivers to previously undocumented backdoors that leverage legitimate services like Microsoft SharePoint and GitHub for command‑and‑control (C2). The activity has been codenamed Operation ShadowCloud by Kaspersky. The Russian cybersecurity company said it identified the campaign in early 2026. "The threat actor behind it is abusing the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two brand-new backdoors," Kaspersky researchers Saurabh Sharma and Noushin Shabab said in a two-part analysis. "These implants hide their command‑and‑control (C2) traffic behind cloud services Microsoft SharePoint, GitHub, and Ably, allowing the implants to blend in with normal traffic, effectively evading network-based detections." The modular backdoors, dubbed GraphDoor and GitDoor for their choice of the cloud platform used for C2, enable the download of additional plugins on demand and the execution of shellcode directly in memory to extend their functionality. Traffic between infected systems and the C2 servers is proxied by deploying a modified Erfrp client and Ably messaging service-based plugins. The starting point of the attack has been traced back to a MeshCentral Agent, a legitimate remote access tool that's used for remote desktop control, command‑line access, and file management. The attack is said to have targeted an unspecified Taiwanese organization. The exact method by which the utility is installed on the host remains unknown. However, signs point to the "reuse of a prior infection already present on the network," Kaspersky added. The MeshCentral Agent is configured to contact a hard-coded C2 server ("wss://27.102.66[.]162:443/agent.ashx") and then fetch three payloads staged on the endpoint - A legitimate binary used for DLL sideloading (start.exe, pythonw.exe, and zoomit.exe) A rogue loader DLL used to unpack and execute the next-stage malware (jli.dll, SbieDll.dll, python39.dll, WINMM.dll, and libcef.dll) An encrypted file containing the core payload At least two different DLL loaders have been identified to date, each employing its own method to decode and launch the encrypted backdoor payload by injecting it into the current process's memory. "Loader (Type 1) employs a hybrid scheme: first running the data through an RC4 stream cipher and then applying an XOR mask, while Loader (Type 2) simplifies the process by using a straight XOR operation alone," Kaspersky noted. The end goal is to deploy backdoors like GitDoor and GraphDoor, which employ a number of encryption and obfuscation techniques like control flow flattening and nested helper functions to complicate analysis efforts and make it harder to trace genuine execution flow. GitDoor, as the name implies, uses GitHub for C2. It relies on two distinct repositories for receiving command payloads ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo") and uploading the results of the execution ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix"). While the Havo repository is public, the Trix repository is private. The creation date of these repositories suggests that preparations for the campaign have been underway since at least the end of 2024. GitDoor supports 26 commands that allow the backdoor to - Perform file management Log keystrokes Launch a proxy, including using Ably Load shellcode to Base64-encoded Common Object File Format (COFF) binaries and terminate the backdoor The custom shellcode feature is used to download and run different modules that facilitate the following functions - Conduct process injection using methods like Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) injection Enumerate and manage Windows services List files and directories, wipe file contents, and recursively delete a directory Conduct network-related activity by displaying active TCP connections and modify firewall rules Manage processes, including dumping the memory of the process with a specified process ID into a file and terminating specific processes Execute commands using "cmd.exe" Enumerate, create, and run scheduled tasks Enumeration Windows Registry keys and values recursively and set a value in the Registry Extract user information, along with local groups and its members Add of a new Windows user account or add a user to a global or a local group Record keystrokes to a file ("%APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat") Dump cookies from Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge directly from the process memory using CookieKatz Use Mimikatz to dump credentials from Windows LSASS Capture screenshots of the entire screen or a specific window identified by its process ID Extract WhatsApp's database decryption key Initiate NTLM authentication to an attacker-controlled destination Calculate system idle time and display the last time a user was active on the host using mouse movement and keyboard input GraphDoor, on the other hand, opens a named pipe, creates a directory named "Intel_Log" inside the system's Application Data folder, and gathers system information to send back to the attacker. To establish communications with the C2 server, it authenticates with a malicious application using "login.microsoftonline.com" on port 443 and uses the access token to communicate with the Microsoft Graph API and ultimately stage the data on the SharePoint drive. The malware then fetches three plugin modules from the server and launches them in parallel to carry out screenshot capture, process listing, and keylogging. It also proceeds to reestablish contact with the SharePoint website to retrieve the commands to be executed on the machine. The complete list of plugins supported by GraphDoor is as follows - kl.ts, to log keystrokes at "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat" pr.ts, to list running processes scr.ts, to take screenshots of the window that matches a supplied process ID and save them as JPEG images moveDir.ts, to move the legitimate executable, the malicious loader DLL, and the encrypted backdoor file to specific target path channel.ts, to launch the proxy abchannel.ts, to use the Ably messaging service to proxy traffic ab2channel.ts, a covert SOCKS5 proxy that tunnels TCP traffic through Ably's Pusher‑compatible WebSocket service In addition, GraphDoor's custom shellcode capability expands on GitDoor to support two additional commands that allow it to run commands using "cmd.exe," as well as MZ executables. The identity of the threat actor behind the campaign is unknown, but Kaspersky said it shares some degree of overlap with a China-nexus activity that Sophos tracks under the moniker Bronze Sandcastle. Tactical similarities have been observed with prior campaigns undertaken by FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle (aka BlackTech). "On several victim systems, these groups shared the same staging directories as the GitDoor backdoor, with their implants deployed within a one-day window of GitDoor deployment," the company concluded. "While this does not prove a direct link, it suggests that a Chinese-speaking group may be developing and/or utilizing the GitDoor and GraphDoor backdoors." "By using cloud-based storage and messaging services, the actors blend in with normal traffic (as cloud API calls to Microsoft Graph, GitHub, and Ably are indistinguishable from legitimate enterprise usage, evading many network-based detections), and enable dynamic payload delivery, where on-demand plug-ins and shellcode are retrieved from cloud repositories, allowing for rapid updates and functional extensions without modifying host files."

1f1xh75.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 17, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Data Privacy Apple on Monday introduced new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents. The changes, currently previewed in macOS 27.3 beta 2, relate to increased transparency and more options for two of its APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. "Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk," Apple said in a statement. "These changes are designed to help them do that and to empower them to make informed decisions about their own data and privacy." To that end, Device Control and Data Access is being split into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. Other changes include - A single method for granting permissions by selecting the requesting app from a list Encouraging users to grant access to just the specific apps (for System & App Protection Override) or folders (for Full Disk Access) that are required for their workflows Increased visibility into the range of data that apps will receive access to or have control over when users grant full permissions An option for users to configure apps to ask every time they require access A transparency indicator when one app is controlling another app using System & App Protection Override Apple stressed that app permissions previously granted by users will remain intact, adding that developers should be prepared to make changes to their onboarding workflows to ensure their apps can handle scenarios where access is granted to only a limited set of folders or apps via these APIs. In addition, apps that use Full Disk Access for disk backup or the new Accessibility settings for assistive technologies can request entitlements to offer the same experience for new installations that they offered before macOS 27.3. "Currently, known apps aren't affected and will keep the same experience without an entitlement," the tech giant added. "Additional entitlement details will be available soon." The development comes a little over a month after Apple began taking steps to tighten controls around a macOS setting called Full Disk Access (FDA) due to security risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

14tp7wt.text: An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation to plant malicious code in some of the scripts that customers' websites load from the service, Optimizely said early today. Visitors to sites run by at least 178 organizations, including CNN, the BBC and Zoom, received the code yesterday, according to Report URI, a firm that monitors the scripts websites run. The code was built to replace crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's own addresses and to capture card details, but the firm cannot see how many card numbers were exposed to the attacker. The vendor says it has fixed the flaw and removed the code. On iPhones and iPads, the code was also set up to load a second stage that the firm identifies as an iOS exploit kit, but it reports no iPhones actually being taken over. In an incident notice posted at 01:02 UTC, Optimizely said the attacker had "exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. The vendor has also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and added protections to stop unauthorized code from being delivered. The notice does not say how the flaw worked, how many projects were changed, when the fix went in, whether the attacker still has any access, or what customers should do. Smartsheet's script was cleaned once and then re-infected with a hidden version of the code, which indicates the attacker still had access at that point, according to the firm. Writing before the notice appeared, the firm said it did not know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: "That's for Optimizely to explain." Sites that use the service to run experiments on their pages load a script from the vendor, called a snippet. The snippet updates itself whenever the customer changes a setting, according to the vendor's snippet documentation. Each time it loads, it runs a field of custom code called Project JavaScript. The attacker wrote a loader into the Project JavaScript of customer projects and left the rest of each snippet untouched, Report URI said in its technical analysis. The snippets were still served from cdn.optimizely.com with the vendor's own certificate, so every page that loaded one also ran the loader. Some sites serve the snippet from their own domain, and those were affected too, because the content comes from the same project. The loader came in three versions. Most snippets loaded 1688360[.]cc/track.js directly, one version hid that address in base64 so a text search for the domain would miss it, and another carried a full copy of the payload that runs if the domain is blocked. Cynet, whose endpoint detection flagged browser connections to the attacker's server, traced the loader to a file served from cdn.optimizely.com in an endpoint investigation. Its researchers also captured the code on CNN and Zoom pages. A site that delivered the code has not necessarily had its own systems compromised, the researchers say. The firm checked 1,611 Optimizely snippets, mostly identified through its own crawl data, and found code in 188 of them, belonging to 178 organizations. It says the real number is likely higher because it could only check the snippets it found in time. Its post lists all 178, with their domains. Besides CNN, the BBC and Zoom, the infected snippets belonged to Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock, among others. The vendor's own main site and login page also carried the code. Some researchers call the campaign OPTIMJACK. The first injection was seen at 04:21 UTC yesterday, in the BBC's snippet. A mass cleanup began at about 20:40 UTC, and by 21:52 UTC only TalkTalk's snippet still carried the code. That first injection loaded webshell[.]lol, which the firm calls the same actor's injector. The injector had also been planted through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts since late last week, and it first appeared on Turkish sites on September 17. The payload, a file called track.js, replaces valid crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's in page text, forms, links, the clipboard and outgoing requests. It swaps only an address that passes its chain's checksum and sits near a payment word such as wallet, deposit or send, according to a payload analysis by StepSecurity. Copying is not safe either: an address a visitor copies from one of these pages may already be the attacker's by the time it is pasted into a wallet. A card skimmer, added at 13:43 UTC, captures the card number, expiry date, and CVV when they are submitted via the site's form fields and sends them to the attacker's server. It cannot read cards entered in a cross-origin payment iframe, such as Stripe's hosted fields or Adyen's. The code sends the visitor's cookies and a screenshot of the page to the attacker only after it swaps an address near wallet or payment wording. It cannot read cookies marked HttpOnly. The firm identifies the iOS exploit kits as Coruna and DarkSword, as documented by Google researchers. The Coruna exploit kit targets iOS 13.0 to 17.2.1, and the DarkSword exploit kit targets iOS 18.4 to 18.7. On iPhones and iPads, the code loads a script called boot.js from two .icu domains. That script reads the iOS version and opens an exploit chain in a hidden iframe: Coruna for iOS 13 to 17, DarkSword for iOS 18, and, for iOS 26, a separate chain that so far only collects details about the device. Between 17:13 and 17:57 UTC, the attacker also added a Coruna iframe to every visit from iOS 18.6 or earlier. Those pages reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, a sign a visitor could notice. The kit's own comments mark iOS 18.7.3 and later, and iOS 26.3 and later, as patched, according to the firm. Cynet's researchers retrieved the second stage using an emulated iPhone browser and describe what they saw as conditional delivery, "not a successful compromise of a physical iPhone or iPad." The firm says crypto has already been stolen. As of 19:25 UTC yesterday, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours. StepSecurity put the total across the same addresses at about $6,600. Two of the addresses were already in use before the injections began, and its analysts wrote that "the chain does not show which transfers came from victims." What Site Owners and Visitors Should Check Report URI recommends these checks for sites that use Optimizely Web Experimentation: Open the Project JavaScript in every project and the custom code in every experiment, and look for 1688360, atob( or any script you did not write. The atob( check finds the base64 version of the loader. Review which users, API tokens and integrations can write to your account, and rotate their credentials. If your own forms take card details, treat cards entered on Monday as possibly exposed. Treat session tokens or other secrets kept in cookies without the HttpOnly flag as exposed, and rotate them. Deploy a Content Security Policy with a strict script-src and connect-src. Allowing cdn.optimizely.com does not help, because the code came from that host, and strict-dynamic or unsafe-eval let the payload run on some sites. Consider telling your customers that your site served them the code. The firm kept a copy of every infected snippet, with hashes and timestamps, and could share them with affected organizations and CERTs (computer emergency response teams) on request. For anyone who visited an affected site on Monday, the firm advises: Update iPhones and iPads to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later. Compare any crypto payment made that day with the address you meant to pay. If the two differ, the address may have been swapped. If you paid by card on one of the sites, watch your card statements. A snippet that is clean now may still have served the code on Monday. StepSecurity also advises: Block the indicators below, and search logs back to 08:00 UTC on Monday. Fetch every snippet you serve, search it for 1688360, .icu and track.js, and record its Last-Modified header. Ask Optimizely which of your project IDs were changed, and when and how. Keep third-party tags off checkout pages, and take card details through the payment provider's own fields in a cross-origin iframe. Replace any card entered on an affected site on Monday, and check wallet addresses on a hardware wallet's screen rather than against copied text. Consider having iPhones and iPads on iOS 18.6 or earlier that visited affected sites checked for signs of compromise. Cynet treats cdn.optimizely.com as a legitimate delivery host rather than an indicator, and it advises against broad blocks of that host or of the affected news sites. The payload changed multiple times during the day, so a single file hash will not capture every version. These indicators come from the researchers' published lists: Domain: 1688360[.]cc, the payload host, with the paths /track.js, /card.php and /hit.php IP: 136.113.106[.]136, the address 1688360[.]cc pointed to Domain: 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu, iOS stage Domain: eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu, iOS stage Domain: webshell[.]lol, the injector loaded by the first injection, seen at 04:21 UTC on Monday SHA-256: f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40, final version of track.js SHA-256: 617df364120adc47fb4f55dcc0c69a9b6c9e108a92c60bc2b64a266254ab02f3, earliest captured version of track.js

5cl0ni.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 17, 2026Endpoint Security / Vulnerability ConnectWise on Monday said it completed its investigation into unauthorized access targeting partner ScreenConnect environments, and recommended customers to ensure that the technician client is running version 26.6.5 or later. The company said additional activity targeting on-premises environments continues to be reported where the identified third-party extensions remain enabled, and ScreenConnect has not been updated to the latest version. "On-premises partners must immediately disable the identified extensions and update ScreenConnect to the latest supported version," the company said. It's worth noting that version 26.6.5 addresses a critical-severity flaw in ScreenConnect client tracked as CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9) that could allow files to be transferred and executed through an active remote session without authorization or Host confirmation in certain circumstances. As highlighted by Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber last week, unknown threat actors are suspected to be exploiting an authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 to execute unauthorized commands while bypassing ScreenConnect's regular authentication controls. The attacks have been found to deploy a multi-component toolkit dubbed SCKit that's capable of spreading from infected customer devices to MSP technicians' computers and compromising additional managed networks by means of a C# module called RelayTrap ("RelayTrap.cs"). Specifically, the malware employs a worm-like technique that exploits CVE-2026-84869 to execute malicious code on a technician's workstation when they connect to an infected device to investigate a problem. There is no evidence this worm-like behavior has succeeded in the latest campaign. Huntress has since said it detected another spike in SCKit-related activity on November 13, 2026, impacting 205 hosts across 41 organizations. "Across the incidents, we saw the new ScreenConnect client being hosted at 185.241.211[.]197, which is associated with 1337 Services GmbH, a bulletproof hosting provider known for previously hosting malicious traffic," the company said. "In one of the incidents, we saw a rogue ScreenConnect client establish persistence via a service called Windows Update Agent, posing as a legitimate system component. The service executable (UpdateConnect.ClientService.exe) was placed in C:\ProgramData\Windows Update Agent (de362a425905bcc4)\ and configured to run under the LocalSystem account." In response to the incident, ConnectWise has taken the step of disabling five third-party extensions, including Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link, across 400 partner environments. That said, the presence of these extensions alone does not imply those environments were impacted. The company is also urging partners not to re-enable or reinstall the extensions until further guidance. "Disabling extensions and updating software do not remove unauthorized access or persistence already established on affected devices," it added.

13pms4a.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 17, 2026Vulnerability / Endpoint Security N-able has released a new security update to address additional critical security flaws impacting N-central. Describing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 as a critical security update, the company said it includes a number of security patches and fixes that enhance the security of the Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) and Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) platform. "HF3 builds on the protections delivered in HF2 and includes further improvements across authentication and access controls, Agent and Probe communications, file handling, server components, legacy APIs, and user management," the company said. The improvements relate to authentication and access control; Agent, Probe, and appliance security; file and import handling; server hardening; and user management controls. As part of the change, the configuration option for legacy APIs has been completely removed, permanently blocking them. As of writing, N-able notes that both Remote control functionality and Intune integration are blocked. Customers running on-premise N-central deployments should upgrade their servers as soon as possible to keep their environments protected. For Hosted N-central servers, no server-side action is required, as the updates are being automatically applied. "All customers, hosted and on-premise, must upgrade all of their Agents and Probes to the latest version to be fully protected," N-able cautioned. "Agents and Probes that are not upgraded are susceptible to impersonation." The complete list of vulnerabilities addressed in the update is listed below - CVE-2026-129271 - N-central Patch Management Local Privilege Escalation CVE-2026-129272 - MMS3 appliance authentication bypass via predictable passcode CVE-2026-129273 - Audit Export syslog injection allows root command execution CVE-2026-129274 - ServerMMS2 task result submission missing authentication CVE-2026-129275 - repositoryItemGet missing authentication discloses policies CVE-2026-129276 - ServerMMS2 asset data submission missing authentication CVE-2026-129277 - ServerMMS maintenance action read missing authentication CVE-2026-129278 - Take Control audit log tampering without authentication CVE-2026-129279 - Password reset response discrepancy allows user enumeration CVE-2026-129280 - ServerUI SOAP operations missing authorisation checks CVE-2026-129281 - View-only users can set DeviceExecute configuration CVE-2026-129282 - Test email sendmail argument injection, missing authorisation CVE-2026-129283 - N-central custom service import XML external entity injection CVE-2026-129284 - Report Manager and Data Export settings SSRF CVE-2026-129285 - XMPP action response origin validation error CVE-2026-129286 - SIS GenericFiles version path traversal leads to RCE CVE-2026-129287 - SIS repository parser XML external entity injection The development comes days after N-able began restricting certain N-central features and integrations following the disclosure of a new set of flaws tracked as 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell. The shortcomings can allow attackers to run arbitrary code as root and gain SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems under specific conditions. Successful exploitation of 4EverAble2Shell hinges on the legacy API mode being enabled. Because the legacy API has been removed from the latest N-central version, it plugs the attack vector. The 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities have since come under active exploitation, with attackers leveraging them to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. Independent security researcher Sean Bales, who disclosed the flaws, has published additional details for 24 CVEs, stating "these are patched vulnerabilities and should not work on the latest patch."

ppq7u.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 16, 2026Agentic AI / Cyber Attacks Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity. In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September. The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The tech giant said the adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber attacks take place at machine speed, allowing the operations to be scaled significantly by chaining together varied attack paths even if the underlying mechanics remain the same. A number of threat actors have been observed experimenting with these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated and suspected espionage actors aligned with China. "These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation," Google said. Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines, allowing threat actors to collapse the window between patch disclosure and active exploitation. "Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws," Google added. Simultaneously, threat actors are also targeting AI infrastructure to illicit profit from LLMjacking attacks by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments, and then reselling the access through underground proxy services like APIMart and JetNight at discounted prices, otherwise known as LLM mixers. The findings show that the emergence of open-source frameworks have further lowered the barrier to entry, enabling bad actors to easily integrate new exploits, autonomously scale attacks, and mount convincing phishing campaigns, further compressing attack timelines. This includes a Chinese-language phishing platform called Jieyou that has integrated an LLM chatbot assistant to allow customers to configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands without necessarily having the technical expertise to do so. "The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier," Google said. "Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly."

haxdtm.text: A default password opened doors it never should have. A trusted update delivered malware. Even a security feature became a way to break in. Different stories, same problem: the things meant to protect us aren't always doing their job. Meanwhile, AI is making bug hunting faster, old flaws are still paying off, and attackers keep finding easy ways in. Some attacks take real skill. Others barely need any. This week's stories show both sides. Here's what happened. ⚡ Threat of the Week N-able 0-Days Exploited for Dropping Crypto Miners — A new set of vulnerabilities tracked as 4EverAble2Shell has come under active exploitation, with attackers exploiting it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. According to Huntback, the activity has successfully compromised 21 N-central servers across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden. Patches for the flaw are expected to be released N-able today. 🔔 Top News Compromised bee-js and Swarm Desktop Steal Swarm Wallet Keys — Threat actors compromised @ethersphere/bee-js, the JavaScript client for the Swarm storage network, with a new postinstall hook in version 13.3.0 that downloads a second stage responsible for stealing the Swarm node's wallet key and installing a backdoor. "On Linux and macOS, the backdoor is a Go remote shell," SafeDep said. "On Windows, it is a hidden ScreenConnect client that runs as SYSTEM." The same malicious code was subsequently distributed via Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 on GitHub. The activity has since been linked to a campaign called SleepyDuck (EtherDuck), which is known to spread malicious Solidity extensions through Open VSX. "The attacker controlled two Ethersphere GitHub accounts. GitHub activity logs attribute 13 pushes on November 6 to long-time maintainer nugaon," SafeDep added. "That day the attacker injected GitHub Actions workflows to steal CI credentials, and the attempts failed. Two days later, the attacker used the release bot bee-worker to publish the malicious releases. How the attacker got into either account remains unknown." Nightmare Eclipse New SignDrop 0-Day — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) released a new Windows zero-day exploit that can let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges. Called SignDrop, it has been described as a Windows Common Log FileSystem (CLFS) authentication zero-day local privilege escalation flaw. "The vulnerability turns a defense into an attack surface," Cyderes said. "Microsoft added HMAC-based authentication codes to CLFS log files specifically to block the class of logic bugs caused by improper validation of CLFS data structures, which accounted for 19 of 24 CLFS CVEs over five years. SignDrop abuses the signing mechanism itself: it forces clfs.sys to create a .cnpf signature file as SYSTEM in an attacker-controlled location, producing a privileged file-creation primitive at an attacker-selected path. Because the resulting file retains attacker-accessible security attributes, the exploit reopens it and replaces the CLFS-generated content with an embedded payload DLL." Microsoft said it's investigating the reported vulnerability. In late September, the researcher also released an exploit for BigDiskBuster, a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw impacting Microsoft Defender that's similar to UnDefend and prevents the application from performing platform/signature updates. Default Admin Password Lets Researchers Unlock and Start Cars — New research found that it's possible to take over customer accounts at two major automakers, and use them to remotely unlock and start a test car, flash headlights, and sound horns after finding an administration console on the brands' login servers still protected by its default password. Both apps signed customers in through ForgeRock, an identity platform now part of Ping Identity. The carmakers remediated the flaw approximately two hours after responsible disclosure. Google Patches Actively Exploited Chrome 0-Day — Google released updates to patch a high-severity vulnerability in Chrome has come under active exploitation in the wild. The flaw, tracked as CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: 8.8), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component. The issue has been addressed in 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Apple macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. Google did not disclose how the vulnerability is being exploited and in what context. Meta Fined by Italy Over Accessing Android Users' Photos with Facebook App — The Italian Data Protection Authority (IDPA) hit Meta with one of its highest fines to date. According to the Italian data regulatory body, Meta has been fined €805 million for failing to disclose that it had access to user photos, videos, and metadata for those using the Facebook app on Android devices. Meta had access to Android users' ​photos and videos through a Facebook app feature that ​suggested content from users' personal galleries that they ⁠could post. The feature has been available since 2023. Meta has 60 ​days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent ​separately. The company said it would appeal the decision. "This is a simple feature ​that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook," Meta told Reuters. ​"Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and ‌they ⁠can change that permission at any time in their settings." ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild. Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-121685, CVE-2026-121686, CVE-2026-121687, CVE-2026-121688, CVE-2026-121689, CVE-2026-121690 (FrodoBots EarthRover Mini+ firmware), CVE-2026-124916 (PrestaShop), CVE-2026-76964, CVE-2026-89126 (aka ICM2SHELL), CVE-2026-89103 (aka PROXYGATE), CVE-2026-120017 (SAP), CVE-2026-98432, CVE-2026-111497, CVE-2026-114406 The flaws, identified by Midnight Blue within the span of an hour, allow full device take-over, persistent access (possibly after reset), and persistent denial-of-service, rendering the device inoperable. Additional technical details are currently withheld. "Through remote code execution, an unauthenticated attacker can remotely run arbitrary code at the operating system level of the AK-SM800A controller," Midnight Blue said. "Due to the lack of secure boot, an attacker with RCE could push malicious firmware that simply renders the device inoperable and irrecoverable without specialized hardware intervention (e.g. by wiping flash memory and/or causing an infinite boot loop). Such a 'bricking' or wiper approach would require full device replacement." The findings unfold against the backdrop of two waves of cyber attacks targeting internet-exposed fridge controllers by Danfoss and Copeland across Europe. Cruciferra has been revealed as a rebrand of the long-running KGB cryptor. It has been sold to cybercriminals since October 2025. ESET said it has prevented over 700,000 compromise attempts from Cruciferra since January 2026, most of them targeting Türkiye, Greece, and Spain. It has been used to deliver payloads like Formbook and PureLogs. "In mid-October the cryptor's domain was seized, and the service went dark," ESET said. "Days later, the same operator resurfaced with a new offering – exclusive $5K-per-build cryptors, pitched against enterprise EDRs and advertised with a claimed bundled kernel 0-day. Seized infrastructure ≠ a dead service." Using AI models on a limited budget and running it against 10 popular TCP/IP stacks has led to the discovery of 99 vulnerabilities in 90 hours. Of these, 66 are new vulnerabilities, 52% of them critical or high severity. This also includes seven vulnerabilities specific to the firmware of a discontinued wireless access point, such as buffer overflow via firmware upload and hard-coded administrator credentials that cannot be changed for web and shell management. "AI cut the analysis time from 9 months to 90 hours and the research cost by 100x when compared to our previous analysis," Forescout said. "It rediscovered 40% of the vulnerabilities we had previously disclosed on those stacks. Total static analysis cost was $935, an average of $2.58 per finding." Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a "90 + 30" vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to address a vulnerability, plus an extra 30 days "soak time" for patch rollout. That's changing now with the emergence of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation. Going forward, Google Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities 90 days after they are reported to the vendor, regardless of whether they are fixed. The deadline drops to 60 days on February 2, 2027, and to 30 days on January 3, 2028. ClickFix-style lures are being used to deliver a macOS-focused, modular information stealer called Phexia. The malware is also capable of deploying an XMRig miner. "The most recent and notable change in Phexia occurred in May 2026, when the threat actor started testing smart contracts on the Polygon blockchain as a command-and-control (C2) dead-drop resolver (DDR)," WithSecure said. "The abuse of smart contracts by threat actors as part of their attack chain is generally known as EtherHiding. The malware previously relied on hardcoded C2 domains as well as Telegram channels and Steam profiles as its C2 DDR. The threat actor was observed actively weaponizing the Polygon smart contracts since late May to early June 2026." The threat actors behind WeedHack have been linked to another cybercriminal operation called Marsalek that expands beyond using Minecraft lures to disguise malicious software as popular gaming tools, cheats, and utilities for games including Roblox, Fortnite, and Counter-Strike 2. "Active from approximately December 2025 through May 2026, Marsalek offered free access to sophisticated information-stealing malware through a publicly accessible platform, complete with a dashboard that allowed users to create malicious files, track victims, and access stolen information," McAfee Labs said. The cybersecurity company identified more than 1,560 registered accounts, over 400 malicious files, and more than 29 distribution URLs associated with the campaign. Marsalek also deploys a second information stealer called PureLog to steal sensitive data and exfiltrate it to another server. "This means that while someone using Marsalek may believe they're collecting stolen passwords and other personal information for themselves, the malware operator could also gain access to that information without their knowledge," McAfee Labs. This tactic is called double theft or a dual-hook infection. New findings from SOCRadar show that ransomware operators have started handing the attack to AI agents, leading to the rise of agentic ransomware attacks. "Agentic ransomware is ransomware where AI agents do the hands-on work: choosing techniques, running tools and writing code, within limits a human sets," SOCRadar said. "In less than a year, AI agents moved from building access for ransomware brands to running live encryption and extortion campaigns." An active campaign discovered in early October 2026 is targeting internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server instances and using Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands to deliver malware such as XMRig miner and Gh0st RAT. The attacks employ predefined username and password lists to brute-force into the servers and exploit their administrative capabilities to execute commands on the underlying Windows systems. "The malware scans IP ranges for exposed SQL Servers and attempts to log in using supplied credentials," Fortinet said. "After a successful login, it remotely executes malicious T-SQL commands on the compromised server to download and run additional malware." It's not known how many servers were compromised or who was behind the campaign. A Europol operation, in collaboration with law enforcement agencies from 14 countries across the globe, has successfully identified vendors and buyers from major dark marketplaces as part of Operation TorNado, a coordinated international effort targeting cybercrime, drug trafficking, and firearms offenses. "The operation, which spanned from May 2025 to October 2026, resulted in 354 arrests and hundreds of house searches worldwide," Europol said. "This effort included a follow-up action focused on the identification of suspects after the takedown of five major dark marketplaces: Archetyp, Bohemia, Nemesis, Kingdom, [and] Tor2Door." The U.S. led with 132 arrests, followed by the U.K. (59). Authorities also seized more than 5.7 metric tonnes of illicit drugs, 209 firearms, and over $234 million in both cash and virtual currencies. Threat actors have been observed using a "convincing device-code phishing attack" that involves a Microsoft Teams calendar invite booking flow to target a company in the construction sector. The attack was observed in mid-October 2026. "While many device code phishing lures leverage a generic Microsoft sign-in form, this attack crafted an email with a believable social engineering lure that impersonated a legitimate senior vice president of another company in the construction sector, complete with a typosquatted email domain," Huntress said. "A link in the message to the victim began a 'Microsoft Teams Meeting Scheduler' booking flow, which included prompts to pick a duration of the call, as well as a date and a time. On the backend, these prompts kicked off the Microsoft device code sign-in process and returned a user code, and when the target clicked the 'Confirm Meeting' prompt on the lure page, they were unknowingly copying the code to their clipboard. Then a pop-up prompt opened to Microsoft's real device sign-in page, asking the target to submit the code, which completed the device-code phishing attempt." Threat actors are probing two of 14 vulnerabilities newly disclosed in XWEB EVO, the Dixell refrigeration supervisor now sold under the Copeland name. According to VulnCheck, the flaws in question are CVE-2026-124014 (an unauthenticated write of the system configuration file via config.lua) and CVE-2026-124010 (an unauthenticated root command execution flaw). 1ur43wb.text: Six flaws in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers could let a remote attacker take over a controller without logging in, Dutch security consultancy Midnight Blue said earlier this week. No patch is available, and the researchers say the newest firmware, version 5.4.0, does not fix the flaws. Government cybersecurity agencies in Belgium, Ireland and Germany told operators this week to take the controllers' management interfaces off the internet. For a controller left on the internet, updating the firmware, changing default passwords or turning on Strict mode is not enough on its own, the Belgian and Irish agencies said. Strict mode is a login protection that requires encrypted connections and session tokens, but one of the six flaws is in the gateway that enforces it. The AK-SM800A runs a store's fridges and freezers, and maintenance firms can manage it remotely. Such controllers were targeted in attacks in France starting October 11, and in a second wave across Europe that began last week. The attacks caused unwanted defrost cycles and destroyed stock. Germany's federal IT security agency, the BSI, says in a security notice that the AK-SM800A was involved in earlier incidents in which refrigeration units in several countries were tampered with. The agency has no information about any exploitation of the six new flaws, and neither other agencies nor researchers link the flaws to those incidents. The researchers examined firmware version 5.3.2, then the newest, and say every version up to and including it is affected. No CVE identifiers have been assigned. The researchers are keeping technical details private while they work on disclosure with Danfoss, the Danish company that makes the controllers. The vendor lists software package 5.4.0, dated November, as its newest release for the AK-SM800A. Its 5.4.0 readme and November update guide cover upgrade steps, and the guide adds a stricter password rule. Neither mentions a fix for any vulnerability. In a follow-up statement carried by trade publication Cooling Post, the researchers said 5.4.0 does not patch the flaws: "It's not really possible either because according to the file timestamp this firmware was likely built on October 29, before the second wave of cyber attacks and well before our vulnerability reports." The German agency first said in a press release this week that 5.4.0 was not affected. Later the same day, it changed that in a corrected statement: it cannot rule out for now that 5.4.0 is affected. The vendor's advisory page lists no advisory for the six flaws as of today, and no date for a fix has been published. Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer found the six flaws in less than an hour of manual review, using firmware the vendor offers for download, and described them in a technical write-up. Five of the flaws are in web request handlers that do not require a login, inside a program that runs as root. Through one of them, the researchers ran code as root on older firmware, version 3.3.0, and they found the same bugs in 5.3.2. Strict mode closes almost all of the controller's web attack surface to users who have not logged in, including the flaw used in that demonstration. The sixth flaw is in the gateway that enforces Strict mode, a separate program that blocks every request except the login until a user has logged in. When the researchers ran firmware 5.3.2 in an emulator with Strict mode on, that flaw crashed the gateway. The crash could be turned into code execution with more work, the researchers say, and the gateway lacks basic exploit defenses such as stack canaries. With code running as root, an attacker could change the controller's settings, start defrost cycles and hide that activity from its logs. The controllers do not use secure boot, the researchers found, so an attacker could plant code that survives a factory reset and a firmware update. An attacker could also make a controller unusable until it is replaced. The researchers say the code almost certainly holds more flaws like these, and they call patching flaws one by one or turning on Strict mode "a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources." What Operators Can Do Removing internet exposure must not wait for a patch, and it is needed even where firmware is current and Strict mode is on, the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium says. The Belgian advisory and a similar Irish advisory recommend these steps: Find every controller whose management interface can be reached from the internet, including through a 4G or 5G modem, and remove that exposure. Give remote access only through a secure VPN or a protected internal network. Allowing only a service company's IP addresses through a firewall is a short-term measure. Check temperature setpoints, defrost schedules, alarm settings, user accounts and remote-access settings for changes you did not make. The German agency adds that anyone who suspects a compromise should change all credentials and check that equipment connected to the controller works properly. Before cutting off the data a controller sends to its refrigeration service company, operators should check contract and insurance terms, the Belgian advisory says. They should also set up protected remote access so that monitoring can continue. Danfoss's own update guide says the AK-SM800A should not be directly reachable from the public internet, adding: “This recommendation applies to all software versions, including those with Strict Mode enabled.” Ireland's National Cyber Security Centre also advises running the latest supported firmware, changing default passwords and turning on Strict mode, but says operators should not rely on those steps alone. Danfoss told Cooling Post on October 12 that most units hit in France were either older models that no longer receive updates or current AK-SM800A units running outdated firmware. The vendor fixed earlier flaws in the AK-SM800A in 2023 and 2025, including login bypass and command injection bugs. Version 5.3.2, which the researchers examined, is newer than all of those fixes.

gqzna8.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 16, 2026Threat Intelligence / Endpoint Security Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new variant of CoffeeLoader, a malware designed to deliver additional payloads to infected machines. "On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named '7z.dll' into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe," Kaspersky said in an analysis published today. "The '7z.dll' file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer." CoffeeLoader was first documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz in March 2025, detailing its use of the Armoury packer to resist analysis and ultimately run Rhadamanthys shellcode. The malware is assessed to share source code similarities with another loader family tracked as SmokeLoader. Malware packed with Armory uses file names like "ArmouryAIOSDK.dll" and "ArmouryA.dll," with the packer hijacking some of the original Armoury Crate functionality with self-decrypting shellcode. Notably, the shellcode extracts code that executes a decryption routine on a system's GPU by making use of the OpenCL library. The end goal is to install CoffeeLoader, establish persistence, and execute it by injecting it into a newly created "dllhost.exe" process. The latest version of the packer continues to use the GPU, but replaces OpenCL with the OpenGL library. In addition, the new version of the packer delivers intermediate shellcode instead of a DLL. This shellcode serves as a downloader responsible for fetching the main CoffeeLoader malware. "To establish persistence, the Trojan copies '7z.dll' to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%," Kaspersky said. "The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information." "To protect itself, the downloader creates a registry key that prevents the user from disabling autorun through Task Manager." Once persistence is successful, the malware launches one of the legitimate processes (e.g., "dllhost.exe," "WerFault.exe," "svchost.exe," "OpenWith.exe," or "AtBroker.exe") and then injects itself into it, after which the malware shellcode is downloaded from a hard-coded command-and-control (C2) server. The shellcode then decrypts and runs the CoffeeLoader payload. It supports the same three commands to run the next-stage malware from the C2 server - Injecting it into a process Saving it to disk as an executable and then running it Saving it as a DLL and then running it via "rundll32.exe" As for how CoffeeLoader is distributed, it takes place via Retadup, a Windows computer worm that was disrupted by French law enforcement authorities in August 2019. The malware, which spreads via infected USB drives, has been used to drop additional payloads like cryptocurrency miners, the Stop ransomware, and the Arkei password stealer. "Two years ago, someone began re-registering the domain names that Retadup had used as C2 servers and using them to issue commands to download third-party malware," Kaspersky said. "At first, this was the SmokeLoader downloader packed using the 32-bit version of Armoury, but in early 2025, the same servers started serving CoffeeLoader." It remains unclear whether the worm's author or some other threat actor was instrumental in bringing the C2 servers back online. Kaspersky said it blocked around 15,000 systems from being infected with the resurrected version of the worm, most of them located in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

13sbva5.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 16, 2026United States A financially motivated threat activity cluster tracked as REF3364 has been attributed to a Linux-focused cryptocurrency mining operation that tampers with the readings used to detect high GPU workloads. Central to the intrusion is a toolkit called SANSAR, a Rust-based orchestrator that receives commands over the TOR anonymity network to manage CPU and GPU miners. The activity was observed in late October 2026. "The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns," Elastic Security Labs said in a report published last week. "This backdoor retrieves its C2 [command-and-control] address from an Ethereum smart contract before connecting to the server directly." In the attack chain documented by the company, initial access is said to have been achieved via an exposed Ray job agent, allowing the threat actor to execute commands. This includes jobs running the NVIDIA System Management Interface (nvidia-smi) to capture and exfiltrate the GPU inventory to an external server. Subsequently, the attacker submitted a Python reverse shell job that connected to a remote listener, after which an SSH key was added to that account's authorized_keys file to establish persistent access. "After obtaining root, the actor staged the toolkit under /opt/vadi_, built the acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support (DKMS) and added an initramfs loader," security researcher Salim Bitam said. "An initramfs is a temporary root file system loaded into RAM during early boot, before Linux switches to its normal root filesystem. The module and loader are stored in the boot image on disk, so the rootkit can load again when the host boots with that image." The installation also delivers a modified NVML wrapper that filters process information and changes GPU telemetry to evade detection. Specifically, the altered wrapper hooks NVML calls used by monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi to report GPU utilization as 0%. In addition, temperature and power readings are substituted with random values between 36 to 46 degree Celsius (96.8 to 114.8 degree Fahrenheit) and 100 to 200 watts.
